Kirby has cited influences ranging from Leonard Cohen to contemporary indie-folk songwriters.

beck|dear life.fact: "Dear Life" opens Beck's 2017 album Colors, produced by Beck alongside Greg Kurstin. The track is built around a jaunty, jazz-tinged piano riff before opening up into rock guitar and vocal harmonies. It was released as an instant-download single when the album was announced, with an accompanying lyric video mixing live-action footage and psychedelic animation.

kilo kish|death fantasy (ft. miguel).fact: "Death Fantasy" is the third track on Kilo Kish's 2022 album American Gurl, featuring a guest vocal from Miguel and a music video directed by Dave Laven. The New York Times described its mood as more of a trance-like spell than a straightforward hook. The collaboration went well enough that Kilo Kish and Miguel teamed up again in 2025 for the song "Negotiate."

yo la tengo|did i tell you.fact: "Did I Tell You" first appeared on Yo La Tengo's 1987 album New Wave Hot Dogs, then was re-recorded as a hushed, late-night ballad for their 1990 covers-and-rarities album Fakebook. On the Fakebook version, Ira Kaplan's conversational lead vocal is paired with Georgia Hubley's airy backing harmonies, giving the song an intimate, heart-to-heart feel.

the beta band|dry the rain.fact: "Dry the Rain" opened The Beta Band's 1997 debut EP Champion Versions and later appeared on the compilation The Three EPs. Bassist Richard Greentree said the song was written to bridge folk music and hip-hop, and it builds from a simple acoustic opening into a brass-heavy, gospel-tinged finale featuring trumpet from Jonathan Levien. The track became the band's best-known song after a memorable cameo in the 2000 film High Fidelity.

mazzy star|flowers in december.fact: "Flowers in December" was the lead single from Mazzy Star's 1996 album Among My Swan, written by Hope Sandoval and David Roback and produced by Roback. It became the band's only UK Top 40 single, reaching No. 40, and its music video was directed by Kevin Kerslake.

youth lagoon|football.fact: "Football" is a 2024 single from Trevor Powers' project Youth Lagoon, reuniting him with producer Rodaidh McDonald. Powers has said the song uses sports as a metaphor, inspired by how throwing a ball was one of the few things he and his father connected over growing up, regardless of skill.

friendship|free association.fact: "Free Association" is the lead single from Friendship's album Caveman Wakes Up on Merge Records, with a video the band shot on Super 8 film on a closed boardwalk in Seaside Heights, New Jersey. Singer Dan Wriggins said he was inspired by folk singer Kath Bloom, and even borrowed the line "born with a weak heart" from David Byrne; the band also said the Mellotron sax and voice sounds on the track started as studio jokes they ended up keeping.

devo|gates of steel.fact: "Gates of Steel" began as an instrumental demo Mark Mothersbaugh recorded with Debbie Smith and Sue Schmidt of the band Chi-Pig, before Gerald Casale added lyrics he'd written separately. It was released as a single on October 6, 1980 from DEVO's album Freedom of Choice.

snocaps|heathcliff.fact: Snocaps is a band formed by twin sisters Allison Crutchfield (of Swearin') and Katie Crutchfield (Waxahatchee), along with MJ Lenderman and Brad Cook. "Heathcliff," the second track on their 2025 self-titled debut, was written and sung by Allison; the album was produced and almost entirely engineered by Cook, with all four musicians switching between instruments.

tame impala|i don't really mind.fact: "I Don't Really Mind" closes out Tame Impala's 2010 debut album InnerSpeaker, giving the record what's been called an "intergalactic bubblegum" finish. Kevin Parker recorded and produced the album himself in a mansion overlooking the Indian Ocean, and it was later mixed by Dave Fridmann, known for his work with MGMT and The Flaming Lips.

the xx|intro.fact: "Intro," the instrumental opening track of The xx's 2009 debut album xx, was composed by the band and produced by Jamie xx. It went on to soundtrack numerous TV commercials, served as the BBC's theme for the UK's 2010 general election coverage, and was later sampled by Rihanna on her 2011 album Talk That Talk.

the beths|jump rope gazers.fact: "Jump Rope Gazers" is the title track of The Beths' 2020 sophomore album. Singer Liz Stokes has described the title as an image of two people holding either end of a jump rope — connected, yet kept apart by the distance between them, which mirrors the song's theme of the push and pull in a relationship. The band performed it, complete with a clarinet solo, for NPR's Tiny Desk concert series.

the feelies|let's go.fact: "Let's Go" is track six on The Feelies' 1986 album The Good Earth, released on Coyote Records. The album was co-produced by R.E.M.'s Peter Buck, who had been a Feelies fan going back to his days working as a record store clerk.

superchunk|like a fool.fact: "Like a Fool" opens Superchunk's 1994 album Foolish, their first full-length for Merge Records, recorded at a breakneck pace at Pachyderm Studio with producer Brian Paulson. The band deliberately put it first because its clean, written-on-acoustic-guitar sound was a surprising change of pace from the crunchy power chords fans expected from them.

day wave|linger.fact: Day Wave, the project of Jackson Phillips, recorded a stripped-down cover of The Cranberries' "Linger" using just two guitars and a couple of voices. It appeared on the deluxe edition of his 2022 album Pastlife, closing the record out.

radiohead|lucky.fact: Radiohead recorded "Lucky" in just five hours on September 4, 1995, at producer Brian Eno's invitation, for The Help Album, a charity compilation benefiting War Child's work with children affected by the Bosnian war. The band considered it some of their best work at the time, and it was later included on their 1997 album OK Computer.

toro y moi|mirage.fact: "Mirage" opens Toro y Moi's fifth album Boo Boo (2017, Carpark Records). Chaz Bear has said he wrote the record as a form of personal therapy during a period of feeling self-conscious about fame after years of touring, drawing on influences like Travis Scott, Daft Punk, Frank Ocean, and Oneohtrix Point Never.

fleet foxes|montezuma.fact: "Montezuma" opens Fleet Foxes' 2011 album Helplessness Blues. The band dressed up the minimal, elegiac arrangement with unusual instrumentation for an indie-folk record, including zithers, tamburas, Tibetan singing bowls, and a Moog synthesizer.

waxahatchee|much ado about nothing.fact: "Much Ado About Nothing" is a Waxahatchee single Katie Crutchfield released in October 2024, in the same twangy folk-rock vein as her album Tigers Blood. It features MJ Lenderman on electric guitar along with Brad and Phil Cook, and later got a dedicated 7-inch release for Record Store Day 2025, backed with two more new recordings, "Mud" and "Next To Me."

the microphones|my roots are strong and.fact: "My Roots Are Strong and Deep" is track B2 on The Microphones' 2001 album The Glow Pt. 2, the project's third studio release. The song has a hymn-like quality, built around a clanging, unsteady piano sound and washes of distorted toy piano.

unknown mortal orchestra|necessary evil.fact: "Necessary Evil" is track 8 on Unknown Mortal Orchestra's 2015 album Multi-Love, and its warm brass chorus was played by frontman Ruban Nielson's father, jazz musician Chris Nielson. The two have continued performing the song together since, including as part of a family trio (with Ruban's brother Kody on drums) at UMO's 2023 NPR Tiny Desk Concert.

the jesus and mary chain|never understan.fact: "Never Understand" was the debut single from The Jesus and Mary Chain, later included on their 1985 album Psychocandy. A demo tape of the song (along with "Upside Down") made its way to Primal Scream's Bobby Gillespie, who passed it to Alan McGee of Creation Records — leading McGee to become the band's manager and launch their career.

sharon van etten|one day.fact: "One Day" is the lead single from Sharon Van Etten's 2010 album Epic. The record's hazy, warm guitar sound carries an obvious Fleetwood Mac Rumours influence, and Van Etten even dedicated the album sleeve to the band, writing: "Dedicated to Fleetwood Mac. You changed my world."

yo la tengo|our way to fall.fact: "Our Way to Fall" appears on Yo La Tengo's 2000 album And Then Nothing Turned Itself Inside-Out, built around gently brushed drums, luminous organ, and Ira Kaplan's hushed vocal. The song later soundtracked a scene in the HBO series Six Feet Under, in the season 2 episode "Driving Mr. Mossback."

hot chip|over and over.fact: "Over and Over" was Hot Chip's breakthrough single, from their 2006 album The Warning. Joe Goddard built the track while trying to recreate the bassline from ESG's "Dance," and Alexis Taylor's lyrics riff on the band's love of hypnotic, repetitive music like Terry Riley's "A Rainbow in Curved Air" — NME later named it the best single of 2006.

joanna newsom|peach, plum, pear.fact: "Peach, Plum, Pear" comes from Joanna Newsom's 2004 debut album The Milk-Eyed Mender and is driven entirely by a harpsichord rather than her signature harp. The song has since been covered by Owen Pallett (performing as Final Fantasy) on his 2006 EP Young Canadian Mothers, as well as by the band Straylight Run.

wilco|quiet amplifier.fact: "Quiet Amplifier" is widely seen as the centerpiece of Wilco's 2019 album Ode to Joy, pairing unusually heavy, march-like percussion with a warm cloud of guitars and cymbal shimmer. Jeff Tweedy's lyrics turn the song toward a hopeful close, singing "Shy little stars will shine."

bon iver|rabi.fact: "RABi" closes Bon Iver's 2019 album i,i, built from an interplay of horns, synths, and layered group vocals. The album itself was rolled out unusually, with tracks released one by one, hour by hour, the day before its official August 9, 2019 release, and features guest contributions from James Blake, Aaron Dessner, Bruce Hornsby, Moses Sumney, and Channy Leaneagh.

future islands|ran.fact: "Ran" was the lead single from Future Islands' 2017 album The Far Field, produced by John Congleton. Its music video, directed by Albert Berney, takes the title literally — following frontman Samuel T. Herring on a run that starts in a Baltimore suburb in daylight and ends in the Maryland countryside after dark.

beth gibbons|reaching out.fact: "Reaching Out" is a single from Beth Gibbons' debut solo album, Lives Outgrown, released in 2024 via Domino Recording Company — her first-ever solo full-length after decades fronting Portishead. The album, produced by Gibbons, James Ford, and Lee Harris, took roughly ten years to record, and the song's video was an interactive piece made with visual artist Weirdcore.

mx lonely|return to sender.fact: "Return to Sender" is a single from Brooklyn alt-rock band MX LONELY, released in January 2026 ahead of their debut album All Monsters, out via Julia's War Recordings. The band is made up of vocalist Rae Haas, guitarist Jake Harms, and bassist Gabriel Garman, and the track features driving rhythms and distorted guitars typical of their sound.

black flag|rise above.fact: "Rise Above" opens Black Flag's 1981 debut album Damaged and became one of hardcore punk's defining anthems about refusing to be controlled by outside pressure. It's also tied to the band's lineup history: singer Henry Rollins joined Black Flag after being pulled onstage to sing at an impromptu New York show, impressing the band enough that they asked him to become their permanent vocalist.

islands|rough gem.fact: "Rough Gem" comes from Islands' 2006 debut album Return to the Sea. Islands was formed by Nicholas Thorburn and Jamie Thompson right after their previous band, The Unicorns, broke up in 2004, and the record — released on Rough Trade in Europe and Equator in North America — blended orchestral pop with playful horn-and-whistle hooks.

chromatics|running up that hill.fact: Chromatics recorded a synth-heavy cover of Kate Bush's 1985 classic "Running Up That Hill" for their 2007 album Night Drive. The cover later reached a much wider audience after being featured in Nicolas Winding Refn's 2011 film Drive, helping cement Chromatics' reputation in the synthwave/neo-'80s revival scene.

devo|s.i.b. (swelling itching brain).fact: "S.I.B. (Swelling Itching Brain)" is track seven on DEVO's 1979 sophomore album Duty Now for the Future. It's one of several songs on the record where the band leaned further into blending synthesizers with guitar, a sonic shift that helped pave the way toward their more keyboard-driven, new-wave sound of the early 1980s.

alvvays|saved by a waif.fact: "Saved by a Waif" is track nine on Alvvays' 2017 album Antisocialites, written by Molly Rankin and Alec O'Hanley. The record was recorded across three studios — Kingsize Soundlabs in Los Angeles, Tarbox Road Studios in upstate New York, and Union Sound Studios in Toronto — with O'Hanley and John Congleton producing.

turnstile|seein' stars.fact: "SEEIN' STARS," from Turnstile's 2025 album Never Enough, is a softer, disco-tinged departure for the hardcore band, featuring guest vocals from Blood Orange's Dev Hynes and Paramore's Hayley Williams. Critics noted its guitar riff echoes The Police's "When the World Is Running Down, You Make the Best of What's Still Around."

the jesus and mary chain|sometimes alway.fact: "Sometimes Always" is a 1994 duet by The Jesus and Mary Chain's Jim Reid with Mazzy Star singer Hope Sandoval, released as the lead single from the album Stoned & Dethroned. In the song the two trade verses playing an ex-couple weighing whether to get back together, and it became a minor UK hit.

guided by voices|space gun.fact: "Space Gun" is the title track and opener of Guided by Voices' 26th studio album, released in 2018. The song famously kicks off with a found-sound recording of an airport restroom paper towel dispenser before launching into Robert Pollard's trademark power-pop guitar charge.

pulp|spike island.fact: "Spike Island," released in 2025 as Pulp's first new song in over a decade, is named after The Stone Roses' legendary 1990 outdoor concert in Widnes, Cheshire, that drew nearly 30,000 fans. Jarvis Cocker said he wasn't actually there, but wrote about the event's lasting cultural ripple through British music — and about a DJ who kept shouting "Spike Island, come alive!" over the PA.

hum|stars.fact: "Stars" was the second single from Hum's 1995 album You'd Prefer an Astronaut, peaking at No. 11 on the Modern Rock Tracks chart and helping the album sell over 250,000 copies. The song's video and track also got an unexpected pop-culture boost from an appearance on MTV's Beavis and Butt-Head.

the white stripes|the big three killed m.fact: "The Big Three Killed My Baby," from The White Stripes' self-titled 1999 debut album, takes aim at Detroit's "Big Three" automakers — Ford, GM, and Chrysler — criticizing the industry's practice of planned obsolescence and its resistance to innovations like electric engines. Jack White wrote the track, which was also released as a 7-inch single.

belle and sebastian|the blues are still.fact: "The Blues Are Still Blue" was the second single from Belle and Sebastian's 2006 album The Life Pursuit, produced by Tony Hoffer. It's an unusually straightforward, rollicking rock song for the famously twee Scottish band, and despite its energy the lyrics are, as critics have noted, nominally about something as mundane as doing laundry.

cheekface|the fringe.fact: "The Fringe" opens Cheekface's 2022 album It's Sorted with the band's signature deadpan, sing-speak style. The lyrics playfully reference musique concrete, avant-garde sculpture, and skeptical art critics, poking fun at the pursuit of being seen as artistically unconventional.

broadcast|the games you play.fact: "The Games You Play" surfaced on Broadcast's 2024 rarities collection Spell Blanket, released via Warp Records. It's actually a vocal version of an earlier instrumental called "DDL," which had previously appeared on the All Tomorrow's Parties 1.0 compilation and the band's 2006 odds-and-ends album The Future Crayon, with the newly unearthed recordings dating from 2006-2009.

king gizzard & the lizard wizard|the riv.fact: "The River" opens King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard's 2015 album Quarters!, clocking in at exactly 10 minutes and 10 seconds to match the record's concept of four equal-length tracks. Built in a non-standard 5/4 time signature inspired by Dave Brubeck's "Take Five," the song moves through a jazzy, improvisational structure, and its parts were pieced together in unusual locations, including harmonica recorded in a touring van and vocals cut in a rented London rehearsal room.

beck|thinking about you.fact: Beck released "Thinking About You" as a surprise single in 2024 with no advance warning, marking his first new material since a 2022 Neil Young cover. The mellow, acoustic track was recorded in the same studio where Beck made his 2003 album Sea Change, and he debuted it live on Jimmy Kimmel Live.

medicine|time baby iii.fact: "Time Baby III" is a special version of Medicine's song recorded for the 1994 film The Crow's soundtrack, featuring guest vocals from Cocteau Twins singer Elizabeth Fraser (a different version, "Time Baby II," appears in the film itself). The Los Angeles shoegaze band, led by guitarist Brad Laner, got its distinctive tone by running guitars through a Yamaha 4-track recorder.

the kills|u r a fever.fact: "U.R.A. Fever" opens The Kills' 2008 album Midnight Boom, built from clattering, scrapyard-style percussion and metallic clunks rather than conventional drums. The duo recorded the album in Benton Harbor, Michigan, working with producer Alex Epton to push their raw blues-rock sound into grittier, more rhythmic territory.

r.e.m.|we walk.fact: On "We Walk," from R.E.M.'s 1983 debut Murmur, the odd dull thud heard throughout the track is actually a slowed-down recording of drummer Bill Berry playing pool. It's one of several unconventional recording tricks producers Mitch Easter and Don Dixon used to give the album its distinctive, hazy atmosphere.

the smiths|well i wonder.fact: "Well I Wonder" was the first song written for The Smiths' 1985 album Meat Is Murder. Guitarist Johnny Marr deliberately moved back to Manchester during pre-production to capture the right rainy atmosphere for the band's more instrumental, textured songs, and the finished track closes with the actual sound of rain and one of Morrissey's rare falsetto vocal turns.

brittany howard|what now.fact: "What Now" is the title track and lead single from Brittany Howard's second solo album, released in 2023 as her label debut on Island Records following 2019's Jaime. Howard wrote and produced the song with longtime Alabama Shakes collaborator Shawn Everett, recording at two storied Nashville studios, Sound Emporium and historic RCA Studio B.

friko|where we've been.fact: "Where We've Been" opens Chicago band Friko's 2024 debut album Where We've Been, Where We Go From Here, and has become the group's de facto theme song. Songwriters Niko Kapetan and Bailey Minzenberger have said the track's live performances typically close their shows, but they deliberately moved it to the album's opening slot so first-time listeners would get the full scope of the band right away.

rilo kiley|with arms outstretched.fact: "With Arms Outstretched," from Rilo Kiley's 2002 album The Execution of All Things, features a makeshift boy choir made up of friends and bandmates, including singer-songwriter Conor Oberst. The song has had a long cultural afterlife, soundtracking the final scene of Showtime's Weeds (mirroring its use in the show's pilot) and later appearing in the Looking for Alaska miniseries.

new order|your silent face.fact: "Your Silent Face," from New Order's 1983 album Power, Corruption & Lies, was written by Bernard Sumner as a tribute to Kraftwerk, carrying a melody reminiscent of the German electronic pioneers' work. Its original working title was simply "KW1," short for "Kraftwerk One," before the band gave it a proper name for release.

angel olsen|fly on your wall.fact: "Fly On Your Wall" grew out of Angel Olsen's fascination with John Cale and the Velvet Underground's wiry art-rock sound, built around a simple strummed guitar and plodding, behind-the-beat drums. The track later found a home on Olsen's 2017 rarities collection "Phases," released through Jagjaguwar.

arctic monkeys|opening night.fact: "Opening Night" was Arctic Monkeys' first new song in four years, written and recorded at London's Abbey Road Studios with longtime producer James Ford after he invited the band to contribute to War Child's charity compilation "Help (2)." The track leans into a restrained, late-night casino atmosphere.

be your own pet|adventure.fact: "Adventure" appears on Be Your Own Pet's self-titled 2006 debut, which the Nashville band recorded over three weeks with producer Steven McDonald of the band Redd Kross. Fronted by singer Jemina Pearl, the breakneck garage-punk record earned acclaim from both NME and Pitchfork.

beach house|irene.fact: "Irene" closes out Beach House's 2012 album "Bloom" with a six-and-a-half-minute build of tremolo guitar and droning synths. True to the duo's playful streak, the track is followed by roughly eight minutes of silence before a hidden bonus song quietly kicks in around the 13:20 mark.

beat happening|tiger trap.fact: "Tiger Trap" is the nearly seven-minute lead track on Beat Happening's fifth and final studio album, "You Turn Me On" (1992), produced by Steve Fisk and Stuart Moxham of Young Marble Giants. Its lush, layered jangle marked a real departure from the stark minimalism of the K Records band's earliest work.

beck|country down.fact: "Country Down" came out of a 2012 recording session Beck held with Jack White, which also produced "Waking Light" and "Blackbird Chain" for his 2014 album "Morning Phase." That record went on to win the Grammy for Album of the Year.

bjork|stonemilker.fact: Bjork wrote "Stonemilker," the opening track of her 2015 album "Vulnicura," on Grotta, a small island beach near Reykjavik, with electronic beats contributed by producer Arca. Director Andrew Thomas Huang later filmed an innovative 360-degree video for the song on that same beach, which premiered at New York's Museum of Modern Art.

black country, new road|opus.fact: "Opus" closes Black Country, New Road's 2021 debut album "For the First Time" with an eight-minute sprawl that swings from quiet, Slint-style interludes into a cacophony of klezmer and prog-rock. Saxophonist Lewis Evans has said it was one of the very first songs the band ever wrote together, back in early 2018.

bully|atom bomb.fact: Bully's Alicia Bognanno originally wrote "Atom Bomb" as a faster song built around drum machine and electric guitar, but producer JT Daly suggested moving it to piano, turning it into the intimate ballad she released as a stand-alone single in February 2024.

caroline|coldplay cover.fact: Despite the title, "Coldplay cover" by the band caroline is not actually a Coldplay song — the joking nickname just stuck. For the track, half of the eight-piece band played in one room of a London house while the other half played in another, with an engineer physically carrying the microphone back and forth between the two rooms.

chicano batman|crosseyed and painless.fact: Chicano Batman's version of "Crosseyed and Painless" is a cover of Talking Heads' 1980 track from "Remain in Light." Featuring keyboardist Money Mark, it closes out A24's 2024 tribute album "Everyone's Getting Involved: A Tribute to Talking Heads' Stop Making Sense," which also features covers by Paramore, Lorde, and Miley Cyrus.

cindy lee|kingdom come.fact: "Kingdom Come" is track 12 on Cindy Lee's sprawling 2024 double album "Diamond Jubilee," which the project's creator, Patrick Flegel, released in a famously unconventional way — as a free, two-hour YouTube stream and a pay-what-you-want download through an old-school Geocities website rather than through standard streaming services.

cindy lee|wild one.fact: "Wild One" is one of 32 tracks on Cindy Lee's 2024 album "Diamond Jubilee," the drag-pop recording project of Patrick Flegel, who previously fronted the acclaimed Canadian band Women. The sprawling double album was shortlisted for Canada's Polaris Music Prize and later ranked by Pitchfork among the best albums of the 2020s so far.

cloud nothings|running through the campu.fact: "Running Through The Campus" is the lead single from Cloud Nothings' 2024 album "Final Summer," produced by Jeff Zeigler. Frontman Dylan Baldi has said the song traces the swirl of thoughts during a late-night run across an empty campus, moving from restlessness toward acceptance and a genuinely upbeat ending.

coach party|do it for love.fact: "Do It For Love" opens Coach Party's 2025 sophomore album "Caramel." Frontwoman Jess Eastwood has described the Isle of Wight band's song as being about the realities of touring as a working-class act — the relentless grind and low financial returns balanced against a genuine love of the music.

courting|throw.fact: "Throw" comes from Courting's 2024 album "New Last Name," produced by Gary and Ryan Jarman of The Cribs. Frontman Sean Murphy-O'Neill said he set out to write "a song with a plot twist" — an epic about a character who returns to his old city and gets lost reminiscing about the past.

courtney barnett|site unseen (featuring.fact: Courtney Barnett tried recording "Site Unseen" three separate times over two years before a fourth attempt finally clicked, landing on her 2026 album "Creature of Habit." For that final version she invited fellow songwriter Katie Crutchfield of Waxahatchee, a longtime favorite of hers, to sing a high harmony on the track.

david byrne|everybody laughs (ft. ghost.fact: "Everybody Laughs" is the lead single from David Byrne's 2025 album "Who Is the Sky?," arranged by trombonist Curtis Hasselbring of the New York chamber group Ghost Train Orchestra. Byrne recruited the ensemble after hearing their tribute album to the blind street composer Moondog and later joining them onstage for a Brooklyn show.

death lens|cold world.fact: Death Lens is a Los Angeles rock band featuring vocalist Bryan Torres, guitarists Matt Silva and Jhon Reyes, bassist Eduardo Contreras, and drummer Tony Rangel. "Cold World" is the title track of their 2024 album on Epitaph Records, produced by New York-based producer Brett Romnes, and marked a heavier, more post-hardcore-tinged direction than the band's earlier releases.

declan mckenna|mulholland's dinner and w.fact: Declan McKenna co-wrote "Mulholland's Dinner & Wine" with Gianluca Buccellati as, in his words, a "weird, warped story about a cartoon-y criminal duo." The quirky title actually combines the name of a real off-licence (liquor store) back home in the UK with Mulholland Drive in Los Angeles, inspired by McKenna's drives through the Hollywood Hills. It was released as the fourth single from his 2024 album "What Happened to the Beach?"

deerhunter|strange lights.fact: "Strange Lights" is written and sung by Deerhunter guitarist Lockett Pundt rather than frontman Bradford Cox, and served as the first single from the band's 2007 album "Cryptograms." It stands out as one of the record's most accessible, pop-leaning moments, with a sunny, sing-song melody that contrasts with the album's hazier, more experimental first half.

dehd|mood ring.fact: "Mood Ring" is the lead single from Dehd's 2025 album "Poetry," recorded at Palisade Studios in Chicago with guitarist/vocalist Jason Balla co-producing alongside Ziyad Asrar of the band Whitney, the first time Dehd brought in an outside producer. Sung by bassist Emily Kempf, the tune is a sweet, fuzzed-out love song about falling for a motorcycle-riding crush.

dr. dog|the old days.fact: "The Old Days" was written by Dr. Dog's Scott McMicken and Toby Leaman for the band's 2008 album "Fate," a record often described as having a '70s-flavored, rock-opera feel. The song is built around a catchy, piano-pounding arrangement with a repeated chorus that became one of the album's most infectious moments.

elliott smith|angeles.fact: "Angeles" appears on Elliott Smith's 1997 album "Either/Or," built from his intricate acoustic fingerpicking, double-tracked vocals, and a single sustained organ-like keyboard chord. Director Gus Van Sant placed the song on the "Good Will Hunting" soundtrack alongside "Between the Bars" and "Say Yes," helping bring Smith to the Academy Awards stage in 1998.

fleet foxes|if you need to, keep time on.fact: "If You Need To, Keep Time on Me" comes from Fleet Foxes' 2017 album "Crack-Up." Frontman Robin Pecknold described it as a deliberate palate-cleanser opening the album's second half, "a breath between some pretty dense pieces of music," built around acoustic guitar, piano, and the band's layered harmonies. It premiered as a World Record on Zane Lowe's Beats 1 radio show in June 2017.

fugazi|bed for the scraping.fact: "Bed for the Scraping" appears on Fugazi's 1995 album "Red Medicine," the first record the band produced and engineered entirely themselves, which gave them room to experiment with studio effects and unconventional song structures. The track's anthemic, stop-start energy later led Swedish hardcore band Refused to record their own cover version.

future islands|seasons (waiting on you).fact: "Seasons (Waiting on You)" is the opening track and lead single from Future Islands' 2014 album "Singles." The band's March 2014 performance of the song on "Late Show with David Letterman," highlighted by singer Samuel T. Herring's unrestrained dance moves, became the show's most-viewed clip and introduced the band to a massive new audience; U2's Bono later called the song "a miracle."

hannah jadagu|my love.fact: "My Love" is a single from Hannah Jadagu's 2025 album "Describe" on Sub Pop, her follow-up to her acclaimed 2023 debut "Aperture." Jadagu has described the song as being about the longing, excitement, and gratitude that comes with missing someone you love, set to an effervescent synth-pop production.

iron and wine|robin's egg (feat. i'm wit.fact: "Robin's Egg" is a 2025 collaboration between Sam Beam's Iron & Wine and the folk trio I'm With Her (Sarah Jarosz, Aoife O'Donovan, and Sara Watkins), who contribute three-part harmonies to the track. The two acts followed the single with a joint "Robin's Egg Tour," capped by both groups performing together at the Newport Folk Festival.

islands|vapours.fact: "Vapours" is the title track of Islands' third album, released in 2009 on ANTI- Records as a follow-up to 2008's "Arm's Way." Frontman Nick Thorburn built the song, and the record as a whole, around a more rhythmic, synth-driven pop sound, pairing jubilant guitars with a bouncing brass arrangement.

jay som|d.h..fact: "D.H." is a track from Jay Som's 2025 album "Belong," her first full-length in six years, released after a stretch of session work that included contributing to boygenius's Grammy-winning album "The Record." The song builds from a heavier, more layered arrangement into the album's simpler, repeated vocal hooks.

kurt vile|kidding around.fact: "Kidding Around" is the penultimate track on Kurt Vile's 2015 album "b'lieve i'm goin down..." It's a largely instrumental showcase for his fingerpicked guitar style, inspired by folk players like Doc Watson and John Fahey, leaning light on vocals and heavy on intricate guitar arpeggios.

l'rain|two face.fact: "Two Face" was the lead single from L'Rain's 2021 album "Fatigue." Songwriter Taja Cheek said the track was inspired by a falling-out with a friend who was a Gemini, which is where the title comes from, pairing spooky instrumental passages with the song's more hopeful lyrics.

lambchop|niv.fact: "NIV" is a track from Lambchop's 2016 album "FLOTUS," with the title referencing the New International Version of the Bible. The song marked a notable sonic shift for the Nashville band, trading their usual chamber-pop sound for jittery, processed synths and a rhythmic bassline.

mac demarco|home.fact: "Home" is a track from Mac DeMarco's 2025 album Guitar, which he wrote, recorded, mixed, and even filmed the music videos for entirely on his own. DeMarco described the song as being about what "home" means to him, written during a solitary creative stretch at his house in Los Angeles in November 2024.

mamalarky|mythical bonds.fact: "Mythical Bonds," from Mamalarky's 2022 album Pocket Fantasy, is singer Livvy Bennett's tribute to her bandmate Noor Khan. Bennett said she wanted to write something that showed how much Khan's friendship meant to her after their years together as musicians, turning marathon studio sessions into what she called a "serotonin rock song."

my bloody valentine|you made me realise.fact: "You Made Me Realise" is the title track of My Bloody Valentine's 1988 EP, their first release for Creation Records, recorded in just a week in January 1988. Live versions became famous for stretching into an extended wall of guitar noise, with the band's 2008-09 reunion shows reportedly pushing the sound to around 130 decibels, among the loudest passages in rock concert history.

nation of language|silhouette.fact: "Silhouette" appears on Dance Called Memory, Nation of Language's 2023 album and their first full-length for Sub Pop. The ten-track record was recorded and produced in New York City by Nick Millhiser of Holy Ghost! and mastered by Heba Kadry in Brooklyn.

nation of language|this fractured mind.fact: "This Fractured Mind," the third single from Nation of Language's 2021 album A Way Forward, was written by Ian Devaney about the frustration of working service jobs while trying to build a music career. For the track's somber, tape-warped atmosphere, the band ran recordings through tape machines at different speeds and backwards, an approach inspired by William Basinski's "Disintegration Loops."

neko case|wreck.fact: "Wreck" is the lead single from Neko Case's 2025 album Neon Grey Midnight Green, her first new solo studio album in seven years. Case has described the song as an homage to the overwhelming, almost disorienting rush of falling for someone new.

nick cave and the bad seeds|do you love.fact: "Do You Love Me?" opens Nick Cave & the Bad Seeds' 1994 album Let Love In and was released as its first single. The recording reunited Cave with his old Birthday Party bandmate Rowland S. Howard on backing vocals alongside Tex Perkins, with Warren Ellis contributing violin; the band also recorded a companion version, "Do You Love Me? (Part 2)," to close out the album.

nilufer yanya|where to look.fact: "Where To Look," from Nilufer Yanya's 2025 EP Dancing Shoes, was co-written with her longtime collaborator Wilma Archer. Yanya said the song was tricky to finish while working on her previous album but "suddenly clicked" once she returned from tour, adding that melodically it's "one of my favourite things ever."

phantastic ferniture|dare to fall in lov.fact: "Dare To Fall In Love" was one of two songs Phantastic Ferniture, the band fronted by Julia Jacklin, released as their first new music in seven years. The group, which traces its origin to a group pact at a Sydney birthday party to start a band, self-produced and co-wrote the track together at Golden Retriever Studios in Sydney.

pixies|bone machine.fact: "Bone Machine" opens the Pixies' 1988 album Surfer Rosa, recorded with engineer Steve Albini in just ten days. Albini used unconventional studio tricks throughout the sessions, including isolating amplifiers and drums in a tiled bathroom to capture the raw, echoing sound heard across the record.

pixies|hey.fact: "Hey," from the Pixies' 1989 album Doolittle, breaks from the band's signature loud-quiet-loud dynamic in favor of a slinking, funky groove built around Kim Deal's bassline, with Joey Santiago's guitar weaving nervous lines above it. Written by Black Francis, it's often singled out by critics as one of the most distinctive tracks in the band's catalog.

r.e.m.|(don't go back to) rockville.fact: Mike Mills wrote "(Don't Go Back to) Rockville" in 1980, in R.E.M.'s earliest days, about a friend from the University of Georgia whose hometown was Rockville, Maryland. The band originally played it as a fast Ramones-style punk song before slowing it into the country-tinged arrangement heard on 1984's Reckoning, partly as a nod to their manager Bertis Downs, who loved the tune.

r.e.m.|at my most beautiful.fact: "At My Most Beautiful," from R.E.M.'s 1998 album Up, became the band's first straightforward love song. Bassist Mike Mills said that after writing the piano part, he realized it sounded like something Brian Wilson could have written for the Beach Boys' Pet Sounds two decades earlier, and Michael Stipe spent about a year on the lyrics before finishing them in a 45-minute burst.

r.e.m.|the sidewinder sleeps tonite.fact: "The Sidewinder Sleeps Tonite," from 1992's Automatic for the People, borrows its title and opening refrain from the Tokens' "The Lion Sleeps Tonight," and R.E.M. paid for the rights to use that earlier song as the single's B-side. Guitarist Peter Buck said the band included the lighter track deliberately to break up the album's heavier mood.

radiohead|no surprises.fact: Radiohead recorded "No Surprises" for 1997's OK Computer with producer Nigel Godrich, who had the band play the instrumental track faster than normal so he could slow the tape down when Thom Yorke recorded his vocal, giving the song its dreamlike, floating feel. The band nailed the arrangement, including its glockenspiel and childlike melody inspired by the Beach Boys' Pet Sounds, on the first take.

radiohead|nude.fact: "Nude" began life during the OK Computer sessions under working titles like "Big Ideas," but Radiohead abandoned several attempts to finish it across the Kid A and Hail to the Thief recording sessions. The band finally completed it a decade later for 2007's In Rainbows, rebuilding the song around a new bassline written by Colin Greenwood.

sebadoh|beauty of the ride.fact: "Beauty of the Ride" comes from Sebadoh's 1996 album Harmacy, written by Lou Barlow and produced by Tim O'Heir. Released as a single, it climbed to number 74 on the UK Singles Chart.

sharon van etten|hands.fact: "Hands" appears on Sharon Van Etten's 2019 album Remind Me Tomorrow, produced by John Congleton, which marked a deliberate shift toward synth-driven production. Van Etten has said the record overall grew out of the sense of transformation she felt after becoming a parent.

siouxsie and the banshees|halloween.fact: "Halloween" appears on Siouxsie and the Banshees' fourth album, Juju, released in June 1981 and recorded at Surrey Sound Studios with producer Nigel Gray. The track pairs guitarist John McGeoch's angular playing with Steven Severin's bass and Budgie's drumming, and its sing-along "trick or treat" refrain gives the album's dark, atmospheric sound a playful, tongue-in-cheek edge. Juju is widely considered a landmark influence on the emerging goth-rock scene.

slowdive|sugar for the pill.fact: "Sugar for the Pill" comes from Slowdive's self-titled 2017 album, the shoegaze band's first new record in 22 years. Its music video, like the album cover, was inspired by beat-era artist Harry Smith's avant-garde animated film "Heaven and Earth Magic," layering swirling geometric shapes over black-and-white footage of the band. The track itself breaks from classic shoegaze walls of distortion, built around a single delay-laden guitar and the dual vocals of Rachel Goswell and Neil Halstead.

snail mail|tonight, tonight.fact: Snail Mail (Lindsey Jordan) recorded a studio cover of the Smashing Pumpkins' 1996 hit "Tonight, Tonight" for the 2024 A24 film "I Saw the TV Glow," in which she also made her acting debut. Jordan had already been playing the cover live on tour before landing the role, and the connection felt serendipitous: she has a tattoo honoring the "man in the moon" imagery from the original Pumpkins video, which echoed imagery tied to the film's story.

songs ohia|vanquisher (cabwaylingo).fact: The song began life as "Cabwaylingo," the brushed-drums-and-banjo opening track of Jason Molina's self-titled 1997 debut album as Songs: Ohia on Secretly Canadian. Molina later reworked it into a sparser, electric-guitar version he retitled "Vanquisher," released in 1998 — an unusual case of an artist renaming and re-recording the same song for a later release.

st. vincent|fast slow disco.fact: "Fast Slow Disco" is St. Vincent's 2018 reworking of "Slow Disco" from her 2017 album MASSEDUCTION, turning the original's string-laden, near-ballad arrangement into a surging, club-ready house track built on the same strings and lyrics. Annie Clark debuted the sped-up version live at Coachella before releasing it, and later created a third variant, the stripped-down piano version "Slow Slow Disco" — three distinct takes on a single song.

sufjan stevens|the dress looks nice on y.fact: "The Dress Looks Nice on You" is a tender love song from Sufjan Stevens' 2004 album Seven Swans, built mainly around banjo and acoustic guitar with a brief organ solo in the bridge. Released as a single that March, it's often cited as a highlight of the record and an early showcase of the gentle, melodic songwriting style Stevens would become known for.

tame impala|lucidity.fact: "Lucidity" was recorded during the sessions for Tame Impala's debut album, Innerspeaker, with the instrumental tracked in Australia in mid-2009 but the vocals not added until that December, at producer Dave Fridmann's Tarbox Road Studio in upstate New York. Released as the album's second single in July 2010, it features cover art by Australian artist Leif Podhajsky, who also designed the artwork for Innerspeaker and its follow-up, Lonerism.

the beths|no joy.fact: "No Joy" was released in June 2025 as the lead single and album-announcement track for The Beths' fourth studio album, Straight Line Was a Lie — the New Zealand band's first release for the label ANTI- Records. The song's punchy, guitar-forward energy signaled a louder, faster direction for the record, which arrived that August.

the cramps|i can't hardly stand it.fact: The Cramps' version of "I Can't Hardly Stand It" is a cover of a 1956 rockabilly single by Charlie Feathers, co-written by Feathers, Jody Chastain, and Jerry Huffman. The Cramps' take appears on their 1983 compilation "...Off the Bone," part of the band's long-running habit of digging up obscure 1950s rock and roll and rockabilly singles and reviving them for a new audience.

the decemberists|oh no!.fact: "Oh No!" is a single from The Decemberists' 2024 album As It Ever Was, So It Will Be Again. Frontman Colin Meloy says the song's rollicking, salsa-tinged groove was partly inspired by filmmaker Emir Kusturica's work and grew out of its opening line, "It was on a wedding night / How they danced by the firelight" — he's described the result as a tune built on mood and momentum rather than any literal story, pairing an earworm melody with the band's trademark wordplay.

the fixx|saved by zero.fact: "Saved by Zero" was the lead single from The Fixx's 1983 album Reach the Beach, which went platinum and became the band's most commercially successful release. Despite its stark title, singer Cy Curnin has said the lyrics draw on Buddhist ideas about non-attachment, encouraging listeners to find contentment in experience rather than material accumulation — set to a Citizen Kane-inspired music video that helped push the song into the Top 40.

the homesick|i celebrate my fantasy.fact: "I Celebrate My Fantasy" is a track from The Homesick's 2020 Sub Pop album The Big Exercise, the follow-up to the Dutch trio's 2017 debut Youth Hunt. Hailing from the small northern Netherlands town of Dokkum, the band built the song around creeping piano and clarinet flourishes, twisting bright, Beach Boys-indebted melodies into something stranger and more off-kilter.

the magnetic fields|strange powers.fact: "Strange Powers" comes from The Magnetic Fields' 1994 album Holiday, written and sung by Stephin Merritt. Its title was later borrowed for "Strange Powers: Stephin Merritt and the Magnetic Fields," a documentary shot over roughly a decade that chronicles Merritt's long creative partnership with bandmate and manager Claudia Gonson.

the magnetic fields|the one you really l.fact: "The One You Really Love" is track 15 on Volume One of The Magnetic Fields' sprawling 1999 triple album 69 Love Songs. Songwriter Stephin Merritt has described the 69-track concept record as "not remotely an album about love" but rather an album about love songs as a genre, with each track sung through an invented character rather than drawn from Merritt's own life.

the national|the perfect song.fact: "The Perfect Song" appears on The National's self-titled 2001 debut album, written by Aaron Dessner, Scott Devendorf, and Bryan Devendorf. The band recorded the entire album on their own before they had ever played a live show, pooling roughly $15,000 to make the record simply "just to do it," years before becoming one of indie rock's most acclaimed acts.

the new pornographers|votive.fact: "Votive" is the lead single from The New Pornographers' tenth studio album, The Former Site Of, announced in January 2026 for release that March on Merge Records. Built around frontman A.C. Newman's mandolin before opening into an atmospheric synth-and-keyboard jam, the song features a call-and-response refrain with keyboardist/vocalist Kathryn Calder and an accompanying video animated by Michael Arthur.

the pogues|a rainy night in soho.fact: "A Rainy Night in Soho" was written by Shane MacGowan and produced by Elvis Costello for The Pogues' 1986 Poguetry in Motion EP. MacGowan called the song "automatic writing," saying he had no real idea what it was about until he reached the fourth verse. He and Costello reportedly clashed over the final mix, with MacGowan favoring a cornet-led arrangement and Costello preferring oboe.

the stone roses|how do you sleep.fact: "How Do You Sleep" appears on The Stone Roses' long-awaited second album, Second Coming, released in December 1994. The record took years to finish, recorded primarily at Rockfield Studios in Wales, where original producer John Leckie departed partway through the sessions and was replaced by Paul Schroeder, who saw the album through to completion in early 1994.

the white stripes|i just don't know what.fact: Jack and Meg White's version of "I Just Don't Know What to Do with Myself" was the second single from 2003's Elephant. The song was written decades earlier by Burt Bacharach and Hal David and became a UK hit for Dusty Springfield in 1964; the White Stripes' stripped-down, hard-driving arrangement gave the old standard an entirely different, raw energy.

the white stripes|you don't know what lo.fact: The song's actual title is "You Don't Know What Love Is (You Just Do As You're Told)," from The White Stripes' 2007 album Icky Thump. It was written and produced by Jack White and recorded in January 2007 at Blackbird Studio in Nashville; White described the tune as essentially a country song at its core, built on a stomping midtempo groove.

this is lorelei|name the band.fact: "Name the Band" began life on This Is Lorelei's lo-fi 2021 release Jimmy Buffet Tape, one of several scrappy home-recorded projects by Nate Amos (also of Water From Your Eyes). He revived and re-recorded the song as the lead single for his 2025 album Holo Boy, which gathers newly polished versions of songs Amos wrote between 2014 and 2021.

tom waits|martha.fact: "Martha" is the standout ballad on Tom Waits' 1973 debut album, Closing Time, released when Waits was still in his early twenties. The song imagines an old man named Tom Frost placing a long-distance phone call to Martha, an old flame he hasn't spoken to in decades, as the two reminisce. It remains one of the most beloved and frequently covered songs of Waits' career.

tunde adebimpe|somebody new.fact: "Somebody New" is a track from Thee Black Boltz, the 2025 debut solo album by TV on the Radio frontman Tunde Adebimpe. Produced by Adebimpe and Wilder Zoby with contributions from TV on the Radio bandmates Jaleel Bunton and Jahphet Landis, the song is a bright, fast-paced synth number built around uplifting trumpet fanfare.

turnstile|i care.fact: "I CARE" is from Turnstile's 2025 album NEVER ENOUGH. The band gave the song its live debut, paired directly with another new track, "DULL," during an appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon on June 3, 2025, just days ahead of the album's release.

u.s. girls|no fruit.fact: "No Fruit" is the closing track and third single from U.S. Girls' (Meghan Remy) 2025 album Scratch It. Co-written with the band's guitarist Dillon Watson, the song is driven by his wah-wah guitar riff and built around a planting-and-harvest metaphor for something that never came to fruition.

vampire weekend|step.fact: "Step," from Vampire Weekend's 2013 album Modern Vampires of the City, has a winding sample history: it was inspired by Souls of Mischief's 1993 track "Step to My Girl," which itself sampled Grover Washington Jr.'s saxophone cover of the 1970s soft-rock hit "Aubrey" by Bread. Because of that chain, Bread's David Gates ended up credited as a co-writer on "Step."

westerman|confirmation (ssbd).fact: "Confirmation" was Westerman's breakout 2018 single, released as a two-track 7" with "I Turned Away" and produced by his friend and frequent collaborator Bullion. The song, which reflects on Westerman's own songwriting process and the paralysis of having infinite creative choices, later appeared on his 2020 debut album Your Hero Is Not Dead.

white reaper|honestly.fact: "Honestly" is the lead single and emotional centerpiece of White Reaper's fifth album, Only Slightly Empty (2025), which the band self-produced with engineer Joey Oaxaca. Frontman Tony Esposito has said the power-pop anthem is about the gap between acting tough and actually shrinking from confrontation.

wilco|kamera.fact: "Kamera," from Wilco's 2002 album Yankee Hotel Foxtrot, exists in multiple studio versions. A heavier "Unified Theory of Everything" take swaps the album's acoustic arrangement for electric guitars and driving drums, and another rendering turned up on the band's The More Like the Moon EP, a collection of outtakes from the same sessions that Wilco eventually gave away for free to fans.

wire|the 15th.fact: "The 15th," written by Colin Newman for Wire's 1979 album 154, was deliberately recorded without guitarist Bruce Gilbert, partly so the band could keep it from being considered single material. The song later found new life when the electroclash act Fischerspooner covered it as the second single from their 2001 debut album.

yo la tengo|beanbag chair.fact: "Beanbag Chair" was the lead single from Yo La Tengo's eleventh studio album, released in 2006. The horn-and-piano pop song, with its lilting trombone melody and falsetto harmonies, has drawn comparisons to a meeting of the Beatles and Burt Bacharach, its wistful chorus adding a touch of melancholy to an otherwise bright arrangement.

yo la tengo|tom courtenay.fact: Yo La Tengo's 1995 song "Tom Courtenay," from the album Electr-o-pura, is named for the British actor known for 1960s films like Billy Liar, The Loneliness of the Long Distance Runner, and Doctor Zhivago. The band never actually says his name in the lyrics, instead referencing Julie Christie, Courtenay's frequent co-star in those films.

young fathers|lowly.fact: "Lowly" comes from the 28 Years Later original motion picture soundtrack, composed entirely by Scottish group Young Fathers for director Danny Boyle's 2025 film. It marked the band's second collaboration with Boyle, who had previously brought them in to score his 2017 film T2 Trainspotting.

youth lagoon|freak.fact: The actual title of this song is "Speed Freak," the lead single from Youth Lagoon's 2025 album Rarely Do I Dream. Mastermind Trevor Powers built the track around home-movie footage he discovered on old camcorder tapes in a shoebox in his parents' basement, sampling the audio directly off the TV he used to watch them.

sbtkrt|lfo (feat. sampha and george rile.fact: SBTRKT and Sampha began sketching this track back in 2018, and the producer says it went through more than 70 versions before it was finished — the final version came together after he connected with singer George Riley. The title is short for 'low-frequency oscillator,' a nod to the analog synth SBTRKT was fiddling with when the song's signature chords first clicked. It also marked the first time SBTRKT and Sampha had worked together in seven years.

animal collective|fireworks.fact: "Fireworks" is the centerpiece of Animal Collective's 2007 album Strawberry Jam, built around a descending guitar gallop and Beach Boys-style vocal harmonies from Avey Tare. The song celebrates finding joy in simple shared moments, like watching a fireworks display with someone else. Critics have called it one of the band's most soulful, emotionally direct performances on the record.

the strokes|12:51.fact: On The Strokes' 'Twelve:Fifty-One,' guitarist Nick Valensi got a synthesizer-like tone purely out of his guitar — no keyboard involved. He later explained he was playing jazz-style lines with his neck pickup and the tone control rolled down when he accidentally hit his amp's channel-switching pedal, instantly producing an analog-synth sound. Dialing in that tone reportedly cost him three blown amplifiers.

amber arcades|odd to even.fact: 'Odd to Even' is a single from Dutch musician Annelotte de Graaf's Amber Arcades project, taken from her 2023 album Barefoot on Diamond Road. De Graaf described it as capturing 'peak new love energy,' the light, almost overwhelming excitement of wanting to feel connected to someone on every level. The track pairs a sweeping, cosmic-rock arrangement with an instantly hummable chorus.

belle and sebastian|like dylan in the mo.fact: 'Like Dylan in the Movies' appears on Belle and Sebastian's 1996 album If You're Feeling Sinister and was written by frontman Stuart Murdoch. The song uses cinematic, old-Hollywood imagery to capture the thrill of losing yourself in music and movies. It's since become a fan favorite, covered by indie artist Telekinesis for The A.V. Club's Undercover series.

the postal service|against all odds.fact: This is The Postal Service's cover of Phil Collins' 1984 hit, recorded by Ben Gibbard and producer Jimmy Tamborello for the Wicker Park movie soundtrack in 2004. Tamborello kept the arrangement spare — slow bass tones and quiet electric piano — to put the focus on Gibbard's vocal. It later resurfaced as a bonus track on the Give Up 10th Anniversary Edition in 2013.

cindy lee|flesh and blood.fact: 'Flesh and Blood' is a track from Cindy Lee's 2024 album Diamond Jubilee, the project of Canadian musician Patrick Flegel, formerly of the band Women. True to the album's lo-fi, retro pop-and-rock sound, Diamond Jubilee was released with no promotion or interviews — fans had to find a 1990s-GeoCities-style website to download it before it eventually landed on YouTube. The sprawling album went on to be shortlisted for the 2024 Polaris Music Prize.

black flag|nervous breakdown.fact: 'Nervous Breakdown' is the title track of Black Flag's debut EP, released in January 1979 as the very first release on Greg Ginn's now-legendary SST Records. Singer Keith Morris originally showed up to the band hoping to play drums and had to be talked into taking the microphone instead. It remains the only non-compilation Black Flag release to feature Morris on vocals before he left to form the Circle Jerks.

militarie gun|very high.fact: 'Very High' was the lead single from Militarie Gun's 2023 debut album Life Under the Gun, blending the urgency of hardcore punk with jangly, '90s alt-rock hooks. The central line, 'I've been feeling pretty down, so I get very high,' was written as a simple way to describe lifting yourself out of day-to-day self-consciousness and embarrassment. Its music video affectionately parodies the opening credits of 1990s sitcoms and dramas.

sufjan stevens|video games.fact: Released in 2020 from Sufjan Stevens' album The Ascension, 'Video Game' uses the metaphor of a video game to talk about public image, ambition, and the pressure to perform for others' approval. Its repeated line, 'I don't wanna play,' functions as the song's thesis — Stevens has said the track's point is that your sense of worth shouldn't depend on other people's validation. The glossy synth-pop sound was a notable departure from his more orchestral, folk-based earlier work.

modest mouse|custom concern.fact: 'Custom Concern' is the third track on Modest Mouse's 1996 debut album, This Is a Long Drive for Someone with Nothing to Think About. Isaac Brock plays dual-tracked acoustic and electric guitar on the song, giving it a slow, country-tinged feel that stands out on the record. His double-tracked vocal, sung both low and high, adds to the song's understated, trudging atmosphere.

wilco|whole love.fact: 'Whole Love' is the title track from Wilco's 2011 album The Whole Love, the first release on the band's own label, dBpm Records. Musically, the song draws on classic soft-pop touches, with critics pointing to echoes of Simon & Garfunkel's 'The 59th Street Bridge Song' and the Small Faces' 'Itchycoo Park.' It gave the band a breezy, summery opener for an album they controlled from top to bottom.

mac demarco|on the level.fact: Mac DeMarco wrote 'On the Level,' from his 2017 album This Old Dog, after buying a new Roland D-50 synthesizer and simply sitting down to experiment with it before adding any lyrics. He's described the lush, synth-driven track as a 'sister song' to 'Chamber of Reflection,' a highlight from his earlier album Salad Days. The album overall leaned into themes about his family and life at the time.

yeah yeah yeahs|heads will roll.fact: 'Heads Will Roll' comes from Yeah Yeah Yeahs' 2009 album It's Blitz!, but it became an even bigger hit after DJ A-Trak released a remix later that year. Unusually, A-Trak approached the band to remix the track himself rather than the other way around. The remix went on to become a dance-club staple and was later named to Rolling Stone's list of the 200 greatest dance songs.

julian casablancas|out of the blue.fact: 'Out of the Blue' is a single from Julian Casablancas' 2009 solo debut, Phrazes for the Young, an album whose concept and title were inspired by Oscar Wilde's witty aphorism collection 'Phrases and Philosophies for the Use of the Young.' The song mixes a quirky, retro-futuristic synth intro with bright, guitar-driven verses. It was Casablancas' first major outing away from The Strokes.

radiohead|follow me around.fact: 'Follow Me Around' dates back to Radiohead's OK Computer era in 1997, when the band played it at soundchecks and it slowly became a legendary fan favorite despite never getting an official release. Fans even lobbied through a dedicated website, followmearound.com, to get the band to perform it live, which finally happened acoustically in Toronto in 2000. The song finally saw official release in November 2021 on the Kid A Mnesia reissue, complete with a music video starring actor Guy Pearce.

mitski|francis forever.fact: "Francis Forever" appears on Mitski's 2014 album Bury Me at Makeout Creek, the lo-fi, guitar-driven record she made after moving away from the classically-composed songwriting of her earlier releases. The track is built from just vocals and a simple guitar line, opening with a music-box chime before the electric guitar arrives.

black country, new road|snow globes.fact: "Snow Globes" is a sprawling, nine-plus-minute track from Black Country, New Road's 2022 album Ants from Up There. The band first previewed its chorus during a Christmas 2020 livestream with fellow London band black midi, then kept developing the song on tour, building from slow strings and woodwinds into a wild, free-jazz-style drum solo from Charlie Wayne.

king gizzard and the lizard wizard|bone.fact: "Bone" appears on King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard's 2015 album Paper Mâché Dream Balloon, an all-acoustic record the Australian band made as a deliberate change of pace from their usual heavier, concept-driven releases. Frontman Stu Mackenzie plays flute as the song's lead melodic instrument, trading the same notes back and forth with a guitar.

the microphones|the moon.fact: "The Moon" is a track from the Microphones' 2001 album The Glow Pt. 2, the influential lo-fi record Phil Elverum built largely on his own in an Anacortes, Washington studio. The song blends hazy, shoegaze-style guitar wash with plainspoken vocals, a combination critics have compared to Neutral Milk Hotel.

real estate|out of tune.fact: "Out of Tune" started as a standalone 7-inch single on True Panther Sounds before Real Estate folded it into their 2011 album Days. The New Jersey band brought in Daniel Lopatin of Oneohtrix Point Never to add synthesizer textures, layering an extra hazy wash over the song's jangly guitar lines.

beirut|the tern.fact: "The Tern" is the penultimate track on Beirut's 2023 album Hadsel, written and recorded by Zach Condon on the remote Norwegian island the album is named for, after a period away from touring. Condon built the song from an old Roland synthesizer and drum machine part, then layered in church organ and hand percussion for a hymn-like feel.

wallows|i don't want to talk.fact: Wallows released "I Don't Want to Talk" as a single in September 2021, working with producer Ariel Rechtshaid (known for his work with Vampire Weekend and HAIM) and spending more than a year refining its fuzzy guitars and harmonica hook. Co-frontman Dylan Minnette has said the song is about the insecurity of shutting down instead of voicing your fears in a relationship.

wild nothing|data world.fact: "Data World" appears on Wild Nothing's 2013 EP Empty Estate, which Jack Tatum recorded in about ten days at Gary's Electric studio in Brooklyn right after a long European tour. The song rides a driving bassline and precise drumming into a bright synth climax, pushing the project's sound in a punchier, more electronic direction.

beach house|other people.fact: "Other People" comes from Beach House's 2012 album Bloom, the Baltimore duo's follow-up to their breakthrough Teen Dream. The track closes with a stretch of ambient field recordings, waves crashing and birds calling, a quiet touch that became one of the album's signature moments.

father john misty|the payoff.fact: "The Payoff" is a 2026 Father John Misty single released on Sub Pop, arriving five months after his single "The Old Law" and following his 2024 album Mahashmashana. Josh Tillman wrote the song and co-produced it with arranger Drew Erickson, with mixing by Michael Harris at Fivestar Studios and mastering by Adam Ayan.

diiv|brown paper bag.fact: DIIV began in Brooklyn in 2011 as frontman Zachary Cole Smith's solo recording project, originally spelled "Dive" after the Nirvana song before he changed the spelling after learning of an earlier Belgian band with the same name. "Brown Paper Bag" served as the lead single from DIIV's 2024 album Frog in Boiling Water.

animal collective|the purple bottle.fact: "The Purple Bottle" is a standout from Animal Collective's 2005 album Feels, a nearly seven-minute track built on a steady percussive groove and the band's layered, chant-like vocal harmonies. Critics have noted its unabashedly poppy, Beach Boys-style surf guitar hooks, a bright contrast to the band's more experimental material.

the clash|lost in the supermarket.fact: Joe Strummer wrote "Lost in the Supermarket" by imagining the suburban upbringing of bandmate Mick Jones, reportedly jotting early lyrics on the back of a guitar-string package. Jones sang lead on the 1979 London Calling track despite Strummer having written the words, giving the song's commentary on consumer culture an extra layer of role-swapping.

the strokes|last nite.fact: The Strokes' 2001 breakout single "Last Nite," from the album Is This It, opens with a guitar riff lifted almost directly from Tom Petty's "American Girl." When fans pointed out the similarity, frontman Julian Casablancas readily admitted, "Yeah, we ripped it off," and Petty later said the admission made him laugh and that he had no hard feelings.

tame impala|it might be time.fact: "It Might Be Time" is a 2019 single from Tame Impala's album The Slow Rush, written, performed, and produced entirely by Kevin Parker, who has said the track grew out of a late-night studio session shaped by his love of 1970s prog and Supertramp. Parker later walked through how the song came together on an episode of the podcast Song Exploder.

black belt eagle scout|my heart dreams.fact: Katherine Paul wrote "My Heart Dreams" during a transitional period in her life, describing the song as capturing the restless, hopeful feeling of wanting to find new love after a relationship had ended. Musically, the 2019 track leans into a warm, '90s-tinged dream-pop sound that critics compared to Mazzy Star.

sonic youth|dirty boots.fact: "Dirty Boots" opens Sonic Youth's 1990 major-label debut Goo and was later released as the album's third single in 1991, backed with five live tracks recorded at a UC Irvine concert that same year. The song's driving, melodic guitar lines gave the famously experimental band one of its most accessible album openers, and its music video follows two teens who meet and fall for each other at a Sonic Youth show.

circulatory system|yesterday's world.fact: "Yesterday's World" opens Circulatory System's self-titled 2001 debut, the project Will Cullen Hart and Bill Doss formed out of the ashes of the Elephant 6 band Olivia Tremor Control. The track layers churning guitars, woodwinds, marching-band-style drums, and a children's chorus into a dense psychedelic-pop collage typical of the Elephant 6 collective's home-recording ethos.

grizzly bear|sleeping ute.fact: "Sleeping Ute," the lead single from Grizzly Bear's 2012 album Shields, is sung by guitarist Daniel Rossen and named after a real mountain in Utah that, according to local legend, resembles a sleeping warrior whose "blanket" changes color with the seasons. Rossen said he had never actually visited the mountain but had driven past it on trips through the Southwest and drew the image from reading about the area.

m. ward|chinese translation.fact: "Chinese Translation," from M. Ward's 2006 album Post-War, features Jim James of My Morning Jacket as a guest musician. The song's rolling, folk-ballad melody and searching lyrics about working through heartbreak made it one of the most memorable tracks on the Merge Records release.

the unicorns|tuff ghost.fact: "Tuff Ghost" is the second track on The Unicorns' 2003 album Who Will Cut Our Hair When We're Gone?, built around a bouncy synth riff and a mix of clean lead vocals with lo-fi, shouted backing vocals. The Vancouver-area band, led by Nicholas Thorburn and Alden Penner, became known for blending whimsical, catchy pop hooks with playfully offbeat lyrics before splitting up shortly after the album's release.

lcd soundsystem|north american scum.fact: James Murphy wrote "North American Scum" as a tongue-in-cheek jab at how Americans are stereotyped abroad, noting that much of the world's impression of the U.S. comes from the media it exports. The song, from LCD Soundsystem's 2007 album Sound of Silver, pokes fun at the gap between the on-screen version of America and the real thing rather than making a serious political statement.

vampire weekend|worship you.fact: "Worship You" appears on Vampire Weekend's 2019 album Father of the Bride, a record frontman Ezra Koenig built around searching, faith-tinged imagery drawn partly from his own upbringing. The song's chant-like vocal hook and steady, driving groove turn a question about devotion into something closer to a communal singalong than a traditional hymn.

beabadoobee|all i did was dream of you (.fact: Beabadoobee's "All I Did Was Dream of You" pairs her lead vocal with a second-verse feature from María Zardoya of The Marías, the result of a long mutual admiration between the two singers. Released in 2026 as beabadoobee's first new single since her 2024 album This Is How Tomorrow Moves, the trip-hop-tinged track arrived with a video shot on location in Vilnius, Lithuania.

t. rex|metal guru.fact: "Metal Guru" became T. Rex's fourth and final UK number-one single, topping the chart for four weeks in 1972. Producer Tony Visconti later said the song was really inspired by Marc Bolan's fascination with a Cadillac, even though Bolan dressed the lyrics up in cosmic language and repeated the title phrase more than twenty times across the track.

siouxsie and the banshees|happy house.fact: "Happy House" was the first single from Siouxsie and the Banshees' 1980 album Kaleidoscope and marked the debut of new drummer Budgie, whose African-polyrhythm-influenced playing combined with John McGeoch's guitar work to give the band what Siouxsie called a "phase two" sound. The single became one of the group's biggest UK hits to that point.

the beths|mother, pray for me.fact: Singer Elizabeth Stokes wrote "Mother, Pray For Me" while reflecting on her relationship with her mother, a first-generation Indonesian immigrant, after the family moved from Jakarta to Auckland when Stokes was four. The stripped-down, finger-picked ballad was released in 2025 as a single from The Beths' album Straight Line Was a Lie, out on ANTI- Records.

guided by voices|echos myron.fact: Widely considered the catchiest, most Beatles-influenced song on Guided by Voices' lo-fi 1994 breakthrough Bee Thousand, the track was recorded by frontman Robert Pollard on a four-track in his home. Its real title is actually spelled "Echoes Myron," one of many playful quirks on an album built from home-recorded fragments.

king gizzard and the lizard wizard|dream.fact: "Dreams" is a synth-driven track from King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard's 2021 album Butterfly 3000, a departure from the band's usual guitar-heavy sound toward dreamy, melodic synth-pop. Its animated music video visualizes the hazy, shifting logic of dreaming, drifting through strange, colorful scenes that never quite resolve into anything concrete.

nick cave and the bad seeds|deanna.fact: "Deanna," from Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds' 1988 album Tender Prey, grew out of an off-the-cuff studio jam: producer Tony Cohen recalled that Cave had only a loose idea for the song, fooling around on a Hammond organ while Mick Harvey kept time on a floor tom before the full band built it into a track. Musically it's rooted in the gospel standard "Oh Happy Day," twisted into the raucous garage-rock sound that became a staple of the band's live shows.

bon iver|beth/rest.fact: "Beth/Rest" closes Bon Iver's self-titled 2011 album with an unabashed detour into 1980s soft-rock and AOR territory, built largely on a Korg M1 synthesizer. Justin Vernon said he wasn't being ironic by embracing the sound, citing genuine admiration for artists like Bruce Hornsby, and described the song as an uplifting ode to finding real love.

wilco|via chicago.fact: Jeff Tweedy wrote "Via Chicago," from Wilco's 1999 album Summerteeth, partly through a word-association exercise: jotting down action verbs tied to a given profession alongside a separate list of words he simply liked the sound of, then connecting them. Tweedy has also noted the irony of fans cheering for a song titled "Via Chicago," since "via" means passing through a place rather than arriving at it.

the waterboys|you in the sky.fact: "You in the Sky" dates back to The Waterboys' mid-1980s Fisherman's Blues sessions, a period when frontman Mike Scott was drawing heavily on Hank Williams and other American roots artists. Long left in the vaults, the track eventually surfaced on later expanded reissues and the band's archival Fisherman's Box set.

big thief|shoulders.fact: "Shoulders" appears on Big Thief's 2019 album Two Hands, which the band tracked live with almost no overdubs at Sonic Ranch studio in Tornillo, Texas. The album was produced by longtime collaborator Andrew Sarlo and released as the "earth twin" companion to the band's other 2019 record, U.F.O.F. Big Thief performed "Shoulders" live on Jimmy Kimmel Live!

foxwarren|sunset canyon.fact: "Sunset Canyon" comes from the 2018 self-titled debut album by Foxwarren, the band Andy Shauf formed with childhood friends Dallas Bryson and brothers Darryl and Avery Kissick. The band has said the song came together quickly late one night while Shauf was home between tours, and it almost didn't make the final album because it felt like such an outlier next to the rest of the record.

the orielles|the room.fact: "The Room" was the first song The Orielles wrote for their album Tableau, recorded at Eve Studios after the Manchester band spent a day jamming together following months of lockdown. The lyrics were written line-by-line by each band member taking turns, starting with the opening image "the moon is in the room," which was inspired by a novel by Brazilian writer Clarice Lispector.

beck|walls.fact: "Walls" is from Beck's 2008 album Modern Guilt, which he co-wrote and produced with Danger Mouse (Brian Burton). Singer Cat Power (Chan Marshall) provides backing vocals on the song's chorus, one of several guest spots across the record.

king krule|slush puppy.fact: "Slush Puppy," from King Krule's 2017 album The OOZ, opens with vocals from Norwegian-American singer Okay Kaya rather than Archy Marshall himself. Marshall has said he distorted and processed his own voice throughout the track to give it its woozy, underwater-sounding tone.

talk talk|it's my life.fact: "It's My Life" was written by Mark Hollis and Tim Friese-Greene and released as the title track and first single from Talk Talk's second album in 1984. It reached number 31 on the Billboard Hot 100, the band's only U.S. Top 40 hit, and was later covered by No Doubt in 2003, whose version became an even bigger hit, peaking at number 10.

radiohead|polyethylene.fact: "Polyethylene (Parts 1 & 2)" was released as a B-side to "Paranoid Android" and later collected on the Airbag/How Am I Driving? EP during the OK Computer era. The track opens with Thom Yorke humming over acoustic guitar before he audibly stops and counts the band in, giving it a raw, in-studio feel.

caribou|sun.fact: "Sun" is a standout track from Caribou's 2010 album Swim, which Dan Snaith set out to make sound "like it's made out of water." The song is built around Snaith chanting the single word "sun" over and over against a shifting, hypnotic techno beat.

whitney|strange overtones.fact: "Strange Overtones" was originally written by David Byrne and Brian Eno for their 2008 collaborative album Everything That Happens Will Happen Today. Chicago duo Whitney covered it for their 2020 covers album Candid, and guitarist Max Kakacek noted that bandmate Malcolm Brown worked out a piano solo for the song, the first time the band had put a keyboard solo on a recorded track.

the white stripes|dead leaves and the di.fact: "Dead Leaves and the Dirty Ground" opens The White Stripes' 2001 breakthrough album White Blood Cells and was written by Jack White about missing someone so much that ordinary life feels changed in their absence, using autumn imagery of dead leaves rather than anything literal. The Guardian's Alexis Petridis later named it the single greatest song in the band's catalog.

caroline polachek|door.fact: "Door" was released in 2019 as the lead single from Caroline Polachek's debut solo album Pang, the first music she released under her own name after earlier recording as Ramona Lisa and as part of the band Chairlift. A lyric from the song, "perpetual novice," later became the name of Polachek's own record imprint.

wolf parade|against the day.fact: "Against the Day," from Wolf Parade's 2020 album Thin Mind, marked the first time co-frontmen Dan Boeckner and Spencer Krug split lead vocals within the same song. Krug has said Boeckner pitched the track's concept as two vampires exploring the human world, with each songwriter voicing one of the characters.

broadcast|come on let's go.fact: "Come On Let's Go" was released in 2000 as a single from Broadcast's debut album The Noise Made by People on Warp Records. The Birmingham band produced the record themselves after being unhappy with earlier sessions handled by outside engineers, giving the album its distinctive lo-fi, analog-synth sound built around singer Trish Keenan's voice.

superchunk|throwing things.fact: "Throwing Things" closes out Superchunk's 1991 album No Pocky for Kitty, which the Chapel Hill band recorded in just three days at Chicago Recording Company with engineer Steve Albini. At three and a half minutes, the jangly, melody-driven track has been singled out by critics as one of the record's standout closing songs.

belle and sebastian|this is just a moder.fact: "This Is Just a Modern Rock Song" is the title track of Belle and Sebastian's fourth EP, released in December 1998 on Jeepster Records. A new UK chart rule capping eligible singles/EPs at three tracks and 20 minutes meant the four-song, nearly 20-minute EP narrowly failed to qualify for the singles chart, and its cover photo features Postcard Records founder Alan Horne.

my morning jacket|out of range, pt. 2.fact: "Out of Range, Pt. 2" appears on My Morning Jacket's self-titled 2021 album, their first new studio record in over six years. The song grew out of a meditative guitar conversation between Jim James and Carl Broemel, with Broemel reportedly feeling their first take was so pure he didn't want to add anything further to it.

c.y.m.|justify.fact: "Justify" comes from C.Y.M., a studio project pairing Vampire Weekend bassist Chris Baio with Berlin-based house producer Michael Greene (aka Fort Romeau). The pair first teamed up on a self-titled EP in 2019 and write, record, and produce all their own material, blending krautrock, shoegaze, and soul influences. "Justify" was part of a batch of 2025 singles that preceded C.Y.M.'s debut full-length album.

sonic youth|silver rocket.fact: "Silver Rocket" is the second track and second single from Sonic Youth's 1988 album Daydream Nation, credited to all four band members and produced by the group with Nick Sansano. It was recorded at Greene St. Recording in Manhattan during the summer of 1988. Its single pressing came paired with a separate, independently-released live version of the song featuring alternate lyrics, pressed in small runs by fanzines.

the smiths|please, please, please let me.fact: Johnny Marr wrote this song's waltz-time melody as a deliberate contrast to the upbeat A-side "William, It Was Really Nothing," drawing inspiration from Del Shannon's "The Answer to Everything," a song his parents played when he was young. Clocking in at under two minutes, the track started life as a 1984 B-side but found a second life on the soundtracks to Pretty in Pink and, via a Dream Academy cover, Ferris Bueller's Day Off, both in 1986.

hana vu|care.fact: "Care" was the lead single from Hana Vu's 2024 sophomore album Romanticism, released on the Ghostly International label. Critics noted the song pulls a melodic page from the Lennon-McCartney songbook while filtering it through Vu's own fuzzy, alt-grunge-tinged indie-pop sound. Vu has said she wrote it while thinking about how differently everyone processes their own thoughts and feelings.
