man man|van helsing boombox.fact: "Van Helsing Boombox" appears on Man Man's 2006 album Six Demon Bag and was later ranked among Pitchfork's best songs of the 2000s. Frontman Honus Honus has described the period when he wrote it as a rough, "dark days" stretch of his life, and it's often singled out by critics as one of the most melodic, emotionally direct moments in the band's otherwise chaotic, carnival-esque catalog.

mgmt|congratulations.fact: The title track to MGMT's 2010 album Congratulations was the record's fourth and final single, released as a limited 7" for Record Store Day's Black Friday with a 20-page illustrated booklet. Frontman Andrew VanWyngarden called the song "a bit more sinister and sarcastic" than a simple pat on the back, saying it partly reflects the band processing everything that happened after their debut took off. The song later soundtracked the closing credits of the Oscar-winning documentary Inside Job.

neutral milk hotel|ghost.fact: Frontman Jeff Mangum wrote much of In the Aeroplane Over the Sea, including "Ghost," after reading The Diary of a Young Girl by Anne Frank, which he has said deeply affected him while making the 1998 album. The record was recorded at Pet Sounds Studio in Denver and is now regarded as one of the most acclaimed indie rock albums of the 1990s.

wallows|hide it away.fact: "Hide It Away" appears on Wallows' 2025 EP More and was produced by Grammy winner John Congleton, who has also worked with St. Vincent and Alvvays. The track leans into a heavier, Strokes-influenced rock sound compared to the band's earlier indie-pop material, reflecting Wallows' continued evolution as a live act.

husker du|makes no sense at all.fact: Written by Bob Mould, "Makes No Sense at All" was released as a single from Hüsker Dü's 1985 album Flip Your Wig and reached number 2 on the UK indie chart. Critics often cite it as proof the Minneapolis trio could write a classic power-pop anthem worthy of the Buzzcocks or the Raspberries without losing their punk identity.

idles|cheerleader.fact: IDLES wrote "Cheerleader" for the soundtrack to Darren Aronofsky's 2025 crime thriller Caught Stealing, one of several original tracks the band contributed alongside a cover of "Police & Thieves." Frontman Joe Talbot has spoken about how the band drew on the gritty energy of the 1990s New York punk scene while scoring the film.

alex g|ain't it easy.fact: "Ain't It Easy" appears on Alex G's 2022 album God Save the Animals, a record where he uses the idea of "God" as a general stand-in for faith and connection rather than any specific religion. Critics have described the song's outlook as one of persistent hope and acceptance of uncertainty, fitting the album's overall arc from hardship toward endurance.

anamanaguchi|buckwild.fact: "Buckwild" is a 2025 single from chiptune-punk band Anamanaguchi, previewing their album Anyway. The upbeat, guitar-driven track celebrates appreciating life and the company of others away from screens and the daily grind, functioning as a kind of answer song to the band's earlier single "Rage (Kitchen Sink)."

soccer mommy|bones.fact: "Bones" was the third single from Soccer Mommy's 2022 album Sometimes, Forever and was produced by Daniel Lopatin, best known for his work as Oneohtrix Point Never. Songwriter Sophie Allison originally wrote the track for a romantic comedy but liked it too much to give away, keeping it for her own record instead.

camera obscura|the sweetest thing.fact: "The Sweetest Thing" comes from Camera Obscura's 2006 album Let's Get Out of This Country, the Glasgow band's commercial breakthrough after signing to 4AD. The gentle, horn-flecked song nods to Paul Simon's "50 Ways to Leave Your Lover" and is sung by Tracyanne Campbell.

font|looking at engines.fact: "Looking at Engines" is the third track on Strange Burden, the 2024 debut album from Austin, Texas indie rock band Font, released via Acrophase Records. The band, fronted by singer-guitarist Thom Waddill, built a local following playing shows with only a couple of songs available online before the album came out.

ginger root|only you.fact: "Only You" is track seven on Ginger Root's 2024 album Shinbangumi, the project's debut for Ghostly International, led by multi-instrumentalist Cameron Lew. The album continues the retro-futuristic, city-pop-inspired concept story Lew began on his 2022 EP Nisemono, and "Only You" has been singled out by reviewers as one of its catchiest, most soaring disco-tinged tracks.

broken social scene|cause = time.fact: "Cause = Time" appears on Broken Social Scene's 2002 breakthrough album You Forgot It in People, with co-founders Kevin Drew and Brendan Canning trading vocal duties alongside guest singers Leslie Feist and Emily Haines. The band Middle Kids released a cover of the song in 2025 as part of a full tribute album celebrating You Forgot It in People.

a certain ratio|do the du (the graveyar.fact: "Do The Du" is the studio-side title track from A Certain Ratio's 1980 debut album The Graveyard and the Ballroom. Despite the ominous-sounding name, "The Graveyard" simply refers to Graveyard Studios in Prestwich, Greater Manchester, where producer Martin Hannett recorded the band's studio tracks in September 1979. The album's other half, "The Ballroom," was captured live at London's Electric Ballroom that same year.

alvvays|after the earthquake.fact: "After the Earthquake" comes from Alvvays' 2022 album Blue Rev, and singer Molly Rankin has said it was partly inspired by Haruki Murakami's short-story collection after the quake. The lyrics also sneak in a nod to the classic mystery series Murder, She Wrote. It was recorded with producer Shawn Everett, known for his work with The War on Drugs and Kacey Musgraves.

andrew bird|plasticities.fact: "Plasticities" appears on Andrew Bird's 2007 album Armchair Apocrypha and shows off his one-man-band style, layering pizzicato violin, whistling, and electric guitar into looping arrangements. Bird performed the song on Late Show with David Letterman in April 2007 to help promote the record.

andy shauf|jaywalker.fact: "Jaywalker" comes from Andy Shauf's 2021 album Wilds, a set of songs written during the same sessions as his earlier record The Neon Skyline. True to his usual process, Shauf played and recorded every instrument himself, and the song unfolds as a quiet, rambling little story about someone too distracted to notice what's coming.

angel olsen|the waiting.fact: "The Waiting" appears on Angel Olsen's 2013 album Half Way Home and leans into a girl-group, Brill Building sound reminiscent of Carole King, complete with ghostly backing harmonies and Olsen's distinctive vibrato. It's an early showcase of the classic pop songcraft she'd become known for beyond her lo-fi roots.

animal collective|alvin row.fact: "Alvin Row" closes out Animal Collective's 2000 debut album Spirit They're Gone, Spirit They've Vanished with a sprawling, nearly 13-minute coda built on layered vocal harmonies from Avey Tare. The album was originally released in a tiny CD-only pressing on the band's own label before later reissues brought it to wider audiences.

animal collective|who could win a rabbit.fact: "Who Could Win a Rabbit" was the first single from Animal Collective's 2004 album Sung Tongs, built around jangly acoustic guitar and playful, nonsensical lyrics. Its music video riffs on Aesop's fable of the tortoise and the hare, with two band members dressed as a rabbit and a turtle racing each other.

bartees strange|too much.fact: "Too Much" opens Bartees Strange's 2024 album Horror and works as a kind of pep talk to himself, growing from self-doubt into something bigger over the course of the song. The track blends noisy indie rock with a confident rap bridge, and its instrumental hook nods to classic soul acts like the Isley Brothers and the Brothers Johnson.

beach fossils|shallow.fact: "Shallow" was the first single from Beach Fossils' 2013 album Clash the Truth, and frontman Dustin Payseur has said he wanted to push against indie rock's tendency to play it safe by making something noisier and more aggressive. The result keeps the band's jangly guitar sound but buries it in extra fuzz and energy.

beach house|superstar.fact: "Superstar" is the second track on Beach House's 2022 double album Once Twice Melody, which was recorded across three studios in Minnesota, Los Angeles, and Baltimore. It marked the first time the Baltimore duo used a live string ensemble, with arrangements by veteran composer David Campbell.

beck|go it alone.fact: "Go It Alone" is a standout cut from Beck's 2005 album Guero, co-written with Jack White of The White Stripes along with Dust Brothers members John King and Mike Simpson. It's one of several songs White has quietly helped pen for other artists over the years.

beck|heart is a drum.fact: "Heart Is a Drum" was released in 2014 as the fourth single from Beck's Grammy-winning album Morning Phase, blending chamber folk with shimmering, Crosby, Stills & Nash-style harmonies. Beck performed the song at the 57th Grammy Awards alongside Coldplay's Chris Martin.

beck|up all night.fact: "Up All Night" is a single from Beck's 2017 album Colors, produced with Greg Kurstin, and it topped Billboard's Alternative Songs chart, becoming Beck's first chart-topper there since 2005's "E-Pro." An earlier version of the song had already appeared on the soundtrack for EA Sports' FIFA 17 video game before the album version was finished.

beirut|villa sacchetti.fact: Beirut's "Villa Sacchetti," from the 2025 album A Study of Losses, was inspired by a real baroque Roman villa that fell into ruin and was later immortalized in paintings by 18th-century romantic artist Hubert Robert. Zach Condon paired a simple piano waltz with lute-like ukulele to try to capture the faded elegance of the once-grand, long-abandoned estate overlooking Rome.

belle and sebastian|another sunny day.fact: "Another Sunny Day" is from Belle and Sebastian's 2006 album The Life Pursuit, recorded at The Sound Factory in Los Angeles with producer Tony Hoffer, who'd also worked with Beck and would later produce Goldfrapp. Hoffer's glossier touch helped push the band's trademark jangle-pop into sturdier, more radio-ready territory.

belle and sebastian|come on home.fact: "Come On Home" appears on Belle and Sebastian's 2022 album A Bit of Previous, their first full-length in seven years. The whole record was recorded in the band's native Glasgow after pandemic travel restrictions scrapped plans to record in Los Angeles, marking the first time since 2000 that they'd made an album in their hometown.

big thief|love in mine.fact: Big Thief's "Love in Mine" came out of the same Texas sessions that produced their 2019 album Two Hands, recorded at the Sonic Ranch studio in the desert near El Paso. The song first reached fans as a mailed 7-inch single before being released as a standalone track in April 2020.

bon iver|u (man like).fact: Bon Iver debuted "U (Man Like)" live at the All Points East festival in June 2019 as one of the first previews of the album that followed 22, A Million. The track is packed with guest voices, including Moses Sumney, Wye Oak's Jenn Wasner, and the Brooklyn Youth Chorus, with Bruce Hornsby playing piano and sharing a songwriting credit.

built to spill|jokerman.fact: Built to Spill covered Bob Dylan's 1983 reggae-tinged song "Jokerman" for the 2014 tribute compilation Bob Dylan in the 80s: Volume One. Where Dylan's original leaned on the rhythm section of Sly and Robbie, the Idaho band reworked it with driving guitars in place of the prominent organ.

califone|frosted tips.fact: Califone takes its name from Califone International, a long-running maker of classroom audio equipment, fitting for a band built around tape loops and old electronics. "Frosted Tips" is track three on 2013's Stitches, the group's first album recorded outside Chicago, with sessions held in Texas, Arizona, and California.

cat power|cross bones style.fact: Chan Marshall wrote and recorded "Cross Bones Style" for 1998's Moon Pix in one sitting, tracking live vocals and guitar together before Dirty Three drummer Jim White added percussion. It became the only song from the album to get a music video, directed by Brett Vapnek.

cat power|lived in bars.fact: "Lived in Bars" is the third track on Cat Power's 2006 album The Greatest, recorded at Ardent Studios in Memphis with a crew of veteran session players, including guitarist Teenie Hodges, billed as the Memphis Rhythm Band. It was the first Cat Power album made entirely of Chan Marshall originals, with no cover songs.

catholic action|i'm no artist.fact: Catholic Action are a Glasgow quartet formed in 2014 around singer-guitarist Chris McCrory. "I'm No Artist" is the third track on their 2020 sophomore album Celebrated by Strangers, which earned the band a nomination for Scotland's SAY Award.

chromatics|i want your love.fact: "I Want Your Love" appears on Chromatics' 2007 album Night Drive, released through Johnny Jewel's Italians Do It Better label. The nearly seven-minute track, with vocals from Ruth Radelet, built the hazy synth sound that became the label's signature.

cocteau twins|donimo.fact: "Donimo" closes out Cocteau Twins' 1984 album Treasure, the record on which the band settled into its classic lineup of Elizabeth Fraser, Robin Guthrie, and Simon Raymonde. Treasure became the group's first album to crack the UK Top 40, with Fraser's vocals favoring invented, non-literal sounds over conventional lyrics.

courtney barnett|kim's caravan.fact: "Kim's Caravan" is the sprawling, seven-minute closing track on Courtney Barnett's 2015 debut, Sometimes I Sit and Think, and Sometimes I Just Sit. Barnett has said the song grew out of concern for the health of Australia's Great Barrier Reef, and its music video, directed by Bec Kingma, opens on a quiet, grey coastline.

drive like jehu|here come the rome plows.fact: "Here Come the Rome Plows" opens Drive Like Jehu's 1994 album Yank Crime, the band's only release for Interscope Records after signing with the major label. When Pitchfork revisited the album for its 2003 reissue, it gave the record a 9.0 and singled out the track's shift from clenched verses to wide-open choruses.

father john misty|chateau lobby #4 (in c.fact: "Chateau Lobby #4 (in C for Two Virgins)" appears on Father John Misty's 2015 album I Love You, Honeybear, built around strings, horns, and Spanish guitar. Josh Tillman shot the song's video with his wife, filmmaker Emma Tillman, on their wedding anniversary, using an iPad and a kaleidoscope filter to capture home-movie-style vacation footage.

fleet foxes|ragged wood.fact: "Ragged Wood" comes from Fleet Foxes' self-titled 2008 debut, produced by Phil Ek, a family friend who had also helped shape the band's earlier Sun Giant EP. An early version of the album was reportedly going to carry the title Ragged Wood before the band released it self-titled instead.

galaxie 500|another day.fact: "Another Day" appears on Galaxie 500's second album, On Fire, released in 1989 on Rough Trade and produced by Kramer. The Rolling Stone Album Guide later called On Fire the band's best record, and Pitchfork ranked it among the top albums of the 1980s.

interpol|obstacle 1.fact: Interpol recorded "Obstacle 1" in November 2001 at Tarquin Studios in Bridgeport, Connecticut, with producers Gareth Jones and Peter Katis. Released as the second single from 2002's Turn on the Bright Lights, Pitchfork later named it one of the best songs of the 2000s.

iron and wine|all in good time feat. fio.fact: "All in Good Time" is a duet between Iron & Wine's Sam Beam and Fiona Apple from Iron & Wine's 2024 album Light Verse. Beam has said the pairing was inspired by classic country duet teams like George Jones and Tammy Wynette, and Dolly Parton and Kenny Rogers.

jamie xx|dafodil (ft. kelsey lu john gl.fact: Jamie xx's 'Dafodil' features Kelsey Lu, John Glacier, and Panda Bear, and samples a 1973 track by R&B singer J.J. Barnes. He first played an early version of it during a 2020 BBC Radio 1 Essential Mix, and finally finishing it years later convinced him he could make a second album. It appears on his 2024 album In Waves, alongside guest spots from Robyn and his xx bandmates Romy and Oliver Sim.

khruangbin|may ninth.fact: Khruangbin's 'May Ninth' is a wistful, mid-tempo track from their 2024 album A La Sala, built on American roots-style guitar lines and airy vocals. The band wove in environmental sound, including birdsong, as texture on the recording. The lyrics capture an early-winter kind of yearning, waiting for May and summer to finally arrive.

kurt vile|another good year for the rose.fact: Kurt Vile's 'Another good year for the roses' is a cover of a country standard written by Jerry Chesnut and first made famous by George Jones. Vile's version, from his 2023 EP Back to Moon Beach, was co-produced by and features Cate Le Bon, with additional contributions from Courtney Barnett and Warpaint drummer Stella Mozgawa. The track grew out of a 2019 recording session at Stinson Beach, California.

la luz|poppies.fact: La Luz's 'Poppies,' from their 2024 Sub Pop album News of the Universe, was written by bandleader Shana Cleveland after coming through breast cancer treatment. She's described the song as capturing the surreal, dreamlike feeling of stepping back out into a bright world and noticing the season's first wildflowers bloom, like a small sense of rebirth.

lael neale|i am the river.fact: Lael Neale has described 'I Am The River' as a kind of mission statement for her album Star Eaters Delight, built on the idea of belonging to nature rather than owning it, with lines like 'I pledge allegiance to tree and meadow.' She wrote the record after moving back to her family's farm in Virginia, and it quietly weaves in nods to Shakespeare and Emerson.

lucy dacus|brando.fact: Lucy Dacus wrote 'Brando' about an intensely dramatic high school friend whose whole personality revolved around the movies and music he introduced her to. The song, from her 2021 album Home Video, is packed with classic-film references including It's a Wonderful Life, A Streetcar Named Desire, and Casablanca, built around the line, 'All I need for you to admit is that you never knew me like you thought you did.'

man man|iguana.fact: Man Man frontman Ryan 'Honus Honus' Kattner has said 'Iguana' was loosely inspired by director Werner Herzog's closing monologue in the documentary Cave of Forgotten Dreams, along with the new wave group the Flying Lizards. The song opens the band's 2024 album Carrot On Strings with a burst of freaked-out art rock.

minutemen|#1 hit song.fact: '#1 Hit Song' was written by guitarist D. Boon and drummer George Hurley for the Minutemen's sprawling 1984 double album Double Nickels on the Dime. The San Pedro, California trio recorded the record's 45 songs quickly and cheaply, and its title was itself a tongue-in-cheek jab at Sammy Hagar's complaints about the national speed limit in 'I Can't Drive 55.'

mitski|where's my phone?.fact: Mitski's 'Where's My Phone?' uses the small panic of a misplaced phone as a stand-in for a deeper craving for mental quiet in an always-connected world. It's the lead single from her 2026 album Nothing's About to Happen to Me, and it returns to the themes of identity and self that ran through earlier work like Puberty 2.

muna|silk chiffon.fact: MUNA wrote 'Silk Chiffon' as an upbeat, celebratory song about queer romance, with guitarist Naomi McPherson calling it 'a song for kids to have their first gay kiss to.' The 2021 single features Phoebe Bridgers, whose label Saddest Factory Records released it, and singer Katie Gavin has said writing it felt like a kind of second coming-out to herself.

nation of language|i've thought about ch.fact: Nation of Language's 'I've Thought About Chicago' is a wistful meditation on all the other lives you might have lived, built on frontman Ian Devaney's love of early-80s synth-pop acts like OMD. Released as a single in 2017, it later appeared on the Brooklyn trio's 2020 debut album, Introduction, Presence, and remains one of their most-streamed songs.

parquet courts|you've got me wondering n.fact: Parquet Courts' 'You've Got Me Wonderin' Now' opens their Tally All the Things That You Broke EP with fuzzed-out guitar and a tootling toy-flute solo that recalls British Invasion garage band the Troggs. The dour, sardonic track offers a glimpse of the band's early lo-fi sound, before producer Danger Mouse helped polish their approach on the following album, Wide Awake!

pavement|shoot the singer (1 sick verse).fact: Pavement's 'Shoot the Singer (1 Sick Verse)' is wordplay rather than literal violence: frontman Stephen Malkmus uses the title to poke at the idea of rock stardom itself, loosely likening a musical prodigy's status to that of a biblical figure. Released on their 1992 debut Slanted and Enchanted, it hints at Malkmus's early unease about being cast as an indie-rock figurehead, delivered with his usual deadpan humor.

perfume genius feat. aldous harding|no f.fact: 'No Front Teeth' pairs Perfume Genius (Mike Hadreas) with New Zealand singer-songwriter Aldous Harding in a delicate, tension-filled duet from Perfume Genius's 2024 album Glory. The song uses the image of losing one's baby teeth as a metaphor for the growing pains that keep showing up well into adulthood.

portishead|numb.fact: 'Numb' was the lead single from Portishead's 1994 debut album Dummy, which went on to win the 1995 Mercury Music Prize. Written and produced by the band, the moody trip-hop track was accompanied by a surreal, black-and-white short film the group directed themselves, evoking a Cold War-era, cinematic atmosphere.

r.e.m.|me in honey.fact: R.E.M. closed their 1991 album Out of Time with 'Me in Honey,' which singer Michael Stipe described as a male perspective on pregnancy. Stipe called it a kind of answer song to his friend Natalie Merchant's 10,000 Maniacs track 'Eat for Two,' which explored similar territory from a different angle. Stipe credited Merchant, a close friend at the time, as a real inspiration for his own songwriting.

radiohead|bones.fact: 'Bones' is the fifth track on Radiohead's 1995 album The Bends, built around an unusually bluesy, boogie-style beat for the band. Years later, Thom Yorke admitted the song never quite worked when they tried to play it live, joking it ended up sounding a bit like the rock band Status Quo. The drum tuning and tempo were worked out during the band's second recording stint at Oxfordshire's Manor Studio.

radiohead|creep.fact: When Radiohead first ran through 'Creep' at a rehearsal, the band considered it a throwaway track, but producers were impressed enough to record it on the spot, and the control room reportedly broke into applause afterward. Guitarist Jonny Greenwood has said his jarring guitar stabs before the chorus were originally meant to sabotage a song he didn't like, but they ended up becoming its most memorable hook. The track became Radiohead's debut single in 1992 off the album Pablo Honey.

radiohead|separator.fact: 'Separator' closes Radiohead's 2011 album The King of Limbs and was written and first performed under the working title 'Mouse, Bird, Dog.' Thom Yorke debuted an early acoustic version solo at a charity concert in Cambridge in February 2010, well before the band finished recording it for the album. Its closing lyric, 'if you think this is over, then you're wrong,' later fueled fan speculation about a possible companion release.

sleater-kinney|call the doctor.fact: Sleater-Kinney wrote the songs for their 1996 album Call the Doctor in just three weeks and recorded the whole record in only four days. It was released that March on Donna Dresch's independent label Chainsaw Records and produced by John Goodmanson, who would go on to work with the band on several later albums. The record is now regarded as a pivotal release in 1990s underground rock.

slowdive|when the sun hits.fact: 'When the Sun Hits' is a standout track from Slowdive's 1993 album Souvlaki, built on layered, reverb-soaked guitar melodies from Neil Halstead and Rachel Goswell. The song is frequently cited as one of the defining recordings of the shoegaze genre and remains a staple of the band's live sets decades later.

spoon|do i have to talk you into it.fact: 'Do I Have to Talk You Into It' is the third track on Spoon's 2017 album Hot Thoughts, which the band co-produced with Dave Fridmann. The song blends the group's indie-rock foundation with disco and electronic flourishes. Its music video, directed by Brook Linder, plays with warped, Photoshop-style visual effects layered over footage of singer Britt Daniel.

spoon|sister jack.fact: 'Sister Jack' appears on Spoon's 2002 album Kill the Moonlight, which the band recorded entirely in drummer Jim Eno's home studio. Eno, who trained as an electrical engineer, built the space himself by converting a detached garage in Austin, Texas, giving the record its stripped-down, do-it-yourself sound.

sufjan stevens|i walked.fact: 'I Walked' was released in August 2010 as an advance single ahead of Sufjan Stevens' album The Age of Adz, his first full studio album since 2005's acclaimed Illinois. The record marked a dramatic shift from his earlier orchestral folk arrangements toward electronic production, with its title and cover art inspired by the outsider artist Royal Robertson.

sugar|changes.fact: 'Changes' comes from Sugar's 1992 debut album Copper Blue, written by frontman Bob Mould and co-produced with Lou Giordano. It was one of the first songs the trio worked up in the studio, since Mould already had a ready demo for it heading into the sessions. Copper Blue went on to be named NME's Album of the Year for 1992.

television|venus.fact: 'Venus' appears on Television's influential 1977 album Marquee Moon, and an early version of the song was recorded back in December 1974 with producer Brian Eno. The final album version is often singled out as the record's most accessible track, built around a hypnotic guitar line and a melodic solo from guitarist Tom Verlaine.

the cure|push.fact: 'Push' is the fifth track on The Cure's 1985 album The Head on the Door, the first Cure record composed entirely by Robert Smith and the first to feature drummer Boris Williams. The song holds off on vocals for more than half of its four-and-a-half-minute runtime, letting the guitar and bass carry an extended instrumental build before Smith's voice finally enters.

the decemberists|traveling on.fact: 'Traveling On' is the title track of a five-song Decemberists EP released in December 2018, made up of outtakes from the sessions that produced their album I'll Be Your Girl with producer John Congleton. It's a gently rolling road song that name-checks tour stops like L.A., London, and Duluth, and it had already become a live favorite before the studio version was released.

the flaming lips|slow motion.fact: "Slow Motion" was recorded during the sessions for The Flaming Lips' 1999 album The Soft Bulletin but left off the U.S. release. It turned out to have an afterlife anyway: the band liked a drum fill from the "Slow Motion" session so much that, at Wayne Coyne's suggestion, they lifted it and dropped it straight into "Do You Realize??," which became one of the band's signature songs.

the magnetic fields|all the umbrellas in.fact: The Magnetic Fields' Stephin Merritt has said the idea for "All the Umbrellas in London" came from something refreshingly literal: it was raining, a lot, in London. Merritt built the song, which appears on the band's 1995 album Get Lost, around that city as an image of persistent, inescapable weather.

the mountain goats|andrew eldritch is mo.fact: This Mountain Goats song, the lead single from the 2017 album Goths, imagines Sisters of Mercy frontman Andrew Eldritch moving back to the English city where his band got its start. Songwriter John Darnielle started the melody on a 1973 Guild guitar at the beach, then finished writing it on piano after deciding the record would have no guitars at all; Goths was recorded at Blackbird Studios in Nashville with woodwinds arranged by Matt Douglas.

the national|fake empire.fact: "Fake Empire" opens The National's 2007 album Boxer and was recorded at Tarquin Studios with producer Peter Katis. The band wasn't sure how to end the song until Aaron Dessner recorded a horn arrangement at his home in Brooklyn for its cathartic brass finale. The song later became well known as Barack Obama's 2008 presidential campaign theme.

the replacements|i will dare.fact: "I Will Dare" opens The Replacements' 1984 album Let It Be and was written by Paul Westerberg partly as his band's answer to U2's "I Will Follow." The track features R.E.M.'s Peter Buck guesting on guitar, plus Westerberg himself playing mandolin, a pop-leaning shuffle that marked a notable step away from the band's earlier punk sound.

the strokes|heart in a cage.fact: "Heart in a Cage" is the second single from The Strokes' 2006 album First Impressions of Earth, recorded at Red Carpet Studios in New York and Allaire Studios in the Catskills with producer David Kahne. The song had actually been kicking around since the band's second album sessions under the working title "Project X" before it finally found a home.

the war on drugs|brothers.fact: "Brothers" is the second track on The War on Drugs' 2011 album Slave Ambient, written by Adam Granduciel along with bandmates Dave Hartley and Kurt Zanghi. Granduciel has said his lyrics often start as loose, semi-conscious improvisations rather than carefully plotted stories, and the song's title nods to the circle of musician friends, including Kurt Vile, who helped shape the record's hazy, textured guitar sound.

vampire weekend|unbelievers.fact: "Unbelievers" was written by Ezra Koenig and Rostam Batmanglij and produced by Batmanglij with Ariel Rechtshaid for Vampire Weekend's 2013 album Modern Vampires of the City. The band first played it live on Jimmy Kimmel Live in October 2012, months before the album came out, and it was later released as the record's third single.

violent femmes|add it up.fact: "Add It Up," from Violent Femmes' self-titled 1983 debut, has had a long second life in pop culture: Ethan Hawke's character covered it with his band in the 1994 film Reality Bites, it showed up on the soundtrack of the skateboarding video game Tony Hawk's Underground 2, and Shawn Mendes recorded his own cover, complete with a music video, for a 2016 episode of The CW's The 100.

wednesday|tv in the gas pump.fact: "TV in the Gas Pump," from Wednesday's 2023 album Rat Saw God, breaks from a typical verse-chorus structure, built instead around the repeated line "TV in the gas pump / Blares into the dark." Singer Karly Hartzman has said it's the first song she wrote about life on tour, written to collect the odd, repetitive imagery of endless gas station stops, rest-area Panera Breads, and Dollar Generals seen from the road.

ween|freedom of '76.fact: "Freedom of '76," from Ween's 1994 album Chocolate and Cheese, is a loving tribute to guitarist Aaron Freeman's hometown of Philadelphia, built as a lush, Al Green-style soul ballad with falsetto vocals and live drums from Claude Coleman Jr. The lyrics work in local landmarks like the Liberty Bell and South Street, and its music video was directed by Spike Jonze.

wet leg|pokemon.fact: "Pokemon" appears on the B-side of Wet Leg's 2025 album Moisturizer, standing out for its breezier, more nostalgic mood compared to the band's more tongue-in-cheek singles. The title comes from a playful chorus line about total devotion to another person, framed through the idea of being chosen like a Pokemon.

wilco|evicted.fact: "Evicted" comes from Wilco's 2023 album Cousin, produced by Welsh musician Cate Le Bon, whose reverberating lead guitar work gives the track its twangy character. Frontman Jeff Tweedy has described the song as being told from the point of view of someone trying to argue their way out of being shut out of someone's heart, despite knowing they probably deserve it.

yo la tengo|she may, she might.fact: "She May, She Might" is the third track on Yo La Tengo's 2018 album There's a Riot Going On. The song leans into dreamy psychedelia, with Ira Kaplan's soft vocals floating over layered guitar, airy synths, and understated rhythm.

yo la tengo|the summer.fact: "The Summer" appears on Yo La Tengo's 1990 album Fakebook, a mostly-acoustic record built largely from covers of artists like Cat Stevens, Gene Clark, and Daniel Johnston, alongside a handful of originals. "The Summer" was one of those originals, and together with their cover of Daniel Johnston's "Speeding Motorcycle," it became one of the band's first songs to reach the alternative charts.

spoon|written in reverse.fact: "Written in Reverse" comes from Spoon's Transference (2010), the first album the band produced entirely on their own, with several tracks built right off the original home demos. The song had already been a staple of Spoon's live set for over a year before they recorded it, and the studio version keeps that raw energy, pairing Britt Daniel's clanging electric guitar with Eric Harvey's piano.

beach house|drunk in la.fact: "Drunk in LA" appears on Beach House's seventh album, 7 (2018), which marked a shift in their sound after the Baltimore duo brought in Sonic Boom (Spacemen 3's Peter Kember) to help shape the record instead of their longtime producer. The song paints a picture of a faded Hollywood starlet looking back on her glory days, fitting the album's bigger, more upfront drum sound.

of montreal|wraith pinned to the mist an.fact: This breakout single from The Sunlandic Twins (2005) marked a turning point for of Montreal, bringing the band its biggest audience yet after an MTV clip helped it take off. Frontman Kevin Barnes built the song's bouncy, programmed drums using the software Reason, citing Prince and Duran Duran as touchstones for its glammy dance-pop feel.

tom waits|time.fact: "Time" is one of the standout ballads on Tom Waits' 1985 album Rain Dogs, recorded at RCA Studios in New York City. It's become one of his most enduring songs, later covered by Tori Amos on her 2001 album Strange Little Girls.

woods|moving to the left.fact: "Moving to the Left" was the lead single from Woods' 2014 album With Light and With Love, the Brooklyn band's eighth record. The song's extended instrumental jam and cleaner, sunnier production marked a noticeably more polished turn for a band usually known for its lo-fi psych-folk sound.

joanna newsom|sadie.fact: "Sadie" is the centerpiece of Joanna Newsom's 2004 debut album The Milk-Eyed Mender, and it's widely understood to have been written about her dog. The song's flowing harp-and-vocal arrangement made it one of the most beloved tracks in her catalog, later covered live by singer-songwriter M. Ward.

waxahatchee|peace and quiet.fact: "Peace and Quiet" comes from Katie Crutchfield's 2013 Waxahatchee album Cerulean Salt, which she recorded in the basement of the West Philadelphia house she shared with her twin sister Allison of the band Swearin'. The record was produced by her housemates Keith Spencer and Kyle Gilbride, who also played in Waxahatchee's touring band.

tune yards|sunlight.fact: "Sunlight" appears on tUnE-yArDs' 2009 debut album BiRd-BrAiNs, which Merrill Garbus recorded almost entirely by herself using a handheld voice recorder and a looping pedal to layer her own vocals, ukulele, and percussion. The lo-fi album was originally self-released on recycled cassette tapes before a label picked it up.

andrew bird|capsized.fact: "Capsized" was the first single from Andrew Bird's 2016 album Are You Serious, and he debuted it live on Conan before the record was even announced. On the track, Bird plays his violin two ways at once, bowing it like a violin while also plucking it guitar-style to drive the song's rock groove.

bon iver|s p e y s i d e.fact: "SPEYSIDE" was Bon Iver's first new song since 2020, released in 2024 and later included on the SABLE EP. Justin Vernon named it after Speyside, a region of the Scottish Highlands known for its whisky distilleries, and recorded the track stripped down to just his voice, acoustic guitar, and bandmate Rob Moose on viola.

margot & the nuclear so and so's|broadri.fact: "Broadripple Is Burning" takes its name from Broad Ripple, the Indianapolis neighborhood where Margot & the Nuclear So and So's played their earliest shows. The song went on to rack up millions of streams and even turned up as an audition song on American Idol, making it the band's best-known track.

rilo kiley|it's a hit.fact: "It's a Hit" appears on Rilo Kiley's 2007 album Under the Blacklight, the band's major-label debut. The record found Jenny Lewis and the band swapping their earlier indie-folk sound on Saddle Creek Records for a glossy, '70s-radio-inspired pop style influenced by acts like Fleetwood Mac and Blondie.

wilco|falling apart (right now).fact: "Falling Apart (Right Now)" was the lead single from Wilco's 2022 double album Cruel Country, the first time all six members recorded together at their Chicago studio, The Loft, since 2011's The Whole Love. The record loosely explores the history and mythology of the United States through a country-leaning sound.

cake|love you madly.fact: "Love You Madly" is from CAKE's 2001 album Comfort Eagle. The band had planned to release the title track as the first single, but switched to "Love You Madly" after deciding its airline and corporate imagery felt out of step so soon after September 11. Its music video features funk legend Rick James and comedian Phyllis Diller judging a cooking contest between band members.

mac demarco|cooking up something good.fact: "Cooking Up Something Good" opens Mac DeMarco's 2012 album 2, his breakthrough release on Captured Tracks. The slide-guitar-laced track is a wistful look back at his childhood and suburban family life, built around the hook "Mommy's in the kitchen, cookin' up something good."

car seat headrest|times to die.fact: "Times to Die" started out as a home-recorded song on one of Will Toledo's early self-released Bandcamp albums, made back when he wrote and recorded Car Seat Headrest material alone in the backseat of his car, which is how the band got its name. It was later revisited as one of ten older songs re-recorded for Teens of Style, his first release on Matador Records in 2015.

sharon van etten & the attachment theory.fact: Sharon Van Etten & The Attachment Theory recorded their self-titled debut album, including this track, at the Church Studios in London — once owned by Eurythmics — with producer Marta Salogni. It was the first time Van Etten wrote and recorded an album in full collaboration with a band rather than largely on her own; the song came together after she asked the group to simply jam, and they wrote it within about an hour.

the sisters of mercy|this corrosion.fact: "This Corrosion" was produced by Jim Steinman, the man behind Meat Loaf's "Bat Out of Hell," who brought in a 40-voice choir from the New York Choral Society to back Andrew Eldritch's gothic rock. Eldritch wanted the song to sound deliberately over-the-top, and Steinman's theatrical touch helped make it the lead single from 1987's Floodland, with the full LP version running nearly 11 minutes.

rahill|fables (feat. beck).fact: Rahill Jamalifard, frontwoman of the Brooklyn band Habibi, wrote "Fables" last for her debut solo album, Flowers at Your Feet, inspired by a summer drive through the mountains near her home. Beck contributes guitar and ethereal backing vocals to the track, which was produced by Alex Epton.

fiona apple|under the table.fact: "Under the Table," from 2020's Fetch the Bolt Cutters, was inspired by a real dinner party where Fiona Apple was expected to stay quiet after someone made an offensive comment. She turned that moment into the song's refrain, "kick me under the table all you want, I won't shut up," making it one of the album's clearest statements about refusing to be silenced in social situations.

lianne la havas|can't fight.fact: "Can't Fight" was written and recorded with producer Mura Masa in Peckham, South London, for Lianne La Havas's 2020 self-titled album. The pair were listening to the funk band Vulfpeck during the sessions, which helped shape the song's soulful, groove-heavy production.

the jesus and mary chain|far gone and ou.fact: "Far Gone and Out" was the second single from The Jesus and Mary Chain's 1992 album Honey's Dead and reached number 23 on the UK singles chart. Unlike the drum-machine sound of the band's earlier records, this track features live human percussion from drummer Monti, on loan from the band Curve, giving it a more organic groove.

thundercat & tame impala|no more lies.fact: "No More Lies" paired Thundercat with Tame Impala's Kevin Parker, who co-wrote and co-produced the track and played guitar, drums, and keyboards alongside Thundercat's falsetto and bass. Thundercat said he'd wanted to collaborate with Parker since Tame Impala's very first album, and the two finally teamed up on this funky, psychedelic single in 2023.

bjork|hyperballad.fact: "Hyperballad" was recorded for Bjork's 1995 album Post at Compass Point Studios in the Bahamas, co-produced with longtime collaborator Nellee Hooper. The song got a completely different arrangement the following year when the Brodsky Quartet reworked it with string instruments for Bjork's remix album Telegram.

grizzly bear|fine for now.fact: "Fine for Now" appears on Grizzly Bear's 2009 album Veckatimest, recorded at Allaire Studios in New York's Catskill Mountains with bassist Chris Taylor producing. True to the album's layered sound, all four band members traded off vocal duties across the record, giving tracks like this one their rich, choir-like harmonies.

big thief|mary.fact: "Mary" is named for and inspired by Adrianne Lenker's grandmother, built around warm memories of childhood winters spent at her grandparents' house. It's the only song on 2017's Capacity centered on piano and organ rather than guitar, giving it a distinct, hymn-like sound on the record.

sufjan stevens|the man of metropolis ste.fact: This track from Sufjan Stevens's 2005 album Illinois takes its title from the Man of Steel himself — Metropolis, Illinois is the only real-life Metropolis in America, and in 1972 both DC Comics and the Illinois legislature officially declared it Superman's hometown. Stevens uses the superhero as a lens for exploring love and vulnerability over the song's airy horns and strings.

radiohead|true love waits.fact: Thom Yorke first performed "True Love Waits" live back in 1995, and for over two decades it remained one of Radiohead's most famous unreleased songs, known only through bootlegs and a 2001 live recording. The band finally settled on a finished arrangement — a stripped-down piano ballad — as the closing track of 2016's A Moon Shaped Pool.

wild nothing|chinatown.fact: "Chinatown" comes from Wild Nothing's 2010 debut album Gemini and remains the project's most-streamed song by a wide margin. Frontman Jack Tatum has described it as an autobiographical snapshot from that period of his life, built on the reverb-soaked, jangly guitar sound that helped define the early-2010s dream-pop revival.

r.e.m.|losing my religion.fact: Peter Buck wrote the music for "Losing My Religion" almost by accident: after playing guitar for hours on end, he picked up a mandolin he'd just bought, and a riff came together with a tape recorder rolling in about five minutes. Both his mandolin part and Michael Stipe's vocal were captured in a single take, and the title itself is actually a Southern US expression for losing one's patience, not a reference to literal religion.

the olivia tremor control|hideaway.fact: "Hideaway" appears on The Olivia Tremor Control's 1999 album Black Foliage: Animation Music, Vol. 1. Within the Athens, Georgia band's experimental Elephant 6 catalog, the song stands out as a sunny, Beach Boys-inspired pop tune, sung by co-founder Bill Doss, which offers a bright counterpoint to the album's more avant-garde sound collages.

the waterboys|the whole of the moon.fact: Mike Scott wrote the key line of "The Whole of the Moon" — "I saw the crescent, you saw the whole of the moon" — almost spontaneously while walking near New York's Gramercy Park Hotel in early 1985, after his girlfriend asked if songwriting came easily to him. The song, from This Is the Sea, is a tribute to a mix of inspiring figures Scott admired, including writer C.S. Lewis and musician Prince, and has since been covered by artists ranging from Prince himself to U2 and the Killers.

toro y moi|empty nesters.fact: "Empty Nesters" was the lead single from Toro y Moi's 2015 album What For?, which Chaz Bear wrote and recorded over eight months at his home studio in Berkeley, California. It's one of his most guitar-driven, rock-leaning tracks, with critics comparing its sunny jangle to bands like Pavement before it breaks into a funky instrumental turn. The album marked his follow-up to 2013's Anything in Return.

alabama shakes|dunes.fact: "Dunes" is the third track on Alabama Shakes' 2015 album Sound & Color, which the band pieced together over four two-week recording sessions at Nashville's Sound Emporium before a final mixing stop at Ocean Way Recording in Los Angeles. Sound & Color debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and picked up four Grammy nominations, including Album of the Year.

smog|let's move to the country.fact: "Let's Move to the Country" first appeared on Bill Callahan's 1999 album Knock Knock, recorded under his old moniker Smog as just voice and guitar. Two decades later, Callahan revisited the song for his 2020 solo album Gold Record, giving it a fuller, more contented acoustic arrangement and even tweaking a few lines. It's a rare case of an artist formally re-recording and updating one of his own older songs on a later album.

the mountain goats|the legend of chavo g.fact: This Mountain Goats song is a tribute to real-life lucha libre star Chavo Guerrero Jr., whom frontman John Darnielle has called a childhood hero. It appears on 2015's wrestling-themed album Beat the Champ, and Guerrero — son of lucha libre legend Gory Guerrero — actually appeared in the song's music video, throwing a body slam and a moonsault alongside the band.

iggy pop|the passenger.fact: Iggy Pop wrote the lyrics to "The Passenger" over music composed by guitarist Ricky Gardiner, drawing partly on a Jim Morrison poem that pictured modern life as a journey by car, as well as Pop's own rides on Berlin's S-Bahn train line. It was recorded at Hansa Studio by the Wall in West Berlin for the 1977 album Lust for Life, which Pop made with David Bowie during their shared time living in the city.

avalon emerson|dreamliner.fact: "Dreamliner" is track six on & the Charm, the 2023 debut album from DJ and producer Avalon Emerson's live band project, Avalon Emerson & the Charm. The record was co-produced with Bullion and features playing from Emerson's wife, Hunter Lombard, marking a deliberate shift from her club-oriented dance records toward warmer, song-based dream pop.

belle and sebastian|this letter.fact: "This Letter" comes from the soundtrack Belle and Sebastian wrote for Days of the Bagnold Summer, the 2019 directorial debut of actor Simon Bird, best known for The Inbetweeners. The hushed track is built around little more than Stuart Murdoch's voice, a plucked acoustic guitar, and a muted trumpet solo over a gentle bossa nova beat.

chromatics|on the wall.fact: "On the Wall" is Chromatics' cover of a song originally by Scottish noise-pop band the Jesus and Mary Chain. It appears on Chromatics' 2019 album Closer to Grey, their first LP in seven years, where Ruth Radelet's cool vocal delivery is layered over the original's fuzzed-out, '80s college-rock guitar sound.

lucy dacus|bullseye.fact: "Bullseye" is a duet between Lucy Dacus and Hozier from her 2025 solo album Forever Is a Feeling. The two first connected when Hozier joined Dacus's band boygenius onstage in Boston in 2023, and they later filmed a performance of "Bullseye" together for the Irish music show Other Voices at the National Gallery of Ireland in Dublin.

dummy|mono retriever.fact: "Mono Retriever" is a 2022 single the L.A. band Dummy recorded for Sub Pop's Singles Club 7-inch series, paired on the B-side with another new track, "Pepsi Vacuum." The band has described the two songs as mirrors of each other, built around droning organ and cycling, hypnotic rhythms in the style of their noise-pop and early-electronic-psychedelia influences.

tom waits|ol' '55.fact: "Ol' '55" opens Tom Waits's 1973 debut album, Closing Time, and takes its title from a 1955-model car Waits once owned. The song got a career boost the following year when the Eagles covered it on their album On the Border — even though Waits himself initially joked their version was "a little antiseptic" compared to his own.

jay som|1 billion dogs.fact: "1 Billion Dogs" is the fourth track on Jay Som's 2017 debut album, Everybody Works. Its quirky title comes from the rough estimate of how many dogs are alive on Earth at any given time, and the song wraps that offbeat idea in Melina Duterte's signature fuzzy guitars and warm, layered vocals.

the clash|the magnificent seven.fact: The Clash built "The Magnificent Seven" around a funky bassline from session player Norman Watt-Roy and recorded it at New York's Electric Lady Studios in 1980 after guitarist Mick Jones became fascinated with early hip-hop acts like the Sugarhill Gang and Grandmaster Flash & the Furious Five. Released on 1980's Sandinista!, it's often cited as one of the first rap-influenced songs by a rock band, predating Blondie's "Rapture" by months — and Grandmaster Flash himself was known to spin it in New York clubs.

bat for lashes|sunday love.fact: "Sunday Love" comes from Natasha Khan's (Bat for Lashes) 2016 album The Bride, and was co-written and produced with Dan Carey, the London producer behind records by Hot Chip, Franz Ferdinand, and Fontaines D.C. Carey also runs the influential label Speedy Wunderground, and the pair had collaborated with him on other sessions around the same period.

cherry glazerr|wasted nun.fact: "Wasted Nun" opens Cherry Glazerr's 2019 album, Stuffed & Ready, which was produced by Carlos de la Garza, also known for his engineering work on Paramore's After Laughter. The band actually scrapped an earlier version of the whole album and re-recorded every song from scratch with de la Garza, and this track's crunchy guitar tone echoes earlier Cherry Glazerr favorites like "Nurse Ratched."

animal collective|strung with everything.fact: "Strung With Everything" opens Animal Collective's 2022 album Time Skiffs, their eleventh studio LP for Domino Records. The nearly seven-minute track was released as the album's lead single in January 2022 and blends sitar textures and gamelan-style percussion with sunny, Beach Boys-esque vocal harmonies.

david byrne|what is the reason for it? (.fact: This duet with Paramore's Hayley Williams comes from David Byrne's 2025 album Who Is the Sky?, his first full album since 2018's American Utopia. Byrne simply texted Williams to ask if she'd sing on the track, and later said "she killed it." The record was produced by Kid Harpoon and arranged with the New York chamber group Ghost Train Orchestra.

turnstile|blackout.fact: "Blackout" was the third single from Turnstile's breakout 2021 album Glow On. The Baltimore hardcore band builds the song around a slow, polyrhythmic groove before it explodes into one of their most anthemic choruses, and Pitchfork later named it one of the best tracks of that year.

cake|sheep go to heaven.fact: "Sheep Go to Heaven" comes from CAKE's third album, 1998's Prolonging the Magic. Released as a single in 1999, it climbed to number 16 on the Modern Rock Tracks chart and stuck around for 14 weeks, with trumpeter Vince DiFiore's horn line giving the track its signature country-funk CAKE sound.

baio|dead hand control.fact: Chris Baio, the bassist of Vampire Weekend, made his third solo album Dead Hand Control partly at Damon Albarn's 13 Studios in London, finishing it at a Los Angeles studio he co-founded with Vampire Weekend bandmate Chris Tomson. The closing track, "O.M.W.," was co-written with fellow Vampire Weekend member Ezra Koenig.

car seat headrest|america (never been).fact: "America (Never Been)" comes from Car Seat Headrest's 2014 EP How to Leave Town, which Will Toledo wrote, recorded, and self-released on Bandcamp. At over seven minutes, it closes out what turned out to be his last do-it-yourself solo release before he expanded Car Seat Headrest into a full band and signed to Matador Records the following year.

greg freeman|point and shoot.fact: "Point and Shoot" opens Vermont songwriter Greg Freeman's 2025 album Burnover. It was recorded with producer Benny Yurco at his Little Jamaica studio in Burlington, filled out by Freeman's friends from the local music scene, including Cam Gilmour on horns and Ben Rodgers on pedal steel. Freeman has said the record is very much "a byproduct of Burlington."

saintseneca|uppercutter.fact: "Uppercutter" came out in October 2013 as a 7-inch single, the first taste of Saintseneca's Anti- Records debut Dark Arc, which followed in April 2014. The Columbus, Ohio band paired the song with a music video that Stereogum premiered ahead of the album's release.

weyes blood|do you need my love.fact: "Do You Need My Love?" was the second single from Weyes Blood's 2016 album Front Row Seat to Earth, her fourth record and first for Mexican Summer. The six-minute track builds from a hushed opening into a sweeping, string-laden finale.

kurt vile|i'm an outlaw.fact: "I'm an Outlaw" is the second track on Kurt Vile's 2015 album b'lieve i'm goin down..., released on Matador Records. The song opens on a drum machine before shifting into some of the cleanest banjo playing on the record, part of what Vile described as a more insular, intimate sound for that album.

sufjan stevens|a little lost.fact: Sufjan Stevens covered Arthur Russell's 1994 song "A Little Lost" for the 2014 various-artists tribute compilation Master Mix: Red Hot + Arthur Russell on Yep Roc Records. The two-disc set gathered more than 20 artists, including Hot Chip, Blood Orange, and Robyn, each reinterpreting one of Russell's songs, and Stevens traded the original's hushed chamber-pop for a bigger, more orchestral arrangement.

jungle|back on 74.fact: "Back On 74" was the fourth and final single from Jungle's 2023 album Volcano. Its one-take music video, choreographed by Shay Latukolan and filmed with 18 dancers at London's Alexandra Palace, went viral on TikTok in late 2023 as fans around the world learned the routine, and the song got an extra boost from a performance at the 2024 Brit Awards.

tops|icu2.fact: "ICU2" is the song TOPS used to announce their signing to Ghostly International in April 2025, shortly after debuting it live at Coachella. It appears on Bury the Key, the Montreal band's first full-length since 2020, self-produced by singer Jane Penny and guitarist David Carriere, and the band has described the track as pure flirtation born from a playful exchange between Penny and bandmate Marta Cikojevic.

talking heads|the good thing.fact: "The Good Thing" comes from Talking Heads' 1978 album More Songs About Buildings and Food, recorded in the Bahamas with producer Brian Eno. For the song's call-and-response backing vocals, the band recruited two of the studio's secretaries, who ended up credited on the record as part of "Tina and the Typing Pool" alongside bassist Tina Weymouth.

local natives|breakers.fact: "Breakers" opens Local Natives' 2012 album Hummingbird, which the band co-produced with Aaron Dessner of The National, who's also credited as a co-writer on this track. Critics at the time pointed to Dessner's and The National's fingerprints on the song's driving drums and widescreen sound, and Pitchfork named it a Best New Track on release.

beach house|wildflower.fact: "Wildflower" appears on Beach House's 2015 album Depression Cherry. After touring behind their previous record with a full live drum kit, Victoria Legrand and Alex Scally said they got tired of it and deliberately built this album back around drum machines and simpler, stripped-down arrangements instead. It was recorded with longtime producer Chris Coady at a studio in Bogalusa, Louisiana.

alex g|june guitar.fact: "June Guitar" is a single from (Sandy) Alex G's 2025 album Headlights, his first release on a major label after a decade of putting out music independently and through Domino. The track was co-produced by Alex G and Jacob Portrait, bassist for Unknown Mortal Orchestra, and Alex G performed it live on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon around the album's release.

built to spill|goin' against your mind.fact: "Goin' Against Your Mind" opens Built to Spill's 2006 album You in Reverse and runs nearly nine minutes long, by far the longest and most guitar-heavy track the band had put on a studio record up to that point. It's built around interlocking solos from the band's three-guitar lineup, led by Doug Martsch.

dr. dog|army of ancients.fact: "Army of Ancients," from Dr. Dog's 2008 album Fate, was written by bassist Toby Leaman as a song about complacency — what happens when people let others do their thinking for them. Leaman has said he wrote it by trying to recall old Aesop's fables and Bible stories dealing with those themes and turning them into rhyming lyrics.

ween|someday.fact: "Someday" started as a Ween outtake from the early-2000s sessions for their album Quebec before the band finally gave it a proper studio version for their 2005 rarities collection Shinola, Vol. 1. It's one of the more straightforwardly sweet, melodic songs in the band's catalog, built around hope and finding love rather than the weirder territory Ween is often known for.

cocteau twins|blue bell knoll.fact: The title track of Cocteau Twins' 1988 album Blue Bell Knoll marked the first time the band ever recorded in a studio of their own, September Sound in Twickenham, London. Bassist Simon Raymonde later said having "our own key and a front door we could shut" changed how freely the band could work, and the album became their first to crack the Billboard 200 in the US.

tame impala|why won't you make up your m.fact: "Why Won't You Make Up Your Mind?" was recorded during the sessions for Tame Impala's 2010 debut album Innerspeaker at Wave House studio in Injidup, Western Australia. At three minutes and nineteen seconds, it's the shortest song on the record, but it's remained one of the few Innerspeaker-era tracks Kevin Parker still plays live today.

grizzly bear|wasted acres.fact: "Wasted Acres," the opening track on Grizzly Bear's 2017 album Painted Ruins, grew out of a surprisingly down-to-earth memory — guitarist Daniel Rossen has said the song started from trying to keep track of a hound dog while hauling firewood on an ATV out in rural upstate New York.

angel olsen|stars.fact: "Stars" appears on Angel Olsen's 2014 breakthrough album Burn Your Fire for No Witness, which was produced by John Congleton and recorded in a former church that had been converted into a recording studio in Asheville, North Carolina. It's one of the album's full-band rock moments, built around chiming electric guitars and a driving rhythm section.

the clash|hitsville u.k..fact: "Hitsville U.K.," from The Clash's 1980 triple album Sandinista!, is a duet between guitarist Mick Jones and singer Ellen Foley. Its title plays on Motown's old "Hitsville U.S.A." nickname, and the lyrics name real British independent record labels of the era — including Rough Trade, Factory, Small Wonder, and Fast Product — as a tribute to the scrappy, DIY label scene of the time.

unknown mortal orchestra|american guilt.fact: The guitar riff driving Unknown Mortal Orchestra's "American Guilt," from 2018's Sex & Food, had been kicking around far longer than the song itself. Ruban Nielson has said he first came up with it years earlier during his time fronting the New Zealand punk band The Mint Chicks, long before Unknown Mortal Orchestra existed, and it simply never found the right song until this one.

pavement|frontwards.fact: "Frontwards" is the second track on Pavement's 1992 EP Watery, Domestic, which was the band's first release featuring bassist Mark Ibold and percussionist Bob Nastanovich and its last with original drummer Gary Young. The song has since been covered by both Los Campesinos! and former Walkmen frontman Hamilton Leithauser.

alex g|sportstar.fact: "Sportstar" is a piano-driven single Alex G released ahead of his 2017 album Rocket, where it appears as track eight. The song stands out for its glossy, polished production compared to the lo-fi home recordings of his earlier career, and its chorus repeats the declarative refrain "I play how I wanna play, I say what I wanna say."

alex g|taking.fact: "Taking" is the fifth track on Alex G's 2019 album House of Sugar, which he began writing in Philadelphia right after touring behind his breakout album Rocket. The song's sparse lyrics repeat just a couple of phrases, and his vocals are blended so tightly with the synthesizer that the track can sound almost entirely instrumental.

alvvays|easy on your own.fact: Alvvays' song is officially titled "Easy on Your Own?" (with a question mark) and appears as the second track on the band's 2022 album Blue Rev. Singer Molly Rankin wrote it about feeling unmoored after leaving school, opening with the line "I dropped out of college, education's a dull knife."

american football|never meant.fact: "Never Meant" opens American Football's self-titled 1999 debut album and is built around an intricate, interlocking guitar riff played in an unusual open tuning and a 12/8 time signature. Decades later the song's gentle opening riff became a popular internet meme, and in 2019 Vulture ranked it the single greatest emo song ever recorded.

andy shauf|spanish on the beach.fact: "Spanish on the Beach" is the second track on Andy Shauf's 2021 album Wilds, a collection of home demos he recorded in 2018 during the same sessions that produced his concept album The Neon Skyline. Set to gentle, jazzy guitar and woodwinds, the song follows Judy, a recurring character in Shauf's songwriting, as she and her companion navigate a language barrier on a tropical vacation.

angel olsen|give it up.fact: "Give It Up" appears on Angel Olsen's 2016 album My Woman and is one of three short, loud, uptempo tracks that give the record's first half its garage-rock energy. Critics have compared its raw, driving sound to grunge bands like Nirvana, a contrast to the more orchestral songs that make up the album's second half.

anna burch|jacket.fact: "Jacket" is a track from Anna Burch's 2020 album If You're Dreaming, which blends 1950s doo-wop melodies with jangly college-rock guitars. The lyrics are built around a simple, relatable image: a jacket an ex-boyfriend left behind.

architecture in helsinki|heart it races.fact: "Heart It Races" was released as a single by the Australian band Architecture in Helsinki in 2007, built around a steel-drum-heavy, percussion-driven melody. The single release included remix and cover treatments by the bands Dr. Dog, Hey Willpower, and YACHT.

arctic monkeys|i bet you look good on th.fact: Arctic Monkeys' debut single "I Bet You Look Good on the Dancefloor" hit number one on the UK Singles Chart in October 2005 before the band had even released a studio album. They had already built a grassroots following by giving away CDs of the song at their own concerts and letting fans trade it online months before its official release.

arlo parks|caroline.fact: Arlo Parks wrote "Caroline," from her 2021 debut album Collapsed in Sunbeams, after witnessing about 30 seconds of an argument between a couple on Oxford Street in London. She imagined the rest of their story from that brief glimpse, turning the moment into a song about watching a relationship fall apart from the outside.

band of horses|the funeral.fact: "The Funeral," from Band of Horses' 2006 debut album Everything All the Time, was recorded in Seattle with producer Phil Ek. Despite its title, the song became one of the most licensed indie-rock tracks of its era, turning up in countless films, TV shows, and ads, getting sampled by Kid Cudi, and receiving an official dance remix from producer Gryffin in 2025.

beach fossils|tangerine.fact: "Tangerine" appears on Beach Fossils' 2017 album Somersault and features guest vocals from Rachel Goswell of the shoegaze band Slowdive. The track also adds a full string arrangement, a departure from the stripped-down guitar sound of the band's earlier records.

beck|fix me.fact: "Fix Me" closes out Beck's 2017 album Colors and plays as a kind of melancholy counterpoint to Coldplay's hit "Fix You." Its string arrangement was composed by Beck's father, the veteran orchestral arranger David Campbell.

belle and sebastian|funny little frog.fact: "Funny Little Frog" was released as a single from Belle and Sebastian's 2006 album The Life Pursuit and became the band's highest-charting UK single, peaking at number 13. Produced by Tony Hoffer, the song later appeared in a different arrangement on Stuart Murdoch's 2009 soundtrack album God Help the Girl.

big thief|los angeles.fact: "Los Angeles" is from Big Thief's 2025 album Double Infinity, recorded at the Power Station studio in New York City. Built around acoustic guitar and layered harmonies, the song is about former romantic partners who have settled into a lasting friendship.

black midi|953.fact: "953" is the noisy, largely instrumental opening track on black midi's 2019 debut album Schlagenheim. Built from abrupt math-rock tempo shifts and heavily filtered, distorted guitar tones, the track sets the chaotic, high-energy tone for the rest of the record.

bon iver|holyfields,.fact: "Holyfields," is a short, atmospheric track from Bon Iver's 2019 album i,i, which the band recorded partly at their home studio in Wisconsin and partly during extended sessions in West Texas. The song's spiky synthesizer pulse echoes minimalist composer Steve Reich, and the backing group known as the Justin Vernon Singers joins partway through for a swelling, choir-like lift.

bully|prism.fact: "Prism," from Bully's 2020 album Sugaregg, was the longest song the band had released at that point and marks a slower, more atmospheric turn from their usual grunge-leaning sound. The track builds from quiet verses into an anthemic, guitar-driven chorus.

car seat headrest|something soon.fact: "Something Soon" started as a lo-fi home recording before Car Seat Headrest's Will Toledo reworked it with a full band for the 2015 album Teens of Style, a collection of re-recorded older songs. The studio version turns the original bedroom-pop sketch into a blown-out, four-on-the-floor power-pop track.

cheekface|hard mode.fact: "Hard Mode" is a standalone single the Los Angeles band Cheekface released in December 2024, produced and recorded by Greg Cortez. It features the band's full lineup of guitarist-vocalist Greg Katz, bassist Amanda Tannen, and drummer Mark Edwards.

cherry glazerr|nuclear bomb.fact: "Nuclear Bomb" is a track from Cherry Glazerr's 2017 album Apocalipstick, released via Secretly Canadian. It was the third song shared ahead of the record, and the band made a music video for it featuring frontwoman Clementine Creevy spending a day around L.A.'s Echo Park with her guitar.

courtney barnett|write a list of things.fact: Courtney Barnett's "Write A List Of Things To Look Forward To," from her 2021 album Things Take Time, Take Time, takes its title from a simple technique a friend once suggested: writing down small, good things to anticipate. Barnett has described the song as a kind of love letter to friendship, and its video shows her sending and receiving a series of handmade gifts and letters.

cut worms|song of the highest tower.fact: Cut Worms' "Song of the Highest Tower" appeared on the 2017 EP Alien Sunset, released through Jagjaguwar. Its title nods to 19th-century French poet Arthur Rimbaud's "Chanson de la plus haute tour," from his book A Season in Hell. Cut Worms is the project of Brooklyn-based songwriter Max Clarke, who named the band itself after a line in William Blake's "Proverbs of Hell."

deep sea diver|what do i know.fact: "What Do I Know" comes from Deep Sea Diver's 2025 album Billboard Heart on Sub Pop. It was the first song for which bandleader Jessica Dobson engineered every instrument herself at her home studio; she originally thought she was just recording a demo, so most of what made the final cut are first takes, imperfections included.

deerhunter|he would have laughed.fact: "He Would Have Laughed" closes out Deerhunter's 2010 album Halcyon Digest. While most of the record was tracked at Chase Park Transduction in Athens, Georgia with producer Ben H. Allen, frontman Bradford Cox recorded this song separately at Notown Sound in Marietta before the rest of the band joined partway through, shifting the track into a looser, dreamier second half.

destroyer|painter in your pocket.fact: "Painter in Your Pocket" is a track from Destroyer's 2006 album Destroyer's Rubies. It opens with a stark acoustic guitar figure that blooms into one of the catchiest, bounciest moments in Dan Bejar's catalog, built around a "Whiter Shade of Pale"-style organ line that critics have singled out as a highlight of the record.

destroyer|rubies.fact: "Rubies" is the nearly ten-minute title track that opens Destroyer's 2006 album Destroyer's Rubies. Dan Bejar, also known for his work with The New Pornographers, builds the song from gossamer acoustic guitar into a full-band, nautical-feeling epic, one of ten sprawling tracks across the album's 53 minutes.

devo|beautiful world.fact: DEVO's "Beautiful World" was written by Gerald Casale and Mark Mothersbaugh and released as the second single from their 1981 album New Traditionalists. Rage Against the Machine later recorded a slower, more somber cover of the song for their 2000 covers album Renegades, the last album that band released.

drive like jehu|luau.fact: "Luau" is the sprawling, nearly nine-and-a-half-minute third track on Drive Like Jehu's 1994 album Yank Crime, the San Diego post-hardcore band's major-label debut for Interscope. Rocket From the Crypt's Rob Crow contributed backing vocals, and years later guitarist Rick Froberg's next band, Hot Snakes, would occasionally revive "Luau" in their live sets.

dum dum girls|coming down.fact: "Coming Down" was issued as a standalone single in July 2011 ahead of Dum Dum Girls' sophomore album, Only in Dreams, released that September on Sub Pop. Early pressings and pre-orders of the album came packaged with a 7" of the track, and Only in Dreams remains the only Dum Dum Girls album to feature all four members of that era's lineup.

fleet foxes|mykonos.fact: "Mykonos" started out as a 1960s-style soul song built around big piano chords, written by Robin Pecknold. After finishing their debut album, Fleet Foxes reworked it into the layered, harmony-driven sound fans know, releasing it on the 2008 Sun Giant EP, produced by Phil Ek. It has since become one of the band's most frequently played live songs.

galaxie 500|decomposing trees.fact: "Decomposing Trees" appears on Galaxie 500's 1989 album On Fire, widely regarded as the Boston trio's finest record. The album was produced by Kramer, with Dean Wareham on vocals and guitar, Damon Krukowski on drums, and Naomi Yang on bass.

grizzly bear|little brother.fact: "Little Brother" appears on Grizzly Bear's 2006 album Yellow House, named for the actual yellow house on Cape Cod belonging to singer Ed Droste's mother, where most of the record was made in a makeshift home studio. The song's live arrangement in particular became known as a highlight of the band's early shows.

hum|iron clad lou.fact: "Iron Clad Lou" opens Hum's second album, Electra 2000, self-released in 1993 on 12 Inch/Cargo Records before the Champaign, Illinois band signed to RCA for 1995's You'd Prefer an Astronaut. The song, which runs just under six minutes, got its own music video and was reissued as part of a 2021 remaster campaign.

idles|the beachland ballroom.fact: "The Beachland Ballroom" is named after the real concert venue in Cleveland, Ohio, and marked a surprising stylistic turn for IDLES into neo-soul territory. The song appears on 2021's Crawler, recorded at Real World Studios in Bath and co-produced by Kenny Beats alongside the band's own guitarist, Mark Bowen.

japanese breakfast|picture window.fact: "Picture Window" appears on Japanese Breakfast's 2025 album For Melancholy Brunettes (& Sad Women), produced by Blake Mills at the famed Sound City studio in Los Angeles - the first time the band recorded in a traditional studio after years of working out of warehouses, lofts, and trailers. Frontwoman Michelle Zauner directed the song's music video herself, filming it on location in Seoul.

joanna newsom|sprout and the bean.fact: "Sprout and the Bean" was the only single from Joanna Newsom's 2004 debut album, The Milk-Eyed Mender, released on Drag City. Pitchfork later ranked it among its list of the 2000s' best songs, and the track has since been covered by other acts, including The Moscow Coup Attempt and Sholi.

khruangbin|pelota.fact: "Pelota" was the third single from Khruangbin's 2020 album Mordechai. The Houston, Texas trio - known for blending global influences despite having a Thai-inspired band name - sang the song in Spanish, where "pelota" means "ball" and also names a traditional Basque sport. Its animated video follows a human figure flying through surreal, geometric landscapes.

king gizzard & the lizard wizard|i'm in.fact: "I'm in Your Mind" is the sprawling opening suite of King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard's fifth album, I'm in Your Mind Fuzz (2014). It was the Melbourne band's first record made in a professional studio, with sessions held at Daptone Studios in Brooklyn, and was written and produced by guitarist Stu Mackenzie.

king gizzard & the lizard wizard|planet.fact: "Planet B" was released in April 2019 as the first single from King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard's album Infest the Rats' Nest. The track marked a sharp genre detour for the Australian band into thrash metal, with critics likening its riffs to early Metallica, and it was written and produced by Stu Mackenzie.

kurt vile|jesus fever.fact: "Jesus Fever" opens Kurt Vile's 2011 album Smoke Ring for My Halo, recorded at the Magic Shop studio in New York City with producer John Agnello. Its breezy, pastoral folk arrangement stood out from Vile's usual fuzzed-out guitar rock, drawing comparisons to the Feelies and the mellower side of R.E.M.

low|dinosaur act.fact: "Dinosaur Act" appears on Low's 2001 album Things We Lost in the Fire, recorded with engineer Steve Albini at his Electrical Audio studio in Chicago. The track broke from the Duluth, Minnesota band's famously slow, minimal style with pounding, timpani-like drums and a horn section, giving the slowcore pioneers one of their most hummable choruses.

lucy dacus|vbs.fact: Lucy Dacus's "VBS," from her 2021 album Home Video, takes its title from Vacation Bible School, a summer program she attended often growing up. She wrote the song in the van on the way to Nashville to record the album, after a church reader board advertising a kids' camp jogged memories of her childhood summers.

mazzy star|halah.fact: "Halah" opens Mazzy Star's 1990 debut album She Hangs Brightly, recorded at Hyde Street Studios in San Francisco with producer David Roback. The song found new life in 1995, when it was reissued as a single on the strength of "Fade into You" and climbed to No. 19 on Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks chart.

my morning jacket|mahgeetah.fact: "Mahgeetah" opens My Morning Jacket's 2003 album It Still Moves, the Louisville band's major-label debut. Like much of their early catalog, Jim James recorded his vocals through the natural echo of a converted grain silo on his family's Kentucky farm, giving the song its cavernous reverb.

my morning jacket|what a wonderful man.fact: "What a Wonderful Man" is a short, high-energy rocker from My Morning Jacket's 2005 album Z, the record that saw the band shift toward a more polished sound with synthesizer and reggae touches. Critics have pointed to its big double-guitar riffing as a nod to power-pop acts like Big Star.

nation of language|the grey commute.fact: "The Grey Commute" appears on A Way Forward (2021), the second album by Brooklyn synth-pop trio Nation of Language. The band built the song's hypnotic, mechanized rhythm as a tribute to pioneering electronic acts like Kraftwerk and Ultravox.

of montreal|suffer for fashion.fact: "Suffer for Fashion" is the propulsive opening track of of Montreal's 2007 album Hissing Fauna, Are You the Destroyer?, widely regarded as a landmark release for the Athens, Georgia band. It begins with a gently strummed acoustic guitar before erupting into a synth-driven disco stomp that sets the tone for the record's genre-blending sound.

ora the molecule|prince of the rhythm.fact: "Prince of the Rhythm" is the fourth track on Dance Therapy (2025), the second album from Norwegian artist Nora Schjelderup's project Ora the Molecule. She wrote, recorded, and produced nearly all of the record herself, drawing inspiration from Italian disco star Raffaella Carrà and the vintage synthesizer sounds of Mort Garson's Mother Earth's Plantasia.

parquet courts|content nausea.fact: "Content Nausea" is the title track of Parquet Courts' 2014 album, released under the band's tongue-in-cheek alter ego Parkay Quarts after two members were largely unavailable to record. Guitarists Andrew Savage and Austin Brown wrote, played, and recorded the entire LP - including cover songs - on a four-track cassette machine in under two weeks.

pavement|silence kid.fact: "Silence Kid" opens Pavement's 1994 album Crooked Rain, Crooked Rain. An ink smudge on the original artwork mangled the song's printed title into "Silence Kit," a misnomer that stuck on later reissues even though the liner notes and Stephen Malkmus's own handwritten lyric sheet show the correct name.

public image ltd.|public image.fact: "Public Image" was the debut single by Public Image Ltd, the band John Lydon formed after leaving the Sex Pistols in 1978. Both the group's name and the song were inspired by Muriel Spark's 1968 novel The Public Image, and the single reached No. 9 on the UK Singles Chart.

quivers|never be lonely.fact: "Never Be Lonely" opens Oyster Cuts (2024), the third album from Quivers, a four-piece band based in Melbourne, Australia, with roots in Tasmania. The track pairs a thumping bassline with a sunshine-soaked, 80s-influenced dream-pop sound.

r.e.m.|get up.fact: Michael Stipe wrote "Get Up," from R.E.M.'s 1988 album Green, as a gentle jab at bandmate Mike Mills, who tended to sleep late during recording sessions - though Mills reportedly didn't realize the song was about him until Stipe announced it at a concert years later. Its chiming bridge features a dozen music boxes played at once, an idea drummer Bill Berry said came to him in a dream.

radiohead|let down.fact: "Let Down," from Radiohead's 1997 album OK Computer, was recorded in the ballroom of St Catherine's Court, a historic manor house the band rented near Bath, England.
