The eerie blips at the song's end were made with a ZX Spectrum, a vintage home computer the members had played with as kids, and guitarist Jonny Greenwood performs his part in a different time signature from the rest of the band.

radiohead|sail to the moon. (brush the c.fact: Officially titled "Sail to the Moon. (Brush the Cobwebs Out of the Sky.)," this track appears on Radiohead's 2003 album Hail to the Thief, where nearly every song carries a parenthetical alternate title. The band recorded the album in about two weeks at Ocean Way Recording in Los Angeles, aiming for a live, spontaneous feel inspired by Neil Young and Crazy Horse.

real estate|flowers.fact: "Flowers" comes from Real Estate's sixth studio album, Daniel (2024), which the band recorded in about two weeks at the famed RCA Studio A in Nashville with producer Daniel Tashian, known for his work on Kacey Musgraves' Golden Hour. It was the first Real Estate album to feature drummer Sammi Niss, and the band has said the plain, human album title was picked partly because it seemed funny.

ride|vapour trail.fact: "Vapour Trail" closes Ride's 1990 debut album Nowhere, recorded at Blackwing Studios in London when the band members were just 20 years old. Guitarist Andy Bell reportedly wrote the song in a single afternoon without realizing how good it was until much later. In 2015, to mark the album's 25th anniversary, The Cure's Robert Smith created an extended remix of the track.

samia|north poles.fact: "North Poles" appears on Samia's third studio album, Bloodless (2025). Samia has said some of the record's most personal moments, including this track, were shaped by her close friendship with fellow musician Raffaella, and that her songwriting style favors elusive, poetic vignettes over literal storytelling.

sasami|honeycrash.fact: "Honeycrash" was released in 2024 as the first single from SASAMI's third album, Blood on the Silver Screen, two years after her 2022 album Squeeze. The music video was directed by Andrew Thomas Huang, who built its look around sweeping American-West imagery and the road movie Thelma & Louise.

sea lemon|crystals (feat. benjamin gibba.fact: Seattle dream-pop artist Natalie Lew records as Sea Lemon, and "Crystals" pairs her with Death Cab for Cutie's Benjamin Gibbard over shimmering, fuzzed-out pop production. The two became friends after Gibbard invited Lew to join him performing a cover of The Vaselines' "Son of a Gun" at a Sub Pop tribute show.

siouxsie and the banshees|arabian knight.fact: "Arabian Knights" was released as a single from Siouxsie and the Banshees' 1981 album Juju, recorded at Surrey Sound Studios with co-producer Nigel Gray. The track is especially noted for guitarist John McGeoch's unconventional playing, long cited by critics as a highlight of the band's post-punk sound.

spoon|wild.fact: "Wild" comes from Spoon's tenth studio album, Lucifer on the Sofa (2022), and was first released exclusively on vinyl ahead of the full album. Frontman Britt Daniel plays out an Old West fantasy in the song's black-and-white music video, directed by Ben Chappell and Brook Linder.

sugar|if i can't change your mind.fact: "If I Can't Change Your Mind" was the fourth single from Sugar's 1992 debut album, Copper Blue, written by frontman Bob Mould and co-produced with Lou Giordano. Copper Blue was voted Album of the Year by NME in 1992 and remains one of the most successful projects of Mould's career after Hüsker Dü.

tame impala|the moment.fact: "The Moment" appears on Tame Impala's 2015 album Currents, a stylistic turn toward synth-driven pop for mastermind Kevin Parker. As with the rest of the record, Parker wrote, played, recorded, and mixed nearly every part of the song himself in his home studio in Fremantle, Australia.

tanlines|the big mess.fact: The title track opens Tanlines' 2023 album The Big Mess, the duo's first release for Merge Records and first new album in eight years. Members Eric Emm and Jesse Cohen made the record after both became fathers and took time away from the band, with Emm writing much of the material from Connecticut.

television|friction.fact: "Friction" appears on Television's influential 1977 debut album, Marquee Moon. The track showcases the interlocking, dueling guitar style of Tom Verlaine and Richard Lloyd, who favored intricate, winding melodic lines over the simple power chords common among their punk and new-wave contemporaries.

the afghan whigs|conjure me.fact: "Conjure Me" was released as a single from The Afghan Whigs' 1992 album Congregation, the Cincinnati band's third record. Pianist Shecky Stein guested on the track, adding to the album's soul-influenced sound, and it's remembered as one of the strongest anthems of the band's early career.

the black keys|10 a.m. automatic.fact: "10 A.M. Automatic" comes from The Black Keys' 2004 album Rubber Factory, which the Akron, Ohio duo recorded inside an actual abandoned tire factory using a reel-to-reel recorder loaded with tape recycled from old fried-chicken commercials. The song later turned up in the video game MLB 06: The Show and on the TV series The O.C.

the black keys|thickfreakness.fact: The title track of The Black Keys' 2003 album Thickfreakness was recorded, along with most of the record, during a single 14-hour session in drummer Patrick Carney's basement on an 8-track recorder. Guitarist Dan Auerbach has said they tracked it live in one day and added just a couple of overdubs the next.

the clash|the guns of brixton.fact: "The Guns of Brixton," from The Clash's 1979 album London Calling, was written and sung by bassist Paul Simonon, the first Clash song on which he took lead vocals. Its dub-inspired bassline later became famous in its own right when it was sampled for Beats International's 1990 UK number-one single, "Dub Be Good to Me."

the cure|close to me.fact: The video for The Cure's "Close to Me," from 1985's The Head on the Door, was directed by longtime collaborator Tim Pope and shows the band crammed into a wardrobe perched on the edge of a cliff at Beachy Head. Pope based the concept on a dream Robert Smith described, in which he was shut in a closet that toppled off a cliff into the sea.

the fall|totally wired.fact: "Totally Wired" was released as a Fall single in September 1980 on Rough Trade, written by Mark E. Smith with bandmates Marc Riley, Craig Scanlon, and Steve Hanley. It reached number two on the UK Independent Singles Chart and later appeared on reissues of the band's album Grotesque (After the Gramme).

the flaming lips|buggin'.fact: "Buggin'" appears on The Flaming Lips' 1999 album The Soft Bulletin, recorded over nearly two years at Tarbox Road Studios in Cassadaga, New York, with producers Dave Fridmann and Scott Booker. Rather than tracking a live orchestra, the band built the album's lush sound by layering and detuning multiple MIDI keyboards, and the song later appeared as a bonus "Mokran remix" on some reissues.

the magnetic fields|fear of trains.fact: "Fear of Trains" is track seven on The Magnetic Fields' 1994 album The Charm of the Highway Strip, a concept record where, per frontman Stephin Merritt, virtually every song deals with roads and travel. It was also the first full-length Magnetic Fields album on which Merritt sang lead vocals on every track, and he designed the cover art himself.

the magnetic fields|promises of eternity.fact: "Promises of Eternity," sung by Stephin Merritt on the second volume of 69 Love Songs (1999), got its backing tracks and arrangement from guest contributor Chris Ewen, who also added theremin to another track on the triple-length record. The sprawling 69-song set was inspired by composer Charles Ives's 114 Songs and became the album that broke the band out of the underground.

the magnetic fields|you must be out of y.fact: "You Must Be Out of Your Mind" opens The Magnetic Fields' 2010 album Realism, which Stephin Merritt called his "folk album" and which completed a self-imposed "no-synth trilogy" following i and Distortion. The largely acoustic record swaps the band's usual drum machines for instruments like dulcimer, giving the opening track a stripped-down, chamber-pop feel.

the national|secret meeting.fact: "Secret Meeting" opens The National's 2005 album Alligator and was written by Aaron Dessner and Scott Devendorf with lyrics by Matt Berninger; the album was recorded at several Connecticut studios with producers Peter Katis and Paul Mahajan. It was later issued as its own single in August 2005, paired with a remix and a live recording of "The Geese of Beverly Road."

the national|start a war.fact: "Start a War" is the eighth track on The National's 2007 album Boxer, written by Matt Berninger and Aaron Dessner. The record was recorded at Peter Katis's Tarquin Studios in Bridgeport, Connecticut, and went on to become one of the most critically acclaimed indie rock albums of 2007.

the replacements|unsatisfied.fact: "Unsatisfied" was written solely by Paul Westerberg for The Replacements' 1984 album Let It Be, recorded at Blackberry Way Studios in Minneapolis. It was one of the first songs Westerberg wrote specifically on acoustic guitar, and though never released as a single, it has grown into one of the band's most acclaimed and frequently played live songs.

the smiths|william, it was really nothin.fact: Released in August 1984, "William, It Was Really Nothing" was written by Johnny Marr and Morrissey and recorded in just days at Jam Studios in London with producer John Porter. At barely over two minutes, its brevity was intentional - Marr wanted to see if a single that short could still work - and it reached number 17 on the UK charts, backed by the classic B-side "How Soon Is Now?"

the sophs|death in the family.fact: The Sophs are a six-piece built around a core of childhood friends from Phoenix, Arizona, who later relocated to Los Angeles and added a Florida-born drummer to round out the lineup. Frontman Ethan Ramon cold-emailed demos to Rough Trade Records founders Geoff Travis and Jeannette Lee without expecting a reply - the label signed the band within a day.

the strokes|machu picchu.fact: "Machu Picchu" opens The Strokes' 2011 album Angles, the first record the band wrote collaboratively as a group rather than having frontman Julian Casablancas write everything alone. The song was later released as the album's third single and featured on the soundtrack to EA Sports' FIFA 12.

the strokes|soma.fact: "Soma," from The Strokes' 2001 debut Is This It, takes its title from Aldous Huxley's 1932 novel Brave New World, which features a fictional mood-regulating substance of the same name used throughout that book's dystopian society. The album was produced by Gordon Raphael at Transporterraum studios in New York City over a six-week stretch in early 2001.

the white stripes|death letter.fact: "Death Letter" is The White Stripes' cover of a Delta blues standard first recorded by Son House in 1965 for Columbia Records, where House played it on a metal-bodied resonator guitar with a slide. Jack White has said discovering Son House's recordings as a teenager changed how he approached music, and the White Stripes dedicated their 1999 debut album to him before cutting their own version of "Death Letter" for 2000's De Stijl.

tv on the radio|family tree.fact: "Family Tree" is track six on TV on the Radio's 2008 album Dear Science, written by Tunde Adebimpe and running five and a half minutes. The album was recorded in Brooklyn at Stay Gold Studio with producer David Andrew Sitek, whose dense, orchestral layering gives this ballad a noticeably different texture from the record's funkier, horn-driven tracks.

wallows|are you bored yet? (feat. clairo.fact: Released in February 2019 as the lead single from Wallows' debut album Nothing Happens, "Are You Bored Yet?" was written by Dylan Minnette, Braeden Lemasters, Cole Preston, and guest vocalist Clairo (Claire Cottrill), whom the band knew through mutual friends before inviting her into the studio. Producer John Congleton helmed the track, which went on to be certified quadruple-platinum by the RIAA.

wild nothing|live in dreams.fact: "Live in Dreams" opens Wild Nothing's 2010 debut album Gemini, released on Captured Tracks. The project is the work of one musician, Jack Tatum, who wrote and largely self-produced every track on the record, drawing on the shimmering guitar sounds of early-1980s dream-pop and post-punk acts like New Order.

wipers|over the edge.fact: The Wipers formed in Portland, Oregon in 1977 around guitarist and songwriter Greg Sage, and by their 1983 album Over the Edge the band had shifted from straightforward punk into a tighter, heavily distorted post-punk sound. Kurt Cobain cited the Wipers as a major influence, and Hole later covered the album's title track both in the studio and live.

yo la tengo|autumn sweater.fact: "Autumn Sweater" was released as a single on April 15, 1997, from Yo La Tengo's album I Can Hear the Heart Beating as One. It was recorded at House of David studio in Nashville with longtime producer Roger Moutenot, whose work helped broaden the band's sound into bossa nova-inflected textures and electronic grooves.

dry cleaning|hit my head all day.fact: "Hit My Head All Day" opens Dry Cleaning's third album, Secret Love, and was produced by Cate Le Bon. During the demo stage the track actually had a harmonica part instead of vocals, and the band has cited Sly and the Family Stone's classic record "There's a Riot Goin' On" as a sonic touchstone while making the album.

wolf alice|white horses.fact: "White Horses" is the one song on Wolf Alice's 2025 album The Clearing where drummer Joel Amey takes the lead vocal, with singer Ellie Rowsell joining him for a duet. Amey wrote the lyrics about family and belonging after a car ride with his mom, aunt, and sister got him thinking about what "home" really means.

beach house|take care.fact: "Take Care" closes out Beach House's 2010 album Teen Dream and, at 5 minutes 48 seconds, is the longest song on the record. The Baltimore dream-pop duo built the track around a simple synth line and electronic percussion before bringing in a live drum kit and piano for the chorus, and the song later turned up on the soundtrack to the 2020 film Chemical Hearts.

sylan esso|wdid.fact: Sylvan Esso formed in Durham, North Carolina, after singer Amelia Meath asked producer Nick Sanborn to remix one of her songs and the two realized their styles clicked. The duo released "WDID" as a 12-inch single, backed with "Keep On," through Psychic Hotline, the independent label they run themselves.

big thief|little things.fact: Big Thief recorded "Little Things" with engineer Shawn Everett at Five Star Studios in Topanga, California, with the band's own drummer, James Krivchenia, producing. It was released as a surprise single alongside "Sparrow" in 2021 before landing as track seven on the band's 2022 double album Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe in You.

westside cowboy|can't see.fact: "Can't See" is the second single from UK band Westside Cowboy's EP So Much Country 'Til We Get There. It was recorded on the very first day of sessions with producer Loren Humphrey, who has also worked with Arctic Monkeys and Lana Del Rey, and the band says it was the first song they tore apart and rebuilt, right down to adding a conga breakdown.

the war on drugs|burning.fact: "Burning" is track eight on The War on Drugs' 2014 album Lost in the Dream, clocking in at 5 minutes 48 seconds. A decade later, the band revisited the song for their 2024 live album Live Drugs Again, recorded across tour stops in the US, UK, Europe, and Australia between 2022 and 2023.

sasami|slugger.fact: "Slugger" is the lead single from SASAMI's third album, Blood on the Silver Screen, co-produced by Jenn Decilveo and Rostam and released in 2025. Over a shuffling drum groove, she flips the old saying "better to have loved and lost than never loved at all" on its head, using it as a jumping-off point for some sharp self-reflection.

sweet pill|starchild.fact: "Starchild" is the title track of Sweet Pill's 2024 EP, which followed the Philadelphia band's 2021 debut album Where the Heart Is and their signing to Hopeless Records. Singer Zayna Youssef has said the song is about the pressure of people-pleasing and carrying other people's expectations, and that its danceable groove marked a new sound for the band.

melody's echo chamber|daisy (feat. el mi.fact: "Daisy" is a collaboration between French psych-pop artist Melody's Echo Chamber and the soul-funk group El Michels Affair, built on shifting key changes and winding, Hendrix-inspired guitar lines. The song was co-written with producer Leon Michels, who has also worked with Clairo and Norah Jones, and mixed by Grammy winner Jens Jungkurth.

phantogram|earthshaker.fact: "Earthshaker" is a 2025 single from New York duo Phantogram, who built the track's groove around late-1960s-style drum breaks and vintage guitar textures. The band has described the resulting sound as landing somewhere between old soul music and Krautrock.

beck|walking light.fact: Beck's "Waking Light" closes his 2014 album Morning Phase, which went on to win the Grammy Award for Album of the Year in 2015, upsetting favorites like Beyonce and Sam Smith. The record earned Beck three Grammys that night in total, also taking home Best Rock Album and Best Engineered Album, Non-Classical.

sufjan stevens|run away with me.fact: "Run Away With Me" is the second track on Sufjan Stevens' 2020 album The Ascension, a record where he set aside the acoustic guitars and orchestral strings of his earlier work in favor of synthesizers and programmed drum machines. The song's reverb-drenched, overlapping vocals ride an upbeat groove that marks a notable departure from his folkier material.

the national|the alcott (feat. taylor sw.fact: "The Alcott" pairs The National's Matt Berninger with Taylor Swift as two voices meeting up at a hotel bar, on the band's 2023 album First Two Pages of Frankenstein. Berninger has said the song's perspective was inspired by his own marriage, with Swift taking on the other half of the conversation.

beirut|gibraltar.fact: "Gibraltar" opens Beirut's 2015 album No No No, trading the band's earlier horn-heavy arrangements for a sparer, more pared-down sound. Its music video follows frontman Zach Condon and the band wandering a stark, fictional version of Gibraltar on a quest to find "the Rock," doubling as a visual nod to caring for the natural world.

spiritualized|a perfect miracle.fact: "A Perfect Miracle" opens Spiritualized's 2018 album "And Nothing Hurt" with gentle ukulele strums and swelling strings, as frontman Jason Pierce sings the romantic line "take the stars and line them up to spell darling I love you." The album's title is deliberately left incomplete — it's the back half of a line from Kurt Vonnegut's novel "Slaughterhouse-Five": "Everything was beautiful, and nothing hurt."

belle and sebastian|sister buddha.fact: "Sister Buddha" became the lead single from Belle and Sebastian's soundtrack to the 2020 film "Days of the Bagnold Summer," based on Joff Winterhart's graphic novel. Frontman Stuart Murdoch had written the song independently of the movie, but director Simon Bird chose it to close the film because he wanted an uplifting final note, and its title nods to Murdoch's longtime interest in Buddhism.

anna burch|quit the curse.fact: Anna Burch named her 2018 debut solo album "Quit the Curse" as a tongue-in-cheek jab at romantic superstition, joking in interviews about being "a cursed Cancer" under astrology. Burch had spent years singing in Frontier Ruckus before stepping out with songs of her own on the record.

cherry glazerr|rabbit hole.fact: Released as a standalone single in December 2020, "Rabbit Hole" marked a turn toward electronic textures for Cherry Glazerr, built around a sample of The Moderations' "All Because of You" and inspired by producers like DJ Koze, Caribou, and Kaytranada. Singer Clementine Creevy has described the song as being about reclaiming your own identity after losing it to conformity.

spoon|i turn my camera on.fact: "I Turn My Camera On," from Spoon's 2005 album "Gimme Fiction," began as a spare home demo built around nothing but acoustic guitar, xylophone, and Britt Daniel's vocal. Daniel has said the song is about reaching a kind of emotional distance from the world, and he was confident enough in the track to push it as the album's lead single over the label's preference for "Sister Jack."

fontaines d.c.|before you i just forget.fact: "Before You I Just Forget" started out as the B-side to the "It's Amazing to Be Young" single before landing on the 2025 deluxe edition of Fontaines D.C.'s acclaimed album "Romance." Produced by James Ford, the track builds and shifts throughout before closing with a string arrangement written by frontman Grian Chatten.

bon iver|if only i could wait (feat. dan.fact: "If Only I Could Wait," a duet between Justin Vernon and Danielle Haim, traces back to a snowstorm in February 2022 that stranded the two musicians together at Vernon's studio. That unplanned session became a starting point for Bon Iver's 2025 album "SABLE, fABLE," and the song was released as an early single alongside "Walk Home."

radiohead|bullet proof..i wish i was.fact: "Bullet Proof..I Wish I Was," from Radiohead's 1995 album "The Bends," is one of the record's most stripped-down tracks, built around hushed acoustic guitar layered with echo and sustain effects under producer John Leckie. Its simple, campfire-style arrangement has made it a favorite choice for solo and acoustic covers in the decades since.

interpol|nyc.fact: "NYC" was one of Interpol's earliest songs, first appearing in re-recorded form on the band's self-titled 2002 EP — their debut release for Matador Records. The same recording later appeared on their breakthrough album "Turn On the Bright Lights" later that year.

interpol|pda.fact: Interpol didn't print lyrics inside their debut album "Turn On the Bright Lights," leaving fans to puzzle out Paul Banks' famously opaque words in "PDA" on their own, including the cryptic line "sleep tight, grim rite, we have two hundred couches where you can sleep tonight." The band eventually posted official lyrics on their website, partly to help non-English-speaking fans in Europe follow along.

whitney|dandelions.fact: On "Dandelions," from Whitney's 2025 album "Small Talk," Julien Ehrlich's falsetto glides over Max Kakacek's slide guitar in a return to the duo's Americana roots. Ehrlich has said the song grew out of a stretch when he and Kakacek were both navigating relationships that fell apart around the same time, which they spun into a story about a city dweller returning home to the Midwest.

phantastic ferniture|change my mind.fact: "Change My Mind" marked the return of Phantastic Ferniture, the Sydney band fronted by Julia Jacklin, after a long gap following their 2018 self-titled debut. Released as a 2022 single alongside "Dare to Fall in Love," it was co-written with Thomas Capell and recorded at Golden Retriever Studios, with the band expanding to a quartet with new bassist Harrison Fuller.

pure carrire|farfouiller.fact: Despite the stylized spelling, the artist behind "Farfouiller" is properly known as Pure Carriere, the project of Quebec musician Jean-Michel Letendre Veilleux. The song, an ode to quiet boredom with loose, playful guitar lines, appears on Pure Carriere's 2025 album "Visions de l'enfer," reflecting the project's deliberately imperfect, DIY approach to indie rock.

runo plum|lemon garland.fact: "Lemon Garland" is the second track on "Patching," the debut album from runo plum, an indie folk-rock artist raised in rural Minnesota. The song arrived as a single in mid-2025 shortly after she signed to the record label Winspear, ahead of the full album's release that November.

westerman|about leaving.fact: "About Leaving," from Westerman's 2025 album "A Jackal's Wedding," is a ruminating, piano-led track with echoes of Arthur Russell and the Beta Band. Westerman wrote the lyrics in fragments while traveling between London, the U.S., and Greece, and that constant movement became the animating idea behind the song's imagery of departure.

tv on the radio|shout me out.fact: "Shout Me Out" appears on TV on the Radio's 2008 album Dear Science and is one of the record's most dynamic tracks, building from a sweet vocal melody into a frantic, horn-driven romp. For the album, the Brooklyn band enlisted the Afrobeat horn section Antibalas to add brassy punch to several songs, helping push Dear Science toward a more danceable sound than the group's earlier records.

cate le bon|jerome.fact: "Jerome" opens Cate Le Bon's 2024 album Michelangelo Dying, a record she wrote and recorded in the wake of a breakup with a longtime musical collaborator. The song eases listeners in with a hypnotic wash of shimmering guitars, setting the dreamy, melancholic tone that runs through the rest of the album.

beach house|master of none.fact: "Master of None" comes from Beach House's self-titled 2006 debut album and was released as a promotional single the following year, complete with two different music videos. The dreamy duo's early funk-tinged track later found new life when it was sampled by The Weeknd and used in the Netflix series "The Future."

the fall|frightened.fact: "Frightened" appears on The Fall's 1979 debut album Live at the Witch Trials, whose title is a bit of a trick: despite sounding like a concert recording, it was actually tracked entirely in a single day in a London studio. Critic Dave McCullough of Sounds magazine called the song "a breathtaking, ominously culminating monster."

nation of language|i'm not ready for the.fact: "I'm Not Ready for the Change" is from Nation of Language's 2025 album Dance Called Memory, the Brooklyn synth-pop trio's fourth record and first for the legendary Sub Pop label. The song's chopped-up drum breaks and glittering arpeggiated synths accompany lyrics about a group of old friends who've all drifted onto separate paths in life.

beat happening|our secret.fact: "Our Secret" was one of the very first songs Beat Happening recorded, laid down in December 1983 at an old, abandoned fire station on the edge of Washington's Evergreen State College campus. It became the band's debut single on the K Records cassette label before later appearing on their self-titled 1985 album.

the smiths|heaven knows i'm miserable no.fact: The Smiths wrote "Heaven Knows I'm Miserable Now" in just about an hour, with Johnny Marr composing the music in a New York City hotel room in January 1984. Its title was a playful nod to Sandie Shaw's 1969 single "Heaven Knows I'm Missing Him Now," and when released that May it became the band's first song to crack the UK Top 10.

the smiths|some girls are bigger than ot.fact: "Some Girls Are Bigger Than Others" closes out The Smiths' acclaimed 1986 album The Queen Is Dead, following the epic "There Is a Light That Never Goes Out." Engineer Stephen Street gave the track its distinctive sound by drenching the drums in reverb so they seemed to echo through a huge hall, then quickly fading it down as the song begins.

dinosaur jr.|freak scene.fact: "Freak Scene" opens Dinosaur Jr.'s 1988 album Bug and was recorded at Fort Apache Studios with engineers Paul Q. Kolderie and Sean Slade. The track, packed with two blistering guitar solos from J Mascis, is widely credited as a key bridge between 1980s indie rock and the grunge sound that followed, with Pitchfork once calling it indie rock's greatest guitar performance.

alabama shakes|i found you.fact: "I Found You" comes from Alabama Shakes' 2012 debut album Boys & Girls, which went on to earn the Athens, Alabama band multiple Grammy nominations and platinum certification. The twangy, feel-good track leans on call-and-response vocals and gospel-style backing harmonies that channel vintage 1960s soul.

spoon|do you.fact: "Do You" was the first single released from Spoon's 2014 album They Want My Soul, the Austin band's comeback record after a four-year break. Produced by Joe Chiccarelli alongside the band, the song is a breezy slice of power-pop built on a skipping acoustic guitar riff and playful "do-do" and "ah-ah" vocal hooks.

benjamin booker|show and tell.fact: "Show and Tell" appears on Benjamin Booker's 2025 album Lower, his first full-length in eight years following 2017's Witness. Produced by Kenny Segal, the track strips things down to an acoustic setting, blending cosmic soul and folk-style storytelling to let Booker's raspy croon take center stage.

blondshell|23's a baby.fact: "23's a Baby" is a single from Blondshell (Sabrina Teitelbaum) that layers harmonies into a girl-group-style chant reminiscent of "Be My Baby." The song reflects on the pressures of your twenties, when you're expected to have life figured out yet still feel like you're just getting started; Teitelbaum has said the song is ultimately about finding compassion rather than casting blame.

courtney barnett|stay in your lane.fact: "Stay In Your Lane" appears on Courtney Barnett's 2026 album Creature of Habit. Rather than aiming at someone else, the song is a gentle self-talk track, with Barnett repeating "please be patient" as a reminder not to rush through big changes in life.

perfume genius|wreath.fact: For "Wreath," off Perfume Genius's 2017 album No Shape, Mike Hadreas turned the song's music video into a true fan collaboration: he launched an open call asking listeners to film themselves dancing to the track, then compiled the submissions into the final video. It's part of Hadreas's long-running interest in dance and movement, an interest that later grew into a full stage collaboration with choreographer Kate Wallich.

boygenius|ketchum, id.fact: "Ketchum, ID" closes out boygenius's self-titled 2018 EP, the first release from the indie-rock trio of Julien Baker, Phoebe Bridgers, and Lucy Dacus. Built around hushed, close three-part harmonies, the song imagines trading the exhausting life of a touring musician for a simpler one in Ketchum, the small Idaho mountain town where novelist Ernest Hemingway spent his final years. It's a fantasy of quitting the road entirely, dressed up in gentle, Americana-tinged folk.

zzzahara|bulletproof (feat. mareux).fact: "Bulletproof" paired rising singer-songwriter zzzahara with producer and vocalist Mareux after zzzahara had kept Mareux's track "Perfect Girl" on repeat for about a year and reached out to collaborate. The session was reportedly Mareux's first time recording in a professional studio, and both artists have said the writing process flowed naturally, with zzzahara calling the moment their two voices overlapped on the chorus "dark, powerful, and moving."

car seat headrest|ccf (i'm gonna stay wi.fact: "CCF (I'm Gonna Stay With You)" comes from Car Seat Headrest's 2025 rock-opera album The Scholars, set at a fictional school called Parnassus University. The song follows one of the record's student characters, Beolco, who believes he's spiritually connected to the university's long-dead founder, a playwright known as the Scop, and it arrived with an animated video continuing the band's elaborate world-building for the album.

english teacher|the world's biggest pavi.fact: English Teacher's "The World's Biggest Paving Slab" was inspired by singer Lily Fontaine's hometown of Colne in East Lancashire, which claims to be home to the world's biggest paving slab. Fontaine has said the song examines "delusions of grandeur and inferiority from the perspective of a small town's local celebrities," and its video traces real locations from her own history up to nearby Pendle Hill. Released in 2023, it was the Leeds band's first single after signing to Island Records.

hippo campus|yippie ki yay.fact: "Yippie Ki Yay" comes from Hippo Campus's 2023 EP Wasteland, which leans hard into Western and cowboy imagery. The band has pointed to the 1936 standard "I'm an Old Cowhand (From the Rio Grande)" as a touchpoint for the song's tone, and the track is structured as a story within a story, with each chorus zooming out from an outlaw character to the perspective of the people narrating his tale.

this heat|paper hats.fact: "Paper Hats" appears on This Heat's 1981 album Deceit, most of which the band recorded inside Cold Storage, a disused refrigerated storeroom at a former meat pie factory in Brixton, London. With the power not yet hooked up, the trio initially worked by torchlight, and they modeled their round-the-clock rehearsal-and-recording routine on the German band Can's own private studio.

variety|plover.fact: "Plover" is the debut single from the Austin band variety, led by former Borzoi drummer Rhys Woodruff, who stepped out from behind the kit to write, perform, and record the song largely on his own. Named after the shorebird, the track is described by the band as "an homage to ornithology," exploring how a dog, a fisherman, and a conservationist can each want something completely different from the same bird.

king gizzard & the lizard wizard|the spi.fact: "The Spider and Me" appears on King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard's 2017 collaborative album Sketches of Brunswick East, made with Los Angeles musician Mild High Club. The gentle, trippy track imagines an affectionate bond between a person and a huntsman spider, a large but harmless species known for wandering into Australian homes, framing humans and arachnids as simply "from the same cloth."

vampire weekend|giving up the gun.fact: Vampire Weekend's "Giving Up the Gun," from 2010's Contra, takes its title from historian Noel Perrin's 1979 book Giving Up the Gun: Japan's Reversion to the Sword, a copy of which was given to frontman Ezra Koenig by his father. The book examines how Japan deliberately phased out firearms between the 16th and 19th centuries in favor of the traditional sword, and the phrase stuck with Koenig as a striking real example of a culture turning away from a dominant technology. The song's music video grew out of an unrelated image Koenig had of a friend playing tennis against a samurai.

the tallest man on earth|the gardener.fact: "The Gardener" appears on The Tallest Man on Earth's 2008 debut album, Shallow Grave, the first release from Swedish singer-songwriter Kristian Matsson under that stage name. The moniker is an inside joke of sorts: Matsson stands at an unremarkable 5-foot-7, and he's said he simply needed "a stupid name" when he began performing solo after leaving his earlier band, the Montezumas. The hushed, fingerpicked record drew early comparisons to a young Bob Dylan.

geese|cobra.fact: "Cobra" is a 2026 single from Brooklyn band Geese, released alongside "Au Pays du Cocaine" as a follow-up to their 2025 album Getting Killed. It was recorded during intensive sessions at Putnam Hill Studio in Los Angeles with producer Kenneth Blume (Kenny Beats) and the band, and compared to the album's heavier material, "Cobra" takes a noticeably relaxed approach, built on interlocking guitar melodies and breezy, Beach Boys-adjacent textures.

portishead|mysterons.fact: "Mysterons" opens Portishead's 1994 debut album, Dummy, taking its title from the Martian villains of the 1967 British sci-fi puppet show Captain Scarlet and the Mysterons. The eerie opening line sounds like a theremin but is actually a keyboard synthesizer tuned to mimic one, a classic trick for conjuring vintage sci-fi atmosphere, and the track helped define the moody, cinematic "trip-hop" sound that emerged from Bristol, England in the early 1990s.

r.e.m.|cuyahoga.fact: R.E.M.'s "Cuyahoga," from their 1986 album Life's Rich Pageant, is named for the Cuyahoga River, which flows through Cleveland, Ohio. The song nods to the river's real history of industrial pollution so severe it famously caught fire on several occasions, most notably in 1969, an event that helped spur the creation of the U.S. Clean Water Act. The music was written by bassist Mike Mills and drummer Bill Berry, though it's credited to the full band.

vegyn|the path less travelled.fact: "The Path Less Travelled" opens Vegyn's 2024 album The Road to Hell Is Paved With Good Intentions. Reviewers have described it as a vaporous, trippy piece of vintage-sounding electronica, built on a skittering beat and warped, garbled tape-delay trails. The London producer, born Joseph Thornalley and best known for his production work with Frank Ocean, built the record with a cast of collaborators including Ethan P. Flynn, Lauren Auder, and Matt Maltese.

arctic monkeys|brianstorm.fact: Arctic Monkeys' "Brianstorm," the lead single from 2007's Favourite Worst Nightmare, is named after a real person: a smooth, LA-styled stranger who left a strong impression on the band backstage after a show in Osaka, Japan. Frontman Alex Turner has said that once the man left the room, the band immediately held a "brainstorm" session about him, complete with a drawing, which became the pun behind the title. The track's blunt, breakneck energy signaled a louder, harder-edged direction for the band.

guided by voices|chasing heather crazy.fact: "Chasing Heather Crazy" was released as a single off Guided by Voices' 2001 album Isolation Drills, produced by Rob Schnapf (known for his work with Beck and Elliott Smith). TVT Records reportedly didn't think the song was strong enough to push as a single, despite its huge, Hollies-meets-Raspberries pop hooks. The band brought it back into regular rotation in their live sets starting in 2019.

manchester orchestra|the silence.fact: "The Silence" closes out Manchester Orchestra's 2017 album A Black Mile to the Surface, a loosely conceptual record inspired by the real mining town of Lead, South Dakota. The album's title nods to the Sanford Underground Research Facility there, home to a neutrino experiment located nearly a mile beneath the surface. The nearly seven-minute closer builds from a quiet, hushed opening into one of the band's biggest, most expansive arrangements.

martin courtney|corncob.fact: "Corncob" is the lead single and opening track from Real Estate frontman Martin Courtney's second solo album, Magic Sign, released in 2022. The song introduced the record with feathery slide guitar and one of Courtney's breeziest melodies, and its music video accompanied the album's announcement.

the strokes|is this it.fact: The title track of The Strokes' 2001 debut was tracked with a deliberately minimal setup by producer Gordon Raphael, who used just one microphone each for vocals and snare drum to preserve the band's raw live sound. Julian Casablancas originally wrote the song without a chorus and only later improvised singing the title phrase over the music to finish it, then picked that same phrase as the album's title because he thought it sounded cool without being pretentious.

wilco|i'm always in love.fact: On Wilco's 1999 album Summerteeth, "I'm Always in Love" was largely built in the studio by Jeff Tweedy and multi-instrumentalist Jay Bennett, who is credited with bass, drums, piano, and keyboards on the track. Its rhythm-heavy, piano-driven groove borrows a few tricks from the Velvet Underground's "I'm Waiting for the Man," and the song was later mixed at Ocean Way Recording in Hollywood.

bright eyes|hot knives.fact: "Hot Knives," from Bright Eyes' 2007 album Cassadaga, was produced by Mike Mogis and features a stacked guest list: guitarist M. Ward, drummer Janet Weiss of Sleater-Kinney and Quasi, and backing vocals from Rachael Yamagata, Z Berg, and sisters Sherri and Stacy DuPree of Eisley. A string arrangement conducted by Bill Meyers rounds out the song's lush, choir-backed sound.

le tigre|deceptacon.fact: "Deceptacon" opens Le Tigre's self-titled 1999 debut album, the first release from the band Kathleen Hanna formed with Johanna Fateman and Sadie Benning after the breakup of her previous band, Bikini Kill. The track's stripped-down, danceable energy made it an instant anthem, and the album went on to be ranked among the best of its decade by outlets like Pitchfork and Spin.

the mountain goats|onions.fact: "Onions" appears on The Mountain Goats' 2000 album The Coroner's Gambit, which came together after John Darnielle went a full year without a release for the first time since starting the project. Like several other tracks on the record, it was recorded in singer-songwriter Simon Joyner's home studio in Omaha, Nebraska, continuing Darnielle's early habit of recording wherever he could set up a cassette deck.

the mountain goats|woke up new.fact: "Woke Up New" appears on The Mountain Goats' 2006 album Get Lonely, a hushed record built around sparse acoustic guitar and upright bass rather than the band's usual boisterous energy. Written entirely by John Darnielle, the track's gentle, murmured arrangement set the tone for the rest of the album.

nick cave and the bad seeds|henry lee.fact: "Henry Lee," from Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds' 1996 album Murder Ballads, is a duet with PJ Harvey and the first time this centuries-old folk ballad had ever been recorded as a male-female duet. Cave's vocal was tracked at studios in Melbourne while Harvey recorded her part separately in London, with bandmate Blixa Bargeld even singing a guide vocal on the demo sent to her. Cave and Harvey got to know each other during these sessions, and by the time they filmed the song's music video together, the two had begun a real-life relationship.

beach house|hurts to love.fact: "Hurts to Love" appears on Beach House's 2022 album Once Twice Melody, which the duo released in four chapters over several months before combining them into a full 18-track record. The song sits in the album's final chapter and leans into a synthpop sound, layering glossy keyboard tones over the band's signature wash of organ and reverb.

beach house|silver soul.fact: "Silver Soul" comes from Beach House's 2010 album Teen Dream, recorded at Dreamland, a studio set in a converted church in upstate New York, with producer Chris Coady (known for his work with TV on the Radio and Yeah Yeah Yeahs). The song's warm, gospel-tinged sound later caught the ear of Kendrick Lamar, who sampled it for "Money Trees" on his 2012 album good kid, m.A.A.d city.

the beths|expert in a dying field.fact: "Expert in a Dying Field" is the title track of The Beths' third album, released in September 2022. Frontwoman Elizabeth Stokes came up with the wry title phrase to describe how much accumulated knowledge of another person, their favorite movies, their habits, their sense of humor, becomes strangely useless once a relationship or friendship changes.

future islands|long flight.fact: "Long Flight," the second track on Future Islands' 2010 album In Evening Air, opens with a sample of real audio from the launch of Space Shuttle Columbia on April 12, 1981, the first orbital shuttle flight ever flown. The clip was originally recorded off the TV by the band's own bassist, William Cashion, long before Future Islands existed, and it resurfaced on the track as a dramatic intro.

the decemberists|california one / youth.fact: "California One/Youth and Beauty Brigade" closes out The Decemberists' 2002 debut album, Castaways and Cutouts, shifting from a gentle, country-tinged ballad into a horn-and-cymbal-driven finale. The album's title is actually drawn from a line in this very song, and its hopeful, forward-looking lyrics about youthful possibility were written as a deliberate contrast to the more somber character sketches that fill the rest of the record.

unknown mortal orchestra|multi-love.fact: For Unknown Mortal Orchestra's 2015 album Multi-Love, bandleader Ruban Nielson built much of the record from scratch in his Portland basement studio, tracking down and rewiring broken vintage 1970s synthesizers to chase the analog sounds of Bowie, Eno, and krautrock records. He eventually brought in his brother Kody Nielson, bassist Jacob Portrait, drummer Riley Geare, and even his father, jazz trumpeter Chris Nielson, to help fill out the arrangements.

sharon van etten|mistakes.fact: "Mistakes" comes from Sharon Van Etten's 2022 album We've Been Going About This All Wrong, which she recorded and engineered largely herself at her new home studio in Los Angeles with co-producer Daniel Knowles. Van Etten played much of the album's instrumentation personally, including synthesizers, drum machine, and Wurlitzer, and later performed "Mistakes" live on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert.

talking heads|wild wild life.fact: "Wild Wild Life" was recorded during Talking Heads' sessions for 1986's True Stories, cut around the same time as material for Little Creatures. The song became the album's breakout hit, reaching number 25 on the Billboard Hot 100 and winning two MTV Video Music Awards in 1987 thanks to its colorful, karaoke-themed video featuring John Goodman, drawn from David Byrne's film of the same name.

the cure|closedown.fact: "Closedown" is the third track on The Cure's 1989 album Disintegration. Robert Smith wrote it as a kind of creative exercise, drafting a list of everything he felt he was losing as he approached his 30th birthday while the band prepared to record the album. The track opens with a long instrumental passage built on Boris Williams's tribal drumming and Roger O'Donnell's layered synthesizers before the vocals finally arrive.

st. vincent|birth in reverse.fact: "Birth in Reverse" was the lead single from St. Vincent's self-titled 2014 album. Annie Clark has said the title came from a phrase in Lorrie Moore's novel Birds of America, and that she wrote the song's melody first, singing nonsense syllables until real words took shape. The accompanying video, directed by Willo Perron, shows Clark delivering a guitar solo amid billowing smoke and a honeycomb-patterned backdrop.

fugazi|full disclosure.fact: "Full Disclosure" appears on Fugazi's final studio album, The Argument (2001). Guy Picciotto has said the song and another track, "Strangelight," started out as the same piece of music before splitting into two very differently-sounding songs during the recording process. The track also features guest backing vocals from Kathi Wilcox of Bikini Kill and Bridget Cross of Unrest.

animal collective|chores.fact: "Chores" is the third track on Animal Collective's 2007 album Strawberry Jam. It was recorded, like the rest of the album, at Wave Lab Studios in Tucson, Arizona in January 2007. The song is one of several on the record where the band folded brighter, Beach Boys-style pop hooks into their usual layered, looping, psychedelic production.

girls|honey bunny.fact: "Honey Bunny" opens Girls' 2011 album Father, Son, Holy Ghost with a burst of '50s-style rock'n'roll and surf guitar. Frontman Christopher Owens said the song has "a bit of swagger to it," with a bridge reflecting on his mother's unconditional love for him. The track helped the album earn a Best New Music nod from Pitchfork.

ian dury|hit me with your rhythm stick.fact: "Hit Me With Your Rhythm Stick" shot to number one on the UK singles chart in January 1979 and sold nearly a million copies. Co-writer Chas Jankel came up with the music during a jam session in Kent, and Ian Dury reportedly had the lyrics ready the same afternoon. At the Workhouse Studio session, saxophonist Davey Payne played two saxophones at once, and the band ultimately used just the second of 28 takes for the single.

elbow|the take off and landing of everyt.fact: The title track of Elbow's 2014 album was written after the amicable end of singer Guy Garvey's long-term relationship. Garvey wanted the lyrics "to be a celebration, not just of the throes of great relationships but of the timely end of things." The album carried the working titles "All at Once" and "Carry Her, Carry Me" before the band renamed it after this sprawling, space-rock-influenced track.

ride|kaleidoscope.fact: "Kaleidoscope" is one of the opening tracks on Ride's 1990 debut album Nowhere, with band members Mark Gardener and Andy Bell trading lead vocals. The band recorded much of the album live in a cavernous Oxford room to capture its natural reverb, deliberately foregrounding a big, booming drum sound on this track. Nowhere went on to help define the shoegaze sound by fusing heavy guitar distortion with melodic, classic pop songwriting.

the white stripes|jimmy the exploder.fact: "Jimmy the Exploder" opens The White Stripes' self-titled 1999 debut album and was actually the first original song the duo ever performed live, at Detroit's Gold Dollar club on July 14, 1997. It's one of the few White Stripes songs to begin with Meg White's drums; since she'd only been playing for about two months at the time, Jack White would coach her through the beat by counting out loud during early shows.

low|california.fact: "California" was the lead single from Low's 2005 album The Great Destroyer, the Duluth, Minnesota band's first release for Sub Pop Records. It was produced by Dave Fridmann, known for his work with the Flaming Lips and Mercury Rev, who also contributed keyboards to the track. Its polished, radio-ready sound marked a notable departure for a band best known for its minimalist "slowcore" style.

silver jews|trains across the sea.fact: "Trains Across the Sea" appears on Silver Jews' 1994 debut album, Starlite Walker, written while David Berman was teaching and taking graduate classes at the University of Massachusetts. Berman later said it was the first song he ever composed. The track features a guest vocal from his college friend and Pavement bandmate Stephen Malkmus.

belle and sebastian|i don't love anyone.fact: "I Don't Love Anyone" is a Stuart Murdoch-written track from Belle and Sebastian's 1996 debut album, Tigermilk. The record began as a project for a music-business course at Glasgow's Stow College, whose student-run Electric Honey label ended up funding a full album after hearing the band's demos. Most of Tigermilk, including this song, was recorded live over just three days at CaVa Studios in Glasgow.

the chemical brothers|block rockin' beat.fact: "Block Rockin' Beats" builds its iconic hook from a sample of rapper Schoolly D saying "back with another one of those block rockin' beats" on his 1989 track "Gucci Again," layered over a Bernard Purdie drum break and a bassline from the Crusaders. It topped the UK singles chart in March 1997 and later won the Grammy Award for Best Rock Instrumental Performance. The track appears on The Chemical Brothers' breakthrough 1997 album, Dig Your Own Hole.

elliott smith|waltz #2 (xo).fact: "Waltz #2 (XO)" was the first single from Elliott Smith's 1998 album XO, his major-label debut, and it reached number 52 on the UK singles chart, his highest UK placement. True to its title, the song is written in genuine 3/4 waltz time. Smith himself is credited as a co-arranger of the song's strings and winds, alongside arrangers Shelly Berg and Tom Halm, part of the more orchestral pop sound he explored on the record.

the english beat|jeanette.fact: "Jeanette" is the second track on The Beat's 1982 album Special Beat Service, released in North America as The English Beat. The lyrics are built around playful rhymes on words ending in "-ette" -- launderette, kitchenette, luncheonette -- telling the story of a brief, memorable romance. Musically, it nods to ska but adds an accordion line that gives it an almost polka-like flavor.

jens lekman|the opposite of hallelujah.fact: "The Opposite of Hallelujah" was originally released as the title track of a 2005 EP before being included on Jens Lekman's 2007 album Night Falls Over Kortedala. Set against a trumpet line, the song finds Lekman taking his sister to the beach, where he tries out one failed metaphor after another -- picking up a seashell to "illustrate his homelessness" -- in a sweetly awkward attempt to explain himself to her. It's a classic example of Lekman's wry, self-deprecating songwriting style.

the clash|tommy gun.fact: "Tommy Gun" was the lead single from The Clash's 1978 album Give 'Em Enough Rope, reaching number 19 on the UK singles chart. Drummer Topper Headon came up with the song's rapid-fire, stuttering snare pattern and nailed it in a single take during recording -- a feat that led producer Sandy Pearlman to nickname him "the Human Drum Machine."

toro y moi|talamak.fact: "Talamak" is a track from Toro y Moi's 2010 debut album, Causers of This, on Carpark Records. Its music video, directed by Jon Casey, reunited him with Toro y Moi's Chaz Bundick after their earlier "Blessa" video, this time trading an indoor party setting for sun-dappled outdoor scenery and a few well-placed explosions. The song is often cited as one of the clearer early examples of the "chillwave" sound Toro y Moi helped popularize.

esg|my love for you.fact: ESG was formed in the South Bronx in the late 1970s by the Scroggins sisters -- Renee, Valerie, Deborah, and Marie -- who named the band after the birthstones and precious metal emerald, sapphire, and gold. Discovered at a local talent show by 99 Records' Ed Bahlman, the minimalist funk-punk group went on to influence house, hip-hop, and post-punk alike. "My Love for You" appears on the retrospective compilation A South Bronx Story, gathering early-1980s recordings from one of New York's most sampled underground bands.

courtney barnett|porcelain.fact: "Porcelain," co-written by Courtney Barnett and Bob Harrow, first appeared on an early EP before being compiled onto 2013's The Double EP: A Sea of Split Peas. The song builds around the image of spotting something fragile and undervalued in a shop -- "pretty as porcelain... worth so much more than what you're going for" -- using the object as a stand-in for not letting yourself be treated cheaply. Barnett and her band stretch the track out past the seven-minute mark, closing with an extended, feedback-laced instrumental jam.

the jam|all around the world.fact: "All Around the World" was The Jam's second single, released in July 1977 just months after their debut album In the City. Written by Paul Weller, it became the band's first UK Top 20 hit, peaking at No. 13, and came out while the trio were in the middle of their first full headlining tour of Britain. The song's lyric later gave its name to a box set celebrating the band's breakout first year.

nation of language|wounds of love.fact: "Wounds of Love," from Nation of Language's 2021 album A Way Forward, grew out of a main guitar riff frontman Ian Devaney wrote under the influence of Kraftwerk. Rather than going fully robotic, the band paired it with a warm, laid-back groove, giving the synth-pop track a spacey, hazy feel. Stereogum praised the song and premiered it ahead of the album's release.

sebadoh|magnet's coil.fact: "Magnet's Coil" was written and sung by Sebadoh bassist Lou Barlow for the band's influential 1994 album Bakesale, where it runs a tight two and a half minutes as track three. It was issued as a single in Australia in 1995, and a stripped-down acoustic version later surfaced on the 2011 deluxe reissue's bonus disc. The song is one of the louder, more driving moments on an album widely considered Sebadoh's turn from lo-fi four-track experiments toward a tighter studio sound.

cocteau twins|aikea-guinea.fact: The title track of Cocteau Twins' 1985 EP, "Aikea-Guinea" takes its name from a Scottish colloquialism guitarist Robin Guthrie used for smooth, bleached seashells washed up on the shore. Released on the 4AD label, the EP reached No. 41 on the UK chart and landed at No. 5 on John Peel's listener-voted Festive Fifty for 1985. The shell imagery fits the EP's broader decorative theme alongside its companion track "Rococo."

beach fossils|saint ivy.fact: "Saint Ivy," from Beach Fossils' 2017 album Somersault, marked a sonic left turn for the Brooklyn band, trading their reverb-heavy guitar sound for orchestral pop touches. The track layers plucked strings, a bouncy staccato string arrangement, and a flute solo underneath its melody. It was released with an accompanying music video in 2017.

sprints|need.fact: "Need" comes from All That Is Over, the 2025 sophomore album by Irish band Sprints, who formed in Dublin in 2019 and are fronted by singer-guitarist Karla Chubb. The song is one of several on the record that swing between desire and anger, matching the band's raw, fuzzed-out post-punk attack. Sprints broke through with their acclaimed 2024 debut Letter to Self before expanding their lineup for the follow-up.

my morning jacket|off the record.fact: "Off the Record" comes from My Morning Jacket's 2005 album Z, recorded at Allaire Studios in upstate New York with producer John Leckie. Written by Jim James with bassist "Two-Tone" Tommy Blankenship and drummer Patrick Hallahan, the track blends the band's Southern rock roots with reggae and chill-out influences. It later soundtracked the closing scene of a How I Met Your Mother episode, and Swedish artist Moneybrother covered it in 2006 as "Under Bordet."

blur|girls & boys.fact: "Girls & Boys" grew out of a Blur holiday in Magaluf, Spain, where frontman Damon Albarn people-watched the raucous British package-tour nightlife of the Club 18-30 scene -- even though, as guitarist Graham Coxon has pointed out, none of the band had actually been on one of those holidays themselves. Released in 1994, it became one of Blur's biggest hits, reaching No. 5 on the UK singles chart. Its Kevin Godley-directed video intercut the band's performance with real package-holiday footage.

haim|the story of us.fact: "The Story of Us" is one of three new songs Haim added to the 2025 deluxe reissue of their fourth album, I Quit, alongside "Even the Bad Times" and a Bon Iver collaboration called "Tie You Down." It keeps the loose, scrappy pop-rock energy of the rest of the record, built around energetic guitar and drum work under a deliberately filtered, muffled vocal hook.

yo la tengo|for you too.fact: "For You Too" is track four on Yo La Tengo's 2018 album There's a Riot Going On, the band's 15th record and their first set of originals since 2013. The band recorded it themselves in their own New Jersey rehearsal space with no outside engineer, letting songs come together gradually, sometimes over the course of a year. The track is built around a hypnotic, slightly distorted guitar line under Ira Kaplan's quietly reassuring vocal.

smith westerns|be my girl.fact: "Be My Girl" appears on Smith Westerns' self-titled 2009 debut, recorded while founding members Max Kakacek and Cullen Omori were still students at a Chicago high school. The pair had taught themselves guitar through 1960s garage-rock compilations like Nuggets and Back from the Grave, then recruited Cullen's brother Cameron on bass before the band started playing Chicago clubs like the Empty Bottle and Schubas.

momma|rodeo.fact: "Rodeo," from Momma's 2025 album Welcome to My Blue Sky, was written from the perspective of partners the band members had left behind while touring in 2022. The rodeo image -- standing in the center of the ring while someone does laps around you -- captures the feeling of being outpaced or replaced in a relationship. The song pairs pummeling riffs and staccato drums with a sweetly delivered vocal.

sleater-kinney|you're no rock n' roll fu.fact: "You're No Rock n' Roll Fun" was released as a single in 2000 from Sleater-Kinney's album All Hands on the Bad One. It's a tongue-in-cheek jab at too-serious indie musicians who forget that playing music is supposed to be fun, written from the band's own perspective of life on tour. The song showcased a more playful, pop-leaning side of the trio's sound.

wilco|if i ever was a child.fact: "If I Ever Was A Child" is a track from Wilco's 2016 album Schmilco, produced by Jeff Tweedy and longtime engineer Tom Schick at the band's Chicago studio. The record arrived just a year after its louder predecessor Star Wars but marked a deliberate shift toward a quieter, more pastoral, largely acoustic folk-rock sound.

the butchies|she's so lovely.fact: "She's So Lovely" appears on The Butchies' 2004 album Make Yr Life, the fourth release from the Durham, North Carolina trio fronted by former Team Dresch guitarist Kaia Wilson. The Washington Post singled out the song as proof the band "lost none of its swagger" on what critics called their poppiest record yet.

radiohead|my iron lung.fact: Radiohead wrote "My Iron Lung" partly as a response to the overwhelming success of "Creep," reflecting on being defined by a single song. Unsatisfied with their studio take, the band used an edited live recording captured at the London Astoria in May 1994 for the released version; the surrounding sessions also marked the first time Radiohead worked with engineer Nigel Godrich and artist Stanley Donwood, both of whom became permanent collaborators.

radiohead|packt like sardines in a crush.fact: The opening track on Radiohead's 2001 album Amnesiac, "Packt Like Sardines in a Crushd Tin Box" grew out of the same marathon sessions that produced Kid A. Producer Nigel Godrich reportedly split the band into two separate working spaces during these sessions, one using conventional instruments and one built entirely from processed, non-acoustic sounds, which helped give the track its mechanical, loop-driven percussion.

mac demarco|freaking out the neighborhoo.fact: "Freaking Out the Neighborhood" appears on Mac DeMarco's 2012 album 2, which he recorded almost entirely by himself in his small Montreal apartment on an 8-track setup, writing, playing every instrument, and mixing the record himself before Josh Bonati mastered it.

grandaddy|he's simple, he's dumb, he's t.fact: This nearly nine-minute track opens Grandaddy's 2000 concept album The Sophtware Slump, introducing the record's themes of technology and alienation through a disoriented "2000 man" piloting a craft he can no longer navigate. It was released as a single later that year.

the clash|london's burning.fact: Joe Strummer wrote "London's Burning" in a disused squat near London's Westway, then finished it with Mick Jones at Jones's flat; its title borrows from the old nursery rhyme about the Great Fire of London. It was recorded at CBS Studios in March 1977 for The Clash's self-titled debut album.

the replacements|can't hardly wait.fact: The closing track on 1987's Pleased to Meet Me, "Can't Hardly Wait" was recorded at Ardent Studios in Memphis with producer Jim Dickinson, who brought in the Memphis Horns (Andrew Love on tenor sax, Ben Cauley on trumpet) and enlisted Big Star's Alex Chilton to add guitar fills to the track.

sunny day real estate|47.fact: "47" is the fifth track on Sunny Day Real Estate's 1994 debut Diary. It continues the band's quirky habit of giving songs plain numerical titles instead of conventional names, a tradition that dates back to early tracks like "Seven," "8," and "9." The song later turned up in the soundtrack of the TV series For All Mankind.

american football|the summer ends.fact: "The Summer Ends" comes from American Football's influential self-titled 1999 debut, recorded that May at Private Studios in Urbana, Illinois with producer Brendan Gamble. Drummer Steve Lamos also doubled on trumpet throughout the album, an unusual instrumental touch for an indie-rock record of that era that drew attention from early reviewers.

american football|i'll see you when we'r.fact: "I'll See You When We're Both Not So Emotional" is from American Football's self-titled 1999 debut, recorded with producer Brendan Gamble at Private Studios in Illinois. For the album's 25th anniversary in 2024, the band M.A.G.S. recorded a cover of the song for a tribute album featuring acts like Manchester Orchestra, Ethel Cain, and Iron & Wine.

melody's echo chamber|eyes closed.fact: "Eyes Closed" is a 2025 single from Melody's Echo Chamber's album Unclouded, featuring propulsive breakbeat drumming from British musician Malcolm Catto. Songwriter Melody Prochet said the title reflects devotion rather than withdrawal, describing her eyes as closed "not in denial, but in devotion — to vibrant memories, to the complexity of human feelings."

the strokes|you talk way too much.fact: "You Talk Way Too Much" is the fifth track on The Strokes' 2003 album Room on Fire. The band initially recorded the album with Radiohead producer Nigel Godrich, but scrapped those sessions and returned to Gordon Raphael, who had produced their debut Is This It, to finish the record within a tight three-month deadline.

ramones|blitzkrieg bop.fact: Tommy Ramone first worked out the music for 'Blitzkrieg Bop' on guitar and originally titled it 'Animal Hop' before the band reworked the lyrics. The signature 'Hey Ho, Let's Go' chant was partly inspired by Tommy wanting a crowd-chant as catchy as the Bay City Rollers' 'Saturday Night,' and the Ramones' debut album was recorded overnight at the studio to save on cheaper night-time rates.

rilo kiley|portions for foxes.fact: 'Portions for Foxes' appeared on Rilo Kiley's 2004 album More Adventurous and became one of the band's best-known tracks, later turning into a favorite for cover versions. Alt-country artists Lydia Loveless and Jason Hawk Harris recorded a duet cover of the song, helping introduce it to a new generation of listeners.

foals|spanish sahara.fact: The chord sequence for Foals' 'Spanish Sahara' was written by guitarist Jimmy Smith in a tour hotel room, then set aside for months before the band finished it in their basement studio. The title itself came from a local Oxford band's cassette tape that singer Yannis Philippakis bought for a pound after a gig. The song was released as a limited 1,000-copy 7-inch for Record Store Day 2010 and was later named NME's Best Track of the Year.

fugazi|suggestion.fact: 'Suggestion' opened Fugazi's debut release, the self-titled EP commonly known as 7 Songs, recorded in June 1988 at Inner Ear Studios in Virginia and put out on Ian MacKaye's own label, Dischord Records. Notably, all the guitar parts on the EP were played by MacKaye alone, since future co-guitarist Guy Picciotto hadn't yet joined the band on guitar.

bright eyes|easy/lucky/free.fact: 'Easy/Lucky/Free' appears on Bright Eyes' 2005 album I'm Wide Awake, It's Morning, which was recorded at Presto! Studio in Lincoln, Nebraska, and produced by longtime collaborator Mike Mogis. For the sessions, the band deliberately stripped back their usual studio effects in favor of a leaner, folk-influenced sound, and brought in outside musicians along with guest vocal appearances from Emmylou Harris and Jim James of My Morning Jacket elsewhere on the record.

squid|cro-magnon man.fact: 'Cro-Magnon Man' was the final single released from Squid's third album, Cowards, in February 2025. The album was recorded at Church Studios in London with producers Marta Salogni and Grace Banks, alongside longtime collaborator Dan Carey, and the track features guitarist Louis Borlase on lead vocals plus guest vocal contributions from Clarissa Connelly, Tony Njoku, and Rosa Brook.

juliana hatfield|scratchers.fact: 'Scratchers' is the lead single from Juliana Hatfield's 21st solo album, Lightning Might Strike, released December 12, 2025 via American Laundromat Records. The song uses scratch-off lottery tickets as a central metaphor for holding onto hope despite long odds, and its guitar riffs deliberately swing between major and minor keys to mirror that push-pull between optimism and gloom.

king gizzard & the lizard wizard|inner c.fact: 'Inner Cell' is a track from King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard's 2017 album Polygondwanaland, whose title is a portmanteau of 'polygon' and 'Gondwanaland.' The band gave the entire album away for free online, releasing high-quality digital, CD, and even separate vinyl master files so that any label or fan could legally press and release their own physical copies, resulting in over 80 different label pressings worldwide.

the shins|australia.fact: 'Australia' is the second track on The Shins' 2007 album Wincing the Night Away, written and produced by frontman James Mercer alongside Joe Chiccarelli. It was released as the album's second UK single on April 9, 2007, and charted on the UK Singles Chart, with the release timed to coincide with the band's tour stop in Australia later that year.

bonny doon|you can't stay the same (feat.fact: Bonny Doon's 'You Can't Stay the Same' features backing vocals from Katie Crutchfield of Waxahatchee, appearing on the band's album Let There Be Music. The pairing grew out of a real touring partnership: Bonny Doon served as Waxahatchee's backing band on the road after collaborating on her acclaimed 2020 album Saint Cloud, and that Americana-leaning chemistry carried over into their own record.

king stingray|milkumana.fact: King Stingray's 'Milkumana' takes its title from a word in Yolngu Matha meaning to show, share, or pass on knowledge through story and song. The band has said the track is about leadership and positive role models, built around the idea of 'mala wangany' -- togetherness -- and its music video was filmed in the band's hometown of Yirrkala in North East Arnhem Land, featuring community elders passing down traditional knowledge.

wolf parade|modern world.fact: 'Modern World' appears on Wolf Parade's 2005 debut album Apologies to the Queen Mary, most of which was produced by Modest Mouse frontman Isaac Brock at his Audible Alchemy studio in Portland, Oregon, while the band self-produced a handful of other tracks back home in Montreal. Brock, who was moonlighting as an A&R scout for Sub Pop, had been following guitarist Dan Boeckner's earlier band and helped broker Wolf Parade's signing to the label; the resulting album went on to earn a 2006 Polaris Music Prize nomination.

blur|parklife.fact: "Parklife" features spoken-word verses by actor Phil Daniels, best known for his role in the 1979 film Quadrophenia. Blur singer Damon Albarn and guitarist Graham Coxon were longtime fans of Daniels, and after an earlier plan to have him recite a poem over a different instrumental fell through, they brought him in to voice "Parklife" instead. Daniels has said he recorded his entire part in well under an hour.

dari bay|river.fact: "River" appears on Dari Bay's 2023 album Longest Day of the Year, the project of Burlington, Vermont musician Zack James, who also plays drums for Unknown Mortal Orchestra. James wrote, produced, and performed most of the record himself, mixing it with Peter Oscar Newton, and the LP was later reissued on vinyl by Double Double Whammy with a bonus track.

the chemical brothers|go.fact: "Go" is the lead single from The Chemical Brothers' 2015 album Born in the Echoes and features a guest verse from rapper Q-Tip of A Tribe Called Quest, who had previously worked with the duo on their hit "Galvanize." The song's music video was directed by Michel Gondry, who also made the band's earlier "Star Guitar" and "Let Forever Be" clips, and depicts dancers forming a human locomotive in an Art Deco setting inspired by Metropolis.

the black keys|act nice and gentle.fact: "Act Nice and Gentle" is a cover of a 1967 song by The Kinks, originally released as the B-side to their single "Waterloo Sunset." The Black Keys recorded their slowed-down, honky-tonk-tinged version for their 2004 album Rubber Factory, turning the Kinks' upbeat original into a sultrier, electrified shuffle.

future islands|aladdin.fact: "Aladdin" opens Future Islands' 2017 album The Far Field, which was recorded in Los Angeles with Grammy-winning producer John Congleton at the famed Sunset Sound studio. The track features string and horn arrangements by Patrick McMinn performed with members of the Section Quartet, giving the band's usual synth-driven sound a fuller, orchestral backdrop.

violent femmes|hallowed ground.fact: The title track of Violent Femmes' 1984 album Hallowed Ground slows the band's usual frantic energy to a meditative crawl, built around Brian Ritchie's droning bass, Gordon Gano's strummed acoustic guitar, and faint, church-like organ flourishes. It's a notable change of pace from the trio's spikier debut, on a record that also brought outside players like avant-garde saxophonist John Zorn and banjo virtuoso Tony Trischka into the fold.

sonic youth|superstar.fact: Sonic Youth covered "Superstar" — written by Bonnie Bramlett and Leon Russell and made famous by The Carpenters — for the 1994 tribute album If I Were a Carpenter, trading the original's lush strings for distorted guitars and a hazy, lo-fi lead vocal from Thurston Moore. The cover later reached a wider audience when it was featured on the soundtrack to the 2007 film Juno.

elbow|leaders of the free world.fact: "Leaders of the Free World" was released as the second and final single from Elbow's 2005 album of the same name, written and self-produced by the band. It peaked at number 53 on the UK Singles Chart and number 6 on the UK Independent Singles Chart.

grizzly bear|knife.fact: "Knife" was the second single from Grizzly Bear's 2007 album Yellow House and became the Brooklyn band's first real breakout song, later landing at No. 109 on Pitchfork's list of the 500 best tracks of the 2000s. Its music video, directed by Isaiah Saxon and Sean Hellfritsch of Encyclopedia Pictura, follows the band operating a strange machine in the desert, and the song has since been covered by acts including Beirut and CSS.

sen morimoto|bad state.fact: "Bad State" is the second track on Sen Morimoto's 2023 album Diagnosis, released on City Slang in partnership with his own Chicago label, Sooper Records. Morimoto has described his reference points for the album as "equal parts Funkadelic and Dinosaur Jr.," and "Bad State" leans into the funkier, brighter side of that mix with its jazz-pop horn-and-groove arrangement.

dow jones & the industrials|can't stand.fact: "Can't Stand the Midwest" is a track by Dow Jones and the Industrials, a punk band from West Lafayette, Indiana active in the late 1970s and early 1980s whose lineup included a keyboardist nicknamed "Mr. Science." The song later gave its name to Can't Stand the Midwest: 1979-1981, a 2016 anthology from Family Vineyard Records gathering the group's scattered singles, demos, and live recordings.

talking heads|take me to the river.fact: "Take Me to the River" is Talking Heads' cover of the Al Green soul classic, and it became the band's first Top 40 hit when it reached No. 26 on the Billboard chart in 1979 off their album More Songs About Buildings and Food. Producer Brian Eno reportedly suggested the band play it as slowly as possible without losing the groove, and it remains the only cover song Talking Heads ever officially released.

siouxsie and the banshees|christine.fact: "Christine" was released in 1980 as the second single from Siouxsie and the Banshees' album Kaleidoscope and reached No. 22 on the UK charts. The song marked a turning point for the band's sound, introducing new guitarist John McGeoch, whose distinctive riff — played on acoustic guitar — opens the track.

sports team|moving together.fact: "Moving Together" appears on Sports Team's 2025 album Boys These Days, which the band recorded over an extended stretch at producer Matias Tellez's studio in Norway. Tellez, who has also worked with Girl in Red, CMAT, and Gracie Abrams, helped push the album toward an '80s-influenced sound, a shift from the band's earlier, scrappier guitar records.

the linda lindas|growing up.fact: The Linda Lindas' 2022 debut album "Growing Up" was produced, engineered, and mixed by bandmates Mila and Lucia de la Garza's father, Carlos de la Garza, a Grammy-winning engineer who has also worked with Paramore and Ziggy Marley. At the time of recording, the band's lineup ranged from 11-year-old drummer Mila to 17-year-old guitarist Bela Salazar, the group's oldest member.

spoon|don't make me a target.fact: "Don't Make Me a Target" opens Spoon's 2007 album "Ga Ga Ga Ga Ga" with a stark, descending guitar riff from frontman Britt Daniel set against a slow, measured beat from drummer Jim Eno. The track builds into an extended instrumental section featuring piano from touring member Eric Harvey before the song winds down.

eric hilton|the dharma lovers.fact: "The Dharma Lovers" was released as the first single from Eric Hilton's solo album "A Sky So Close." Hilton is best known as co-founder of Thievery Corporation, which he formed in Washington, D.C. in 1995 with Rob Garza after the two discovered a shared admiration for Brazilian composers Antonio Carlos Jobim and Joao Gilberto.

junior boys|waiting game.fact: "Waiting Game" is the title track and closing song on Junior Boys' 2016 album of the same name, the Hamilton, Ontario duo's first new record in six years. Bandmate Jeremy Greenspan called it an "ode to inactivity," written in a patchwork style where he jotted down striking phrases and descriptions verbatim before piecing them into lyrics.

fiona apple|o' sailor.fact: "O' Sailor" appears on Fiona Apple's 2005 album "Extraordinary Machine" and was one of two tracks Epic Records streamed early on Apple's website that August, ahead of the album's October release. Its music video, directed by Floria Sigismondi and filmed aboard the retired ocean liner RMS Queen Mary, was nominated for eight Music Video Production Awards and won two, including Direction of a Female Artist.

blur|coffee & tv.fact: "Coffee & TV," the second single from Blur's 1999 album "13," was sung by guitarist Graham Coxon rather than usual frontman Damon Albarn. Its award-winning video starred a wandering, sentient milk carton named "Milky," built by Jim Henson's Creature Shop, and won the MTV Europe Music Award for Best Video.

happy mondays|wrote for luck.fact: "Wrote for Luck" was remixed and retitled "W.F.L." for a 1989 single reissue. One version, produced by Paul Oakenfold and Steve Osborne, helped kick-start the "indie dance" crossover sound, while a second version came from Erasure's Vince Clarke, marking the very first remix he ever attempted.

yo la tengo|cherry chapstick.fact: "Cherry Chapstick," from Yo La Tengo's 2000 album "And Then Nothing Turned Itself Inside-Out," was later reworked into a hushed, half-tempo acoustic arrangement recorded for Australian radio station JJJ. That stripped-down version closed out the band's 2003 "Today Is the Day" EP on Matador Records.

yeasayer|tightrope.fact: Yeasayer contributed "Tightrope" to the 2009 two-disc compilation "Dark Was the Night," curated by The National's Aaron and Bryce Dessner and released on 4AD to benefit the Red Hot Organization. The track layers frontman Chris Keating's lead vocal under the band's signature group harmonies, handclaps, and chattering percussion.

king gizzard & the lizard wizard|nuclear.fact: "Nuclear Fusion" appears on King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard's 2017 album "Flying Microtonal Banana," named after a custom yellow guitar that bandleader Stu Mackenzie had built with extra frets to access microtonal, in-between notes. The whole record was made using guitars and even a bass that the band customized specifically to explore that unconventional tuning.

my bloody valentine|sometimes.fact: "Sometimes" appears on My Bloody Valentine's landmark 1991 album "Loveless," a record that reportedly took the band more than two years and around 20 different recording studios to complete. One signature guitar loop on the album alone is said to have cost roughly £15,000 to get right, reflecting just how painstaking and perfectionist the sessions were.

the white stripes|the denial twist.fact: "The Denial Twist," from The White Stripes' 2005 album "Get Behind Me Satan," went through three different takes during recording, more than most tracks on the album.
